issues.body:
## Bug type

Behavior bug (incorrect output/state without crash)

## Beta release blocker

No

## Summary

When `secrets.egressProxy.enabled` is on, Gateway-hosted exec receives `HTTP_PROXY`/`HTTPS_PROXY` (plus `NODE_USE_ENV_PROXY=1`) but no `NO_PROXY`. The proxy refuses plain HTTP by design, so every plain-HTTP call from a proxy-aware client in exec is refused with `502 Secret egress proxy refused the request.`, including loopback and LAN services. That covers Ollama on `http://127.0.0.1:11434`, LAN model servers such as vLLM, and anything else local over plain HTTP.

## Steps to reproduce

1. Enable `secrets.egressProxy.enabled` and restart the Gateway, with no `NO_PROXY` in the Gateway's environment.
2. From Gateway-hosted exec:
   - `python3 -c 'import urllib.request as u; print(u.urlopen("http://127.0.0.1:11434/api/version").status)'` returns HTTP 502 from the egress proxy.
   - `node -e 'fetch("http://127.0.0.1:11434/api/version").then(r=>console.log(r.status))'` is also routed to the proxy via `NODE_USE_ENV_PROXY`.

## Expected behavior

Loopback is exempt by default, as the managed proxy already does: `src/infra/net/proxy/proxy-lifecycle.ts` sets `LOOPBACK_NO_PROXY = "127.0.0.1,localhost,localhost.,::1,[::1],127.0.0.0/8"`. Loopback plain HTTP can't carry a destination-bound secret anyway, since bindings are HTTPS-only.

## Actual behavior

`src/secrets/egress-proxy/proxy-server.ts` returns only `HTTPS_PROXY`, `HTTP_PROXY`, `NODE_USE_ENV_PROXY` and the CA variables for the exec environment. Local plain-HTTP services are unreachable from exec unless the operator adds `NO_PROXY` to the Gateway's environment by hand. That workaround does work, because the proxy env is merged over the inherited env and never touches `NO_PROXY`.

## Suggested fix

- Set `NO_PROXY`/`no_proxy` for loopback in the exec proxy env, merging with any operator-provided value rather than replacing it.
- Mention in the egress proxy docs that operators must add LAN plain-HTTP hosts to `NO_PROXY`. Python (`urllib`/`requests`) ignores CIDR entries there, so hosts must be listed by name or IP.

## Environment

OpenClaw 2026.9.6 (eb377ac), Node 24.21.0, Ubuntu 24.04, gateway as a systemd service.

Related: #135955 (egress proxy upstream CA trust).

issues.body:
**Title:** `agents.files.*` cannot read/write symlinked workspace files — agent identity save fails with `unsafe workspace file "IDENTITY.md"`

## Summary

Saving an agent display name in the UI fails with:

```
unsafe workspace file "IDENTITY.md"
```

for any agent whose `IDENTITY.md` in its workspace is a **symlink** to a file outside the workspace root.

`agents.files.get` / `agents.files.set` route through `@openclaw/fs-safe`, which refuses to traverse symlinks. Because the identity save writes *both* `openclaw.json` and a merged `IDENTITY.md`, the file error aborts the entire operation and **the display name is silently never persisted** — the UI only surfaces the file error, giving no hint that the config write was rolled back too.

Notably, `@openclaw/fs-safe` already supports the options needed (`allowSymlink`, `allowSymlinkBase`, `followSymlinks`), and OpenClaw already exposes a configurable trust list for the *skills* loader — but nothing equivalent is wired to agent workspace files.

## Environment

- openclaw `2026.9.1-beta.1` (`1d96e5a`), installed via Homebrew
- `@openclaw/fs-safe` `0.5.6` (pinned exact in `dependencies`)
- Node v26.5.0, Linux 6.8.0

## Repro

Minimal, standalone — no OpenClaw config required:

```js
// repro.mjs  (run from a dir with openclaw's node_modules resolvable)
import { root } from '@openclaw/fs-safe/root';

// workspace/IDENTITY.md -> ../shared/IDENTITY.md  (symlink escaping the root)
const r = await root('./workspace/');
try { await r.read('IDENTITY.md', { hardlinks: 'reject', nonBlockingRead: true }); }
catch (e) { console.log('read  ->', e.constructor.name + ':', e.message); }
try { await r.write('IDENTITY.md', '- Name: Test\n', { encoding: 'utf8' }); }
catch (e) { console.log('write ->', e.constructor.name + ':', e.message); }
```

```
$ mkdir -p shared workspace
$ printf '# IDENTITY.md\n\n- **Name:**\n' > shared/IDENTITY.md
$ ln -s "$PWD/shared/IDENTITY.md" workspace/IDENTITY.md
$ node repro.mjs
read  -> FsSafeError: symlink path component not allowed
write -> FsSafeError: path alias escape blocked
```

End-to-end: point an agent's workspace at a dir whose `IDENTITY.md` is such a symlink, then set a display
name in the UI (or `openclaw agents set-identity --agent <id> --name X`). It fails, and
`agents.entries.<id>.identity` / `.name` is never written. An otherwise identical agent with a **regular**
`IDENTITY.md` succeeds.

## Expected

Operators can opt into a narrow set of trusted symlink target roots for agent workspace files, the same way
`skills.load.allowSymlinkTargets` already allows it for skills. Symlinking agent definition files into a
shared/synced directory is a reasonable and common layout.

## Actual

Hard failure with no opt-in, and a partial-write abort that leaves the display name unsaved.

## Where it comes from

In the agents handler (bundled as `dist/agents-Dvcyjl9o.js`), both file ops call fs-safe with no symlink
options:

```js
await (await agentsHandlerDeps.root(workspaceDir)).read(name, { hardlinks: "reject", nonBlockingRead: true })
await (await agentsHandlerDeps.root(params.workspaceDir)).write(params.name, params.content, { encoding: "utf8" })
```

Any `FsSafeError` is mapped to a single opaque response:

```js
function respondWorkspaceFileUnsafe(respond, name) {
  respond(false, void 0, errorShape(ErrorCodes.INVALID_REQUEST, `unsafe workspace file "${name}"`));
}
```

Meanwhile the schema already documents a skills-only trust list:

- `skills.load.allowSymlinkTargets` — *"Trusted real target roots that skill symlinks may resolve into when they sit outside their configured source root. Keep this narrow, such as a sibling repo skills directory."*
- `skills.workshop.allowSymlinkTargetWrites` — *"Allows Skill Workshop apply to write through symlinked workspace skill paths whose real target is already trusted by `skills.load.allowSymlinkTargets`."*

So the precedent, the config surface pattern, and the underlying library support all exist; agent files just
don't use them.

## Related issues / prior art

- **#54235** (closed, completed) — *Symlinked workspace context files show as `[MISSING]` on session startup.*
  Fixed. This established that symlinked `IDENTITY.md` / `SOUL.md` / `USER.md` in a workspace **are** expected
  to resolve. The present bug is the same class of file failing through a *different* code path
  (`agents.files.*` rather than context injection), so the two subsystems now disagree about whether a
  symlinked `IDENTITY.md` is valid.
- **#118016** (closed, not-planned — auto-closed by the stale bot, not a maintainer decision) — same symptom,
  with the closing message inviting a fresh issue with new repro steps on the latest release. This is that
  refile, reproduced on `2026.9.1-beta.1`.
- **#121238** (closed, completed) — *Skill Workshop update fails through an explicitly allowed workspace
  symlink.* Direct precedent for the proposed fix: skills already have `skills.load.allowSymlinkTargets` +
  `skills.workshop.allowSymlinkTargetWrites`, and writing through an explicitly trusted symlink is treated as
  a supported scenario worth fixing. Agent workspace files have no equivalent.
- **#134967** (closed, completed) — *Symlinked `USER.md`/`MEMORY.md` aborts the entire memory sync.* Sibling
  in `memory-host-sdk`. There the right fix was to **skip** the symlink gracefully, because enumeration is
  incidental. That is *not* sufficient here: `agents.files.set` is an explicit, user-initiated write to that
  exact file, so silently skipping it would still lose the user's data. Hence the opt-in trust list.

## Suggested fix

1. Add an `agents`-scoped analogue, e.g. `agents.files.allowSymlinkTargets` (+ an explicit
   `allowSymlinkTargetWrites` opt-in for writes, mirroring the skills split), and pass the corresponding
   `allowSymlinkBase` / `followSymlinks` options through to the fs-safe root in `agents.files.get/set`.
2. Independently of (1), improve the failure mode:
   - Surface the fs-safe `reason` (`symlink path component not allowed` vs `path alias escape blocked` vs
     `outside-workspace`) rather than one generic `unsafe workspace file` string — the current message gives
     no indication that a symlink is the problem.
   - Make the identity save's failure atomic *and legible*: right now the config portion is discarded on a
     file error with no indication the name wasn't saved.

## Workaround (for anyone hitting this)

`openclaw agents set-identity` accepts `--identity-file`, which reads the target directly and bypasses the
workspace symlink. It does not modify the agent's `workspace` config, and applies without a gateway restart:

```
openclaw agents set-identity --agent <id> --from-identity --identity-file /real/path/to/IDENTITY.md --json
```

Two caveats: it parses unfilled template placeholders literally (`- **Avatar:** *(none yet)*` becomes
`avatar: "(none yet)"`, and `--avatar ""` will not clear it — use
`openclaw config unset agents.entries.<id>.identity.avatar`), and the UI save button still fails.

issues.body:
### Bug type
Behavior bug (incorrect output/state without crash)

### Summary
Android node `notifications.changed` events are enqueued as system events with `contextKey: notification:<key>` but without `replace: true`. An ongoing notification whose text updates often (battery/charging monitors, media or download progress) creates a new queued event on every update, instead of replacing the earlier one with the same key. A `removed` change is also appended, and the queued `posted` entry for that key stays in the queue. A single notification can therefore fill most of the 20-entry per-session queue (`MAX_EVENTS`). After that, other producers are refused with `SystemEventQueueFullError`, and `POST /hooks/wake` returns 503.

### Steps to reproduce
1. Pair an Android app as a node with notification forwarding enabled (default target: the agent's main session).
2. Use an app that keeps an ongoing notification whose text changes every 1-2 minutes (e.g. a battery monitor while charging).
3. Don't let the main session run a turn for a while (e.g. the heartbeat interval hasn't elapsed yet).
4. Inspect `openclaw status --json` -> `queuedSystemEvents`, then call `POST /hooks/wake`.

### Expected behavior
At most one queued event per notification key. The latest `posted` state replaces earlier ones. A `removed` change drops the still-queued `posted` entry for that key instead of adding a second entry.

### Actual behavior
On 2026.10.5, 16 of the 20 queued events in `agent:main:main` were updates of the same notification key, each with slightly different text. Notification wakes use `intent: "event"`, which the heartbeat cooldown defers as `not-due` until the next heartbeat (1h interval here), so the queue drained hourly and was full again within ~28 minutes. While it was full, every `/hooks/wake` call from an unrelated producer got a 503 (`System event queue is full (20 pending)`).

### Source (main `dea6ff0`, 2026.10.7)
`src/gateway/server-node-events-notifications.ts`:
```ts
const eventOptions = withSystemEventOwner(
  {
    sessionKey,
    contextKey: `notification:${key}`,
    deliveryContext: expectedTarget.deliveryContext,
  },
  agentId,
);
const occurrence = enqueueSystemEventEntry(summary, eventOptions);
```
`src/infra/system-events.ts` already supports per-context-key supersession: with `replace: true`, matching entries are removed and retired, and the capacity check is skipped when a match exists (`entry.queue.length >= MAX_EVENTS && !(options.replace && entry.queue.some(matches))`). The notification handler doesn't use it. The existing duplicate-text check doesn't help because each update has different text.

Note: on main the wake now goes through `enqueueSessionEventForHost` instead of `requestSessionEventWake({ intent: "event" })` (2026.10.5), so how long the queue stays full may differ. I have not reproduced the hourly pattern on main; the per-key accumulation is unchanged.

### Proposed fix
- Enqueue `posted` changes with `replace: true` on `notification:<key>`, so the latest state replaces earlier ones and repeated updates never hit the capacity refusal.
- For `removed`: if a `posted` entry for the same key is still queued and not yet consumed, retire it and don't enqueue the removal (the agent never saw the notification). Otherwise enqueue the removal with `replace: true`.
- Make sure retiring a replaced occurrence settles its `enqueueSessionEventForHost` receipt cleanly, so it isn't logged as `notification event not delivered`.
- Test: N `posted` updates for one key followed by `removed` leave at most one queued entry and never raise `SystemEventQueueFullError`.

### Related
- #149383: Android node events cause high-frequency main-session turns (notification noise; this issue is a specific mechanism that makes it worse)
- #167854: 20-entry system-event queue overflow from session notices (different producer, same capacity refusal)

### OpenClaw version
2026.10.5 (observed); handler code unchanged on main `dea6ff0` (2026.10.7)

### Operating system
Linux x64 (gateway), Android app as node

### Install method
npm global

### Workaround
Turn off notification forwarding on the Android app, or block the noisy app in its notification package filter.

issues.body:
## Problem

Changing an agent's default model can leave existing inherited-model automations failing before execution, without an actionable automation compatibility warning during the change. Please add a read-only impact/preflight check and clearer model-change guidance; do not silently transfer account ownership or broaden model policy.

## Observed installation

- OpenClaw CLI reports 2026.10.8, checkout bf6a97a1761.
- An upgrade occurred first; the default model was changed separately afterwards through the assistant, from `openai/gpt-6-sol` to `openai/gpt-6.1-sol`.
- Nine enabled recurring agent-turn jobs had no `payload.model` override.
- Morning Brief and an energy usage review succeeded on 28 October using the old model, then failed on 29–30 October after correctly inheriting the new model.
- Error (account anonymised): `Automation has no recorded inference account. Runtime codex would run openai/gpt-6.1-sol with stored account openai:<owner>. Record the account with openclaw automations edit <jobId> --model openai/gpt-6.1-sol@openai:<owner>, or with openclaw doctor --fix.`
- A separate scheduled continuation failed with `Scheduled model "openai/gpt-6.1-sol" is not allowed by agents.entries.*.modelPolicy.allow`.
- The global allow-list contained the new model, while the main agent's explicit allow-list did not, despite its primary model being the new model.

This does **not** establish that changing defaults caused the missing account bindings, nor that upgrade migration itself failed. It establishes that the model-change workflow did not surface existing/new incompatibilities before the next scheduled execution. Interactive chat success was insufficient validation.

## Existing behaviour reviewed

- `src/cron/isolated-agent/model-selection.ts` resolves inherited defaults at run time; per-job edits for each new model are not inherently required.
- `src/agents/scheduled-unrecorded-account.ts` deliberately fails closed before inference and stops fallback from bypassing account choice.
- `src/commands/doctor/cron/inference-binding-migration.ts` can adopt legacy accounts without pinning inherited models; personal-account adoption has separate owner-authorisation requirements.
- `docs/automation/cron-jobs/payloads.md` and `troubleshooting.md` explain account continuity and Doctor migration, but this is easy to miss when changing the default independently of an upgrade.
- Related merged work: #173509 (legacy account adoption), #185070 (scheduled runtime continuity).

## Requested outcome

1. Provide an automation-impact/preflight check when changing default models through supported model/config workflows, and make it available to agents/tools.
2. Identify affected enabled jobs, effective model source (job/session/subagent/agent default), per-agent vs global policy conflicts, missing account bindings, and account/provider/runtime compatibility failures.
3. Keep the check read-only. Explain exact owner-authorised recovery options; never silently select a different account, credential route, runtime, or widen an allow-list.
4. Preserve default inheritance after account adoption. Avoid presenting a permanent per-job model pin as the only recovery option.
5. Add a short model-change checklist to the relevant docs/agent-facing guidance, linking to account continuity and policy precedence.
6. Cover inherited jobs, explicit pins, global/per-agent policy disagreement, legacy unbound accounts, compatible same-account model changes, incompatible provider/runtime changes, and expired one-shots. Do not auto-restart expired work.

## Local workaround

With the owner's explicit authorisation, align the main-agent allow-list with the chosen default, adopt the already-identified existing account through the automation API, and clear the temporary model/profile override before execution. Preserve original prompts, schedules, destinations, tool permissions and fallbacks. An energy-review force-run then completed successfully with confirmed delivery. Other job configuration repairs were reread; this issue does not claim every scheduled workload was exhaustively exercised.

issues.body:
## Bug description

When configuring `channels.telegram.apiRoot` to point at a self-hosted [Telegram Bot API server](https://github.com/tdlib/telegram-bot-api), the gateway receives raw updates from the local server but **never dispatches them to any agent session**. The bot can send messages, but inbound messages are silently dropped after the raw-update middleware.

## Environment

- **OpenClaw version:** 2026.3.23-2 (7ffe7e4)
- **OS:** Ubuntu 24.04, Contabo VPS
- **Node:** 22.22.0
- **Telegram Bot API server:** official Docker image (`aiogram/telegram-bot-api`), running with `--local` flag
- **Container port mapping:** `127.0.0.1:8083->8081/tcp`

## Configuration

```json
{
  "channels": {
    "telegram": {
      "enabled": true,
      "botToken": "<redacted>",
      "apiRoot": "http://127.0.0.1:8083",
      "dmPolicy": "allowlist",
      "groupPolicy": "allowlist",
      "allowFrom": [128586066],
      "groups": {
        "-1003841627937": { "requireMention": false }
      }
    }
  }
}
```

## Steps to reproduce

1. Set up a local Telegram Bot API server container with valid `TELEGRAM_API_ID` and `TELEGRAM_API_HASH`
2. Call `logOut` on the official API (`https://api.telegram.org/bot<token>/logOut`) and wait 10 minutes
3. Set `channels.telegram.apiRoot` to `http://127.0.0.1:8083`
4. Start the gateway

## What happens

### 1. Raw updates are received but not dispatched

The gateway polls successfully and receives updates (visible in the detailed log as `gateway/channels/telegram/raw-update`):

```
[gateway/channels/telegram/raw-update] telegram update: {"update_id":401179648,"message":{"message_id":56,"from":{"id":128586066,...},"chat":{"id":-1003841627937,"title":"Jarvis HQ","is_forum":true,"type":"supergroup"},"date":1774449757,"text":"Jarvis"}}
```

But **no session is created, no `Inbound message` log appears, and no agent processes the message**. The update is silently dropped after the raw-update logging middleware calls `next()`.

Outbound works fine — `sendMessage`, `getMe`, `getChat` all succeed through the local server.

### 2. Update offset incompatibility

The file `~/.openclaw/telegram/update-offset-default.json` stores the `lastUpdateId` from the official API (e.g., `841948744`). The local Bot API server uses a completely different update ID sequence (e.g., `401179648`). When the gateway switches to the local server, it requests `getUpdates?offset=841948745`, which the local server will never satisfy — returning empty forever.

**Expected behavior:** OpenClaw should detect the endpoint change and reset the offset, or at minimum document that the offset file must be reset manually.

### 3. `deleteWebhook` crash loop during logOut cooldown

After calling `logOut` on the official API, there is a mandatory 10-minute cooldown. If the gateway restarts during this window, the startup `deleteWebhook` call fails with:

```
[gateway/channels/telegram] telegram deleteWebhook failed: Call to 'deleteWebhook' failed! (400: Logged out)
[gateway/channels/telegram] [default] channel exited: Call to 'deleteWebhook' failed! (400: Logged out)
[gateway/channels/telegram] [default] auto-restart attempt 1/10 in 5s
```

The gateway treats the `400: Logged out` response as a fatal error and enters a crash loop (up to 10 retries). This happens even when `apiRoot` is set to the local server — suggesting `deleteWebhook` may be hitting the official API instead of the configured `apiRoot`.

## What I expected

1. Messages received via the local Bot API server should be dispatched to agent sessions exactly like messages from the official API
2. The update offset should be reset or handled gracefully when `apiRoot` changes
3. `deleteWebhook` should use the configured `apiRoot`, and a `400: Logged out` response should not be treated as fatal (it's an expected transient state during migration)

## Debugging notes

- Confirmed the local server works: `getMe`, `sendMessage`, `getChat`, `getUpdates` (manual curl) all return correct results
- Confirmed the local server connects to Telegram's DC (active TCP connection to `149.154.175.52:443`)
- Confirmed raw updates arrive in the grammY middleware (logged as `raw-update`)
- The dispatch failure is silent — no error, no warning, no session state change after the raw update
- Reverting to official API (`api.telegram.org`) immediately restores full functionality

## Related issues

- #19454 — Same symptom (raw updates received but never dispatched), though that issue may have a different root cause
- #25877, #28535 — Feature requests that led to apiRoot implementation
- #27453 — PR that added apiRoot support

## Suggested fix areas

- Check if the inbound message adapter between grammY and the OpenClaw session dispatcher has assumptions about the API endpoint or response format
- The update offset file should be scoped per `apiRoot` or reset when the endpoint changes
- `deleteWebhook` should respect `apiRoot` and handle `400: Logged out` gracefully during local server migration

issues.body:
## Summary

Support European Portuguese (`pt-PT`) across OpenClaw's user-visible interfaces and native apps, using its existing localization systems.

## Problem to solve

European Portuguese users need consistent regional language throughout the product, rather than a translated web interface surrounded by English native screens, onboarding or plugin controls. Brazilian Portuguese should remain a separate choice.

The initial version of this request covered only the Control UI. The intended outcome now includes the native apps and other user-visible product surfaces. PR #188794 is an initial Control UI registration slice, not completion of this request.

## Proposed solution

- Register `pt-PT` through the existing regional locale resolvers, catalogs and platform resource generators. Preserve explicit and saved choices; keep bare `pt` mapped to `pt-BR` where that is the existing contract.
- Cover the Control UI, native app screens, onboarding, settings, permissions and errors, plus bundled-plugin interfaces and user-facing help. Inventory CLI/help localization and platform-specific gaps explicitly instead of silently treating them as translated.
- Generate and review the real European Portuguese catalogs through their native owners. English bootstrap copy may support an intermediate source-registration slice; it does not satisfy the completed translation outcome.
- Preserve internal IDs, protocol names, command tokens, saved human names and user-authored content. Do not introduce a parallel translation service or a maintained engine fork.

## Acceptance

- Each supported app and interface has an identified native localization owner and recorded PT-PT coverage, including any remaining untranslated surface.
- European Portuguese can be selected separately from Brazilian Portuguese, with regional detection and saved preferences behaving correctly where supported.
- Actual generated translations render in the relevant apps and plugin interfaces, with placeholders and platform resource formats preserved.
- Relevant checks and inspectable behavior evidence cover the delivered surfaces. Existing explicit language preferences are preserved during the supported upgrade path.

## Alternatives considered

Using Brazilian Portuguese does not provide the requested regional wording. Hand-maintaining duplicate catalogs or a translation overlay would bypass the systems already responsible for localization.

## Impact

This is a product-wide localization request. Its platform and generation slices may be delivered incrementally; a Control UI-only merge must not close the wider request. Maintainer direction on that scope is still needed.

## Evidence/examples

The inspected Control UI source lacked `pt-PT` registration and mapped the regional browser language to `pt-BR`. PR #188794 addresses registration and catalog-backed default titles; its generated Portuguese output, real-Gateway proof and normal CI qualification remain separate requirements.

The current native-app locale registry also lacks `pt-PT`. Platform resource mappings, generated-artifact rules and native shell copy are being audited before choosing the next source slice. No complete native-app translation or maintainer approval is claimed.

Related context is #3460. Earlier PT-PT proposals #28482 and #28500 closed without merge. The Control UI slice follows `ui/AGENTS.md`; other surfaces must follow their own current generator and contribution policies.

## Do you plan to open a PR for this?

Yes. PR #188794 is the first bounded delivery; the remaining app and localization work stays tracked here.

labels.name: P2
labels.description: Normal backlog priority with limited blast radius.

issues.body:
## Summary

On OpenClaw 2026.10.8 (dc2523e), a NAS/Docker install spends **58.1 s of every startup** in `resolvePluginMetadataSnapshotAsync` — **96 % of `workspaceFactsMs` (60.2 s)**, inside `sidecars.model-runtime` (60.6 s). Startup already takes 157–245 s on this host, so this single stage is **24–39%** of total startup.

The cost is filesystem metadata operations (`stat` / manifest reads) over the whole plugin tree — 101 MB / 6 495 files / 603 directories, of which one plugin's `node_modules` holds 4 553 files. It re-runs on **every** startup, not once per install.

Cross-host comparison pins the mechanism: same build, same concurrency setting, only file count and filesystem differ — and the slowdown decomposes as **48× ≈ 7.3× (file count) × 6.5× (per-file cost)**. It is an I/O-count problem, not an algorithmic one.

## Minimal repro

1. Install a plugin with a large `node_modules` (the `feishu` plugin here contributes 4 553 files).
2. Apply the patch in [How to reproduce the instrumentation](#how-to-reproduce-the-instrumentation) and start the Gateway once. Record `runtimePluginMs`.
3. Disable that plugin, restart, record `runtimePluginMs` again.

The delta is that plugin's scan cost. On this host removing 6 small stock plugins (18 → 12 loaded, confirmed in the log) changed `model-runtime` by −1.6 % — the bulk is one plugin's dependency tree, not plugin count.

## Measured breakdown (via instrumentation patch)

The `onBuildStats` callback already computes 20 metrics, but routes them to `startupTrace.detail("sidecars.model-runtime-build", …)` → the diagnostic events channel, **not** the log file. That is why this was hard to see. Patching that one line to also `console.error(JSON.stringify(stats))` produced:

```
workspaceFactsMs               60247.4 ms   ← the whole phase
runtimePluginMs                58123.9 ms   ← 96 %, nested inside
agentFactsMs                    1316.7 ms
registryMs                       593.6 ms
staticProviderCatalogMs           28.4 ms
configuredProjectionMs            14.7 ms
ambientCredentialsMs               8.0 ms
pluginMetadataMs                   0.1 ms
catalogSourceMs                    0.0 ms
```

Total phase wall time `sidecars.model-runtime` = **60.6 s**, so `workspaceFactsMs` accounts for essentially all of it.

Scale metrics from the same payload:

```
agentCount=3  workspaceGroupCount=3  configuredFactsGroupCount=3
catalogSourceCount=0  credentialGroupCount=1  catalogGroupCount=0
runtimeRegistryCount=3  configuredRuntimeModelCount=21
generatedCatalogPluginCount=2  generatedCatalogReadCount=6
sourceConcurrencyLimit=2  fullCatalogConcurrencyLimit=1
```

## Where the time goes

Inside `prepareWorkspaceBuildGroup`, the `reportStage` labels map 1:1 onto those metrics:

| stage | metric | value |
|---|---|---:|
| `workspace plugins` | `runtimePluginMs` | 58 124 ms |
| `static provider catalog` | `staticProviderCatalogMs` | 28 ms |
| `ambient credentials` | `ambientCredentialsMs` | 8 ms |
| `agent facts` | `agentFactsMs` | 1 317 ms |
| `configured model projection` | `configuredProjectionMs` | 15 ms |

The `workspace plugins` stage's only `await` is `resolvePluginMetadataSnapshotAsync`, which goes through `createPluginCache` / `retainPluginCache` / `selectPluginMetadataSnapshot`.

> Scope caveat: `plugin-metadata-snapshot-*.mjs` itself contains only
> one `scan` call (with 14 `stat` and 45 `manifest` references). The
> 6,495-entry filesystem walk therefore happens **beneath** that call —
> inside `createPluginCache` / `selectPluginMetadataSnapshot` and their
> transitive helpers — not in this module. The 58 s is attributed to
> this stage by the `onBuildStats` instrumentation, which measures the
> whole `runtimePluginMs` span around the single `await`.

### Code locations

| what | path | line |
|---|---|---:|
| `prepareWorkspaceBuildGroup` | `dist/prepared-model-runtime.facts-*.mjs` | 400 |
| the `await` that owns the 58 s | `dist/prepared-model-runtime.facts-*.mjs` | 413 |
| `resolvePluginMetadataSnapshotAsync` | `dist/plugin-metadata-snapshot-*.mjs` | 550 |

```js
// dist/prepared-model-runtime.facts-*.mjs:413
await resolvePluginMetadataSnapshotAsync(prepareOwnedPluginMetadataSnapshotParams(input, env));
```

## The tree being walked

```
~/.openclaw/npm/projects/    6495 files / 603 dirs / 101 MB
└─ feishu plugin              4553 files in node_modules (2 files are its own)
   @larksuiteoapi/node-sdk     7 files, 28.83 MB
   typebox                  1409 files
   zod                       840 files
   @openclaw/fs-safe          672 files
   protobufjs                 108 files
   @openclaw/fs-safe-*        8 platform variants, ~24 MB
```

## The two instances are a natural A/B

Same OpenClaw version (2026.10.8 / dc2523e), same code path, same
`fullCatalogConcurrencyLimit` (= 1), same `MAX_CONCURRENT_MODEL_RUNTIME_AGENT_SOURCE_BUILDS`.
Only two variables differ: plugin-tree size and filesystem.

| | Comparison host (bare metal, local SSD) | This host (Docker on Synology NAS) |
|---|---|---|
| `runtimePluginMs` | **1,209 ms** | **58,124 ms** (48×) |
| plugin-tree files | **885** = `extensions/` 849 + `npm/projects/` 36 | **6,495** = `npm/projects/` only |
| plugin-tree size | 7.2 MB | 101 MB |
| per-file cost | **1.37 ms** | **8.95 ms** (6.5×) |

Scope note: the two columns are **not** counted identically. The 885
figure includes `extensions/`; the 6,495 figure does not. This host's
`extensions/` tree was not counted, so both the 7.3× file-count ratio
and the 6.5× per-file ratio are **lower bounds** for the true gap.

Decomposition (conservative, given the scope note above):

    48× total ≈ 7.3× more files × 6.5× higher per-file cost

The first factor is ordinary data volume. The second is filesystem:
Docker overlay2 + NAS spindle/network storage makes each `stat`
substantially more expensive. This also explains why the host's ~100%
SQLite page cache does not help — `stat` does not go through it.

Note the fix target is *operation count*, not *operation scheduling*.

## What does not explain it (ruled out)

Single-variable experiments, each verified with a restart. Format: *hypothesis → how it was tested → result*.

1. Hollow `node-llama-cpp` install / provider pointing at a dead host → removed plugin + provider + aliases + install dir + install record → **−2 %** (62.9 s vs 64.4 s)
2. Plugin *count* → disabled 6 unused plugins, 18 → 12 loaded (confirmed in log) → **−1.6 %**
3. DB size → checked what the phase reads → `memory_embedding_cache` / `memory_index_chunks` / `embedding` referenced **0 times**
4. Memory / CPU → `mem_limit` 3 g→5 g, `cpu_shares` 512→4096 → `eventLoopUtilization` 0.997→0.999, **unchanged**
5. Disk I/O on the DB → page cache 100 % resident, `diskBytes=0` → **only covers SQLite**, not the plugin tree
6. External-service probe timeouts → 72 × 5 s `generativelanguage.googleapis.com` timeouts/day → **zero** fall inside the `model-runtime` window (first is 11 s after it ends)

Disabling 6 plugins changed nothing because those were small stock plugins; the bulk is one plugin's `node_modules`.

## Why this matters

- The scan runs on **every** startup, not once per install.
- On containers and NAS/NFS hosts the per-`stat` cost is amplified, so the effect is far larger than the tree-size ratio suggests.
- The metrics that reveal it already exist but never reach the log (see last section).

## Suggested directions (in priority order)

1. **Bounded, manifest-first lookup (largest win).** Check for `openclaw.plugin.json` at the known layouts — the package root, and `node_modules/<pkg>/` directly under each plugin root — and fall back to a full walk only when nothing is found. This preserves support for arbitrary-depth installs while removing the walk from the common case.
2. **Cache the metadata snapshot**, keyed on `pluginGeneration` or directory mtime, so startup does not re-scan an unchanged tree. Pushes steady-state operation count toward 0. A cold install or upgrade would still scan once.
3. **Parallelism — consider last, and probably not at all on network filesystems.** Little's law predicts it will not help:

   ```
   throughput = concurrency / latency_per_operation
   ```

   On NAS / overlay2 the per-operation latency **already includes queueing**. Raise concurrency → queue deepens → latency rises with it → throughput stays flat → total time does not drop. The bottleneck is the metadata path, not the workers feeding it.

   **A measurable guard for anyone tempted to try it:** after raising concurrency, if `runtimePluginMs / fileCount` (cost per file) **rises instead of falling**, the metadata path is saturated and concurrency is a negative optimization. This holds for NAS, containers, and network filesystems generally.

The fix target is *operation count*, not *operation scheduling* — see the per-file cost table above.

## How to reproduce the instrumentation

Patch `onBuildStats` in `dist/server-startup-post-attach-*.mjs` to also print (comma operator, one line, original trace unchanged):

```js
onBuildStats: (stats) => (console.error("MODELRUNTIME_BUILD_STATS " + JSON.stringify(stats)), params.startupTrace?.detail("sidecars.model-runtime-build", [ /* unchanged */ ]))
```

One startup then prints all 20 values to stderr.

## Observability gap (this cost is currently invisible)

`onBuildStats` computes all 20 metrics and then discards them into `startupTrace.detail`, which reaches the diagnostic events channel and never the log file. So a phase can burn 58 s of every startup and leave no trace in any log the operator can read.

**Suggestion:** emit these at debug level by default, or behind a verbose flag. They already exist — surfacing them would make the next occurrence diagnosable without patching the bundle. This issue took a plugin-tree audit and a bundle patch to attribute; with the numbers in the log it would have been one `grep`.

## Environment

- Gateway 2026.10.8 (dc2523e), Linux x64, Node 24.22.1, **Docker on Synology NAS**
- Plugin tree `~/.openclaw/npm/projects/`: 101 MB / 6 495 files / 603 dirs
- 3 agents, 12 plugins enabled, 21 configured runtime models
- Container: 5 GiB memory, 4 cores, no cgroup CPU limit
- Comparison instance (different host, same version): 885-file / 7.2 MB tree, `runtimePluginMs` 1 209 ms

issues.title: Telegram isolated polling re-fetches the same completed update in a tight loop (local Bot API, 2026.10.9), pegging CPU

labels.name: P1
labels.description: High-priority user-facing bug, regression, or broken workflow.

labels.name: impact:crash-loop
labels.description: Crash, hang, restart loop, or process-level availability failure.

issues.body:
## Summary

With Telegram isolated polling against a local Bot API server (`channels.telegram.apiRoot: http://127.0.0.1:8081`), the gateway keeps receiving the **same, already completed** update over and over, several times per second, and never moves past it. The gateway sits at 120-170% CPU and writes roughly 100 MB of logs every 40 minutes until it is stopped and the offset is confirmed by hand.

It recurs after ordinary messages. On 2026-10-31 it looped on update `N`, I cleared it, and about an hour later it was looping on the next message, `N+3`, after that message had been answered.

## Environment

- OpenClaw 2026.10.9 (8b18b55), Node 24.22.2
- Raspberry Pi, aarch64, Debian 13 (trixie), 4 GB RAM
- Gateway as a systemd user service, `--max-old-space-size=3072`
- Self-hosted `telegram-bot-api` on `127.0.0.1:8081` (2 GB file limit), one bot account, private chat only

## What the logs show

The same three lines repeat for one updateId every 100-300 ms (411 times in about 2 minutes in one sample):

```
[telegram][diag] isolated polling worker update received updateId=699162895 queued=1
[telegram][diag] isolated polling update spooled updateId=699162895
[telegram][diag] isolated polling offset queued updateId=699162895
```

- `channel_ingress_events` in `~/.openclaw/state/openclaw.sqlite` has that event as `status = completed`, as well as the two that came after it.
- There are **no** `telegram: failed to persist update offset` lines and no `isolated polling update spool failed` lines.
- `isolated polling ingress started` is logged only once per gateway start, so the polling session is not cycling.
- Alongside the loop there are `slow SQLite transaction hold`, `slow SQLite session write` and `slow agent database reservation` warnings.

## Workaround that clears it

1. `systemctl --user stop openclaw-gateway`
2. `GET {apiRoot}/bot<token>/getUpdates?offset=<stuck_id + 1>&limit=1&timeout=0`
3. Start the gateway again.

After that, CPU settles at about 5-10% until the next time it happens. I'm currently running this from a 1-minute systemd timer as a self-healing workaround.

## Where I looked (`dist` of 2026.10.9)

- In `telegram-ingress-worker.runtime-*.mjs`, the worker advances its in-memory `lastUpdateId` after each `spool-ack` and polls with `offset = lastUpdateId + 1`. Going by that, the same id should not come back while the worker stays alive.
- In `polling-session-*.mjs`, a worker is created with `initialUpdateId: this.opts.getCommittedUpdateId()`. Separately, `createTelegramUpdateOffsetPersistence` (in `probe-*.mjs`) moves `acceptedUpdateId` forward before the write lands and drops any later `persistUpdateId` call with `id <= acceptedUpdateId`.

So my guess is that something recreates the worker, or resets its `lastUpdateId`, without logging `ingress started`, while `committedUpdateId` is still behind (possibly a slow or stuck `writeTelegramUpdateOffset` while SQLite is contended). Each new worker then re-fetches the same update, and `persistUpdateId` treats the re-delivery as already accepted and never retries the commit. I haven't confirmed this. Some extra diagnostics would show it directly: logging `poll-start` offsets, worker creation, and `writeUpdateId` start and finish.

Possibly related: #176731 (a different trigger: the persisted offset was ahead of the real update_ids), #159990 (SQLite contention).

## Expected

Once an update is spooled and acked, it is never fetched again, and the committed offset eventually catches up even after a slow write.

issues.body:
### Bug type

Behavior bug (incorrect output/state without crash)

### Beta release blocker

No

### Summary

A plugin whose manifest id has uppercase letters (for example `MyProv`) is enabled again by plugin auto-enable after the user disables it. `openclaw plugins disable MyProv` stores the disable under the canonical lowercase key, `plugins.entries.myprov.enabled: false`. Auto-enable looks the disable up under the manifest spelling `MyProv`, does not find it, and appends `plugins.entries.MyProv.enabled: true`. When the entries fold onto the canonical id, the later key wins, so the plugin loads, and `openclaw doctor --fix` writes the re-enable into `openclaw.json`. https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/pull/180789 moved install persistence onto the canonical id (https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/issues/180071); auto-enable still reads the raw id.

### Steps to reproduce

1. Install a local provider plugin whose manifest has `"id": "MyProv"`, `"providers": ["myprov"]` and `"autoEnableWhenConfiguredProviders": ["myprov"]`: `openclaw plugins install --force --accept-capabilities ./myprov`.
2. Configure its provider: `openclaw config set models.providers.myprov '{"baseUrl":"http://127.0.0.1:9/v1","api":"openai-completions","models":[{"id":"m1","name":"m1"}]}' --strict-json`.
3. `openclaw plugins disable MyProv`.
4. `openclaw doctor --fix --non-interactive`.
5. `openclaw plugins list --json` and read the `MyProv` status.

### Expected behavior

The plugin stays disabled; `doctor --fix` does not enable it and `plugins.entries` keeps only `myprov: { enabled: false }`.

### Actual behavior

`doctor --fix` prints `myprov auth configured, enabled automatically.`, `plugins.entries` becomes `{"myprov":{"enabled":false},"MyProv":{"enabled":true}}`, and `plugins list` reports `MyProv: loaded`. The same raw lookups affect deny and enable: with `plugins.deny: ["myprov"]`, or after `openclaw plugins enable MyProv`, `doctor --fix` still writes `MyProv: {enabled: true}` beside the canonical entry and prints `myprov auth configured, enabled automatically.` (the denied plugin stays blocked).

### OpenClaw version

Source build at 24e37a12ddc

### Operating system

Ubuntu 22.04

### Install method

Source build

### Model

None (the plugin is never called)

### Provider / routing chain

None; local CLI only

### Additional provider/model setup details

Isolated state and config directories; a synthetic local plugin with no network access and no credentials.

### Logs

```shell
after plugins disable: plugins.entries: {"myprov":{"enabled":false}}
doctor --fix:          myprov auth configured, enabled automatically.
after doctor --fix:    plugins.entries: {"myprov":{"enabled":false},"MyProv":{"enabled":true}}
plugins list:          MyProv: loaded
```

### Screenshots, recordings, and evidence

The before and after captures are in the pull request.

### Impact and severity

- Affected: users of third-party plugins whose manifest id is not all lowercase and that auto-enable (configured provider, channel, tool or model reference).
- Severity: an explicit disable is silently undone; `plugins list` shows the plugin loaded, and `doctor --fix` persists the re-enable.
- Frequency: every auto-enable pass for such a plugin after it was disabled.
- Consequence: the user cannot keep the plugin off without removing its configuration. Lowercase ids are unaffected.

prs.title: fix: avoid unrelated validator churn when schemas change
prs.body:
## What Problem This Solves

Fixes: validator regeneration produces large unrelated diffs when developers add or reorder protocol schemas.

## User Impact

No user-visible behavior change is intended. Generated validators should retain the same validation behavior. This introduces a large one-time regeneration; no configuration changes or migrations are required.

## Why This Change Was Made

Use deterministic names and ordering for shared predicates so unrelated schema changes do not renumber existing output. Preserve schema data and property names during rewriting, and retain tree-shaking of unused predicates.

<details>
<summary>Requested diff breakdown</summary>

prs.title: fix(ui): keep remote session loading ahead of offline downloads
prs.body:
## What Problem This Solves

Fixes delayed session switches and reconnect recovery on remote Gateways when offline asset downloads compete with foreground traffic.

Related: #188922.

## User Impact

Foreground conversations and route loads take priority over optional offline downloads. Reconnecting to the same Gateway starts the sidebar refresh alongside cached-history recovery. First loads keep conversation-first ordering.

## Why This Change Was Made

The existing first history page already uses compression, intent prefetch, and cursor deltas. The measured waste was elsewhere: service-worker installation did not see WebSocket traffic, offline downloads filled the link, and reconnect roster refresh waited for history. This change lets the existing cache owner yield to foreground requests/imports, bounds offline batches, and removes that reconnect dependency. Declared next-route preloads remain. Three shared sandbox transport helpers also share one lazy chunk, saving two requests and avoiding another HTTP/1.1 request wave on first Board visit. Automatic menu warmups and their queue are removed: a single root import could fan out across all six HTTP connections and delay a new document.

The sandbox grouping keeps renderer boundaries unchanged; some optional MCP/Website views receive about 1.5 KB gzip of sibling transport helpers. No protocol or persistence format changes. Menus and pickers load on first use, which can briefly show their existing loading fallback; later opens reuse the loaded body. Offline preparation remains best effort and retains its existing deadline and completed assets.

## Evidence

**Timing acceptance is pending: the final 20-pair cohorts run on the current head before auto-merge is armed.**

Acceptance: 20 serial AB/BA pairs for local, 100 ms RTT/10 Mbps, and 250 ms RTT/3 Mbps, plus 20 mobile base/base A/A pairs. Measure cold/warm transcript and composer, session switch, New Session, first Board/Usage/Appearance visits, and reconnect after a five-second outage. Use renderer CPU and structural counts when the shared-host A/A timing control is noisy. Session switch target: local plus one RTT. Attribute queueing, Gateway time, compressed transfer, parse, and remaining presentation time.

| Check | Result |
| --- | --- |
| UI typecheck | Passed |
| Focused navigation, offline-cache, reconnect roster tests | Passed; regression assertions fail on base |
| Production Knip | Passed |
| Scoped lint and independent review | Passed |
| Startup JS gzip, same-machine base → head | 88,766 → 88,965 B (+199 B) |
| Startup CSS requests / gzip | 1 / 33,568 B on both |
| Production build and strict asset check | Passed |
| Final latency/CPU cohorts | Running; results to follow before readiness |

The diagnostic first history page was 127,703 B decoded and about 10.7 KB compressed on the wire (about 28.4 ms transfer at 3 Mbps); JSON.parse was about 0.2 ms. Reconnect already used zero-message cursor deltas, so this PR adds no duplicate cache or delta protocol. Final round-trip tables, LOC totals, and representative synthetic screenshots will be recorded here after the run.

prs.title: fix(openai): avoid repacing GPT-Live carrier audio
prs.body:
Closes #189012

## What Problem This Solves

Fixes delayed GPT-Live phone replies when audio captured during connection startup remains queued behind incoming carrier audio.

## User Impact

GPT-Live phone calls can catch up after startup without discarding buffered speech. In a controlled ten-session comparison, median model reply latency dropped from **3.53 to 1.57 seconds**. No configuration change is required. This measurement ends at model audio arrival, not handset playback.

## Why This Change Was Made

The carrier already delivers G.711 audio at real-time speed. Applying another clock preserves any initial backlog because it consumes audio only as fast as new audio arrives. The existing socket runtime now forwards public `gpt-live-1` mono 8 kHz G.711 capture through its unpaced path, retaining readiness buffering, conversion, ordering, backpressure, and shutdown. PCM, other models, and WebRTC keep their current behavior.

## Evidence

- A new Gateway regression fails on upstream `dda109cacbbefd3a6dfcc442ac97e2107b6c62c8`: only 960 PCM bytes are sent after readiness despite two seconds of queued capture. The repair immediately sends over 95,000 ordered bytes, forwards continuing capture, adds no idle silence, and stops sending after close. A strengthened other-model case guards the remaining clock behavior.
- Focused tests: **58 passed**. OpenAI plugin lane: **1,124 passed across 87 files** in 45.89 s. Targeted format, lint, and typecheck passed for all changed TypeScript. The script erasability check, test-line ratchet, and Knip production/full-tree unused-file scans pass (zero unused files).
- Local autoreview (Codex, P0–P3) completed with `scoped-clean`, no findings, against base `dda109cacbbefd3a6dfcc442ac97e2107b6c62c8` and the production, regression-test, and workload snapshot. A separate independent review of the production/regression change also found no actionable issues. Neither reviewer reran the tests. The final documentation-only follow-up clarifies the G.711 exception in the provider and SDK guides; format, MDX, and Markdown lint checks passed, and the production and regression-test bytes are unchanged.
- Published head `3228456b583fa6397b8188016e4665cc1bd5f2e6` has tree `bd86b0a8a92b576ddabd2a1f3240e4bb5b1652ef`, verified identical to the checked local source.
- CI caught a broad SDK import in the standalone workload that exposed a deprecated compatibility API. The workload now imports the same RMS helper directly from its owner. Independent review, the database-worker ratchet, targeted typecheck/lint/format, script erasability, and a fresh live smoke sample pass. The sample delivered all 896 input frames, recognized and answered correctly, and closed cleanly with zero errors.
- Five serial ABAB baseline/candidate pairs through the real source bridge, media worker, and public GPT-Live WebSocket: **10/10 recognized the question, answered correctly, and closed cleanly**, with zero provider/runtime errors or delegation attempts.

| Metric | Upstream | Candidate |
| --- | ---: | ---: |
| Reply latency, median / p95 | 3.529 / 3.675 s | 1.574 / 1.744 s |
| Reply latency, min–max | 3.309–3.675 s | 1.290–1.744 s |
| Session ready, median / p95 | 1.018 / 1.429 s | 0.989 / 1.020 s |
| Process CPU, median / p95 | 1,749.7 / 1,877.9 ms | 1,683.9 / 1,710.6 ms |
| Main-thread CPU, median / p95 | 597.2 / 628.5 ms | 592.3 / 632.5 ms |
| Peak RSS, median / p95 | 688.0 / 702.5 MiB | 677.1 / 687.1 MiB |
| Graceful close, median / p95 | 657.2 / 686.4 ms | 680.6 / 688.5 ms |
| Input frames per session | 896 | 896 |
| Output chunks, min–max | 152 | 151–155 |
| Output bytes, min–max | 121,595 | 120,795–123,995 |

Median latency improves by **1.955 s (55.4%)**. Graceful-close median is 23.3 ms higher; main-thread CPU p95 is 4.0 ms higher. No measured resource or delivery metric regressed by 20%; all samples completed. This small live-service sample is evidence for this route, not a general latency guarantee; nearest-rank p95 is the maximum of five samples.

<details>
<summary>Reproduction, acceptance rule, and scope</summary>

The acceptance rule was saved before measurement: identical synthetic question/model/voice/instructions, a fixed 1,920 ms pre-ready backlog, five baseline and five candidate sessions interleaved, median reply-latency improvement of at least 1,000 ms, no worse p95, correct recognition/answer and clean closure in every sample. Any loss/error rejects the change; a 20% startup/CPU/RSS/output regression requires investigation. The comparison meets that rule.

Use the committed workload from each pinned source checkout:

```sh
ffmpeg -i question.wav -ac 1 -ar 8000 -c:a pcm_mulaw -f mulaw question.ulaw
mkdir -p .artifacts/gpt-live-profile
node --cpu-prof --cpu-prof-dir .artifacts/gpt-live-profile \
  --import ./scripts/tsx.mjs scripts/perf/gpt-live-telephony-input.ts \
  --live --input question.ulaw
```

Supply `OPENAI_API_KEY` through the environment and generate the synthetic phrase “What is seven plus five?” once. The fixture used here is 10,886 mu-law bytes; its SHA-256 is `57676adcb3e7d2e5b84418a5b0d36bae8537bb34900b59513534b6adbc50f64b`. Run the same workload on upstream and candidate in alternating order, five times each. The workload queues 96 silence frames, then submits 800 160-byte frames on an absolute 20 ms cadence, including trailing silence. It emits aggregate JSON and boolean recognition/answer checks, never raw transcripts or credentials.

The ten comparison samples used the workload at `f5f3d005f534c8ae236fb3211c04777620ee44e5`. The later import-only CI repair leaves the measured loop and RMS implementation unchanged; the table retains the original workload’s absolute memory measurements. Its separate final-workload smoke sample is excluded from the comparison.

Every comparison sample used a fresh process and session, Node 26.12.1 on macOS 26.6.2 arm64. OS and provider caches were uncontrolled. One-minute host load ranged from 1.91 to 3.03; worst frame scheduling lag was 3.19 ms. CPU and RSS describe source processes, including worker startup. One initial empty-fixture setup attempt stopped before any provider session; it is excluded from the ten valid samples. Separate baseline/candidate worker profiling runs passed and captured both the media worker and loader thread; main-thread profiles were captured with the timing runs. Raw profiles remain private. These diagnostic runs are excluded from the latency table.

The deterministic test covers the real bridge/runtime with a fake wire; the live workload covers the real bridge/worker/provider. It does not measure carrier network timing, handset playout, or a production Gateway deployment. Existing worker tests cover batching and queue bounds.

The simplification pass removes the second clock from this route at its existing owner. Production delta: +14/-2 lines; tests: +53 lines in existing suites, with a scoped allocation. The standalone workload exists to make the comparison rerunnable; generated evidence is not committed.

</details>

prs.title: fix: cancel usage pricing preparation when the Gateway stops
prs.body:
## What Problem This Solves

Fixes: Gateway shutdown can hang on usage backfill while catalog pricing preparation is pending.

## User Impact

Stopping the usage sidecar now cancels its pricing wait and releases its refresh lock. Committed cost-cache rows remain intact; unfinished refresh work is rebuilt on the next startup. No configuration, schema, or migration changes.

## Why This Change Was Made

The sidecar already aborts its work scope, but `prepareUsageCostPricing` awaited catalog preparation without observing that signal. The worker runtime holds its refresh lock across this await. Race this optional preparation against the existing scope signal, retaining the existing joins for native workers and admitted cache writes. Shared catalog preparation may finish independently; the cancelled refresh cannot continue to scan or write.

The incident journal identifies the usage sidecar as the only pending named owner at the 82-second shutdown deadline, but cannot identify its inner await. This regression proves a remaining cancellation hole after #187877; it does not establish that every production SIGKILL has this cause. Earlier stops with no pending close steps also recorded service-child cleanup failures, which need separate investigation.

## Evidence

- Real sidecar, queue, refresh runtime, and pricing owner; only the inner catalog-preparation step is held pending. On base `9902334873c1c00649c1cfe1ff484621635ece49`, the pricing case fails because stop never settles within 100 ms; discovery and scan-admission cases pass. The fix passes all three cases.
- Focused single-file tests, each timeout-wrapped with `--maxWorkers=1`, using the pinned Bun fork: sidecar **7 passed** (17.15 s wrapper wall time); pricing-context **1 passed** (7.15 s); real incognito close/accepted memory usage and trajectory settlement **1 passed** (14.99 s). Existing sidecar coverage includes committed usage, exact reads, deferred appends, and recovery after restart.
- Focused type-aware lint, formatting, and `git diff --check` pass. Full typechecks and broad suites are left to PR CI under the host IO restriction. The initial installed-Bun lint attempts timed out because that runtime invoked the package script; the documented focused oxlint fallback passed.
- Fresh local autoreview through **P0–P2: scoped-clean**, reviewing the complete local candidate against `9902334873c1c00649c1cfe1ff484621635ece49` (committed unchanged as `c4b1ba1695b46e903c05425a5ea39659d59e4fc0`). Catalog preparation internals were outside the reviewer bundle; source inspection confirms the refresh exits before any scan dispatch and uses existing lock cleanup.
- Simplification: reuse the pricing owner and abort helper; remove single-use test fixture indirection. Whole-PR production delta **+8 lines**, test delta **−1 line**, with all previous assertions retained.
- No live Gateway or production data was modified. Production restart confirmation remains an operator follow-up.

prs.title: feat(cron): skip scheduled runs when a shell precheck finds no work
prs.body:
Supersedes #171738 and links the closed replay #112375. ## What Problem This Solves Scheduled jobs that poll for work still start a model turn when the inbox, queue, or watch target is empty. This supersedes https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/pull/171738 and replaces the closed replay of https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/pull/112375. Those branches targeted the previous cron store and could not be applied to current main. This branch is based on current `openclaw/openclaw` main (`7559fb21a57059bd7483fb8c0a7117aff9794f92`). ## User Impact User impact: an operator can attach a host shell precheck to an `at`, `every`, or `cron` job. Exit code 0 continues into the trigger and payload. Exit code 2 records a skipped run with summary `precheck-no-work` and does not start the model turn. Denied, unapproved, timed out, or unexpected results fail closed and skip the payload. Agent turns cannot create or edit the command. Docs: https://docs.openclaw.ai/automation/cron-jobs/schedules#shell-precheck ## Why This Change Was Made Current cron jobs live in SQLite `job_json`, with validation in the cron service and execution in `executeJobCore`. The precheck is an optional field on that job, not a new config key or schema version. The probe runs through `createExecTool` with `nonInteractiveApproval` and no host-approval bypass, then the existing gateway allowlist and approval floors. `cron.triggers.enabled: false` disables it. Forced manual runs still run the probe; they do not skip it the way they skip a condition script. ## Evidence Local validation on `7712f5df3648054ff2bd2ecdd0c90d96b73d71c5`: - `pnpm test src/cron/job-precheck.test.ts src/cron/job-precheck-run.test.ts src/cron/service/timer-execution.precheck.test.ts src/cron/service/timer-execution.occurrence.test.ts src/cli/cron-cli/register.cron-precheck.test.ts` — passed. Cron shard: 4 files, 86 tests. CLI shard: 1 file, 3 tests. The exec-policy file proves a marker file is not created when security is deny, ask is always, the job pin requires ask always, `toolsAllow` excludes exec, or run authority is rejected. An allowed `full`/`off` policy covers exit 2 (no work) and exit 0 (work). - `node scripts/run-oxlint.mjs` on the changed TypeScript files — passed. - `node_modules/.bin/oxfmt --check` on the 29 changed files — all matched files use the correct format. - `pnpm tsgo:core` — passed. - `node scripts/run-tsgo.mjs -p test/tsconfig/tsconfig.core.test.services-cron.json --incremental --tsBuildInfoFile .artifacts/tsgo-cache/core-test-services-cron.tsbuildinfo` — passed. ## Security review ### Threat model A precheck is an unattended host command. The realistic attackers are a model turn that tries to persist one, an operator who saved a command and later tightened exec policy, and a forced or restarted run that might otherwise skip the gate. The command can do anything the exec tool would allow, including reading or writing files on the gateway host. The feature must not add a second spawn path with weaker defaults. ### How approvals are enforced - The runner calls `createExecTool` with the resolved `tools.exec` host, mode, security, and ask, plus the live exec-approvals file that the tool already re-reads. It does not pass `bypassHostApprovalFloors`. - `nonInteractiveApproval: true` makes approval-requiring commands return `approval_required` before spawn. `ask: "always"`, an allowlist miss, and `security: "deny"` therefore do not run the command. - A stored `toolsAllowExecTarget` pin is applied with `pinExecToolTarget`, so a creator floor of `ask: "always"` still denies a headless run when global policy is `full`/`off`. - A defined `toolsAllow` that does not include `exec` denies the probe before the tool is built. - `assertRunCurrent` is awaited in `executeJobCore` and again inside the runner immediately before `tool.execute`. A rejected run does not spawn. - If the gateway does not wire `runJobPrecheck`, or `cron.triggers.enabled` is false, the job errors and the payload does not start. - Agent creates and patches that set a non-null `precheck` are rejected in the automations tool and again in `assertCronModelJobAllowed`. Clearing the field is allowed. `cron.run` of an existing job is not treated as authoring. - Invalid persisted prechecks quarantine the row instead of being dropped, so a bad write cannot fall open into an unguarded payload. - Each run re-reads current policy. A command saved under a looser policy is denied after the operator tightens it. ### Residual risks - Command payloads (`runCronCommandJob`) still spawn from their own runner and do not use this exec-tool gate. That path is unchanged. - Operators who can already persist command jobs can persist a precheck through the CLI or Gateway API. The protection is the run-time policy check, not a second save-time approval dialog. Reusing the stream approval dialog would describe the wrong effect. - `mode: "auto"` remains the existing exec auto-review path. With `nonInteractiveApproval`, a reviewer that approves can still allow a spawn. Tests pin `mode: "full"` so they do not depend on a reviewer. This change does not weaken or special-case auto-review. - When config omits security, the exec tool keeps its own non-sandbox default and the approvals file still applies its floors. That is the same default as other exec callers. - Exit codes are the only work signal. A command that prints a success banner and exits 2 is no-work. A command that exits 0 after doing nothing is work. Overlapping codes are rejected. - The probe runs on the exec host selected by `tools.exec` unless a gateway pin forces the gateway host. It cannot target a node or sandbox that the exec tool itself would refuse.
  
--- > [!NOTE] > **High Risk** > Introduces unattended host command execution on the gateway before scheduled agent turns, gated by exec policy but still a security-sensitive automation surface. > > Reviewed by [Cursor Bugbot](https://cursor.com/bugbot) for commit 7712f5df3648054ff2bd2ecdd0c90d96b73d71c5. Bugbot is set up for automated code reviews on this repo. Configure [here](https://www.cursor.com/dashboard/bugbot). Updated by merging current upstream main (merge commit `ce9c3641f4`); the precheck, occurrence and CLI cron tests (89 tests) and `pnpm tsgo:core` pass on the merged head.
