prs.title: fix(exec): explain what a running background result proves and warn against unpolled promises
prs.body:
## What Problem This Solves

On 2026-04-27 I asked my OpenClaw agent over Telegram to fix two failing evals in one of my repositories. It handed the work to a coding agent running in the background, and six seconds after the exec tool reported the session as running it told me the work had started and promised to report back. It never did, twice. The exchange, condensed (times UTC):

```text
13:13  me     Can you use the good-oss-citizen tile to get the two failing evals to 100%?

13:14  agent  I set up a fresh worktree and I'm handing the implementation to a
              coding agent now.

13:15:14 exec Command still running (session crisp-breeze, pid 3469063).
              Use process (list/poll/log/write/kill/clear/remove) for follow-up.

13:15:20 agent Started. Worktree, branch, and session are set up.
              I'll report back when it has a commit and gate results, or if it blocks.

13:23  (the coding agent finishes with a local commit; the agent is woken with the
        completion event but that turn is told user delivery is disabled, so I am
        not notified)

13:26  me     Is it still going

13:26  agent  No, the coding agent finished and exited cleanly. There is already a
              local commit. I'm not calling it done yet because I still need to verify.

13:26  (no tool call and no message follow; the agent is idle until my next question)

13:27  me     I'm confused, are you still doing something

13:27  agent  Sorry, yes, that was confusing. The coding agent is no longer running.
              I'm doing the final verification myself now.

13:27  (it amends the commit and starts the gates as another background command)

13:27:55 exec Command still running (session mild-rook, pid 3477273).
              Use process (list/poll/log/write/kill/clear/remove) for follow-up.

13:27:55 agent Yes, but only final verification now. Gates are running now.
              I'll report DONE/BLOCKED when those gates finish.

13:28  (the gates finish; the agent is woken again and again told that user
        delivery is disabled; it writes a "successfully completed" message inside
        that turn, and I am not notified)

13:33  me     Are the gates still running.

13:33  agent  No. Gates finished successfully.

13:33  me     Why didn't you notify me then?

13:33  agent  Because the completion event explicitly said "user delivery is disabled"
              and told me to handle it internally. I should have stayed quiet there.
              But after that, I also failed to proactively send a normal concise DONE
              update once I confirmed the gates had finished. That's on me. I made
              you ask twice.
```

### What the transcript shows

- A running result means a process was spawned and was alive when the result was written. "Started." was true.
- What the agent could not know from that result: whether the command was making progress, was waiting for input, or had since exited or failed.
- The harm was not a false start. It was a promise to report back that could not be kept, twice.
- When a background command finishes, the agent is woken with a completion event by default (`tools.exec.notifyOnExit`, [background process docs](https://docs.openclaw.ai/gateway/background-process#disable-automatic-completion-turns)), but that turn may not be allowed to message the user. That is decided when the turn runs, from the heartbeat delivery route and visibility settings ([heartbeat docs, "Delivery behavior"](https://docs.openclaw.ai/gateway/heartbeat#delivery-behavior)). On 2026-04-27 the agent was woken both times and told both times that delivery was disabled.
- At the moment the running result is written, the exec tool knows whether a completion event will be queued, but not whether that later turn will be allowed to message the user.

That leaves two ways to stop an agent from promising a report it cannot deliver:

1. Tell the agent, in the running result itself, what "running" does and does not mean, and that the completion turn may not be allowed to reach the user, so a promise of updates has to be backed by the agent polling the session to the end and reporting itself.
2. Resolve at exec time whether the completion turn will be allowed to deliver, and put that answer into the result.

This PR takes the first. It is one sentence group in one producer, it is true in every configuration, and it needs no knowledge of delivery routing inside the exec tool. The second would couple the exec tool to heartbeat delivery resolution and still could not promise delivery, because the route can change before the command exits.

## Why This Change Was Made

The shared running result from `createExecTool` currently reads:

> `Command still running (session ..., pid ...). Use process (...) for follow-up.`

#161780 (merged 2026-10-02) split the follow-up route into three notification modes. This PR adds the same first sentences to all three, then folds the delivery caveat into each mode's own wake wording:

> `Command still running (session ..., pid ...). Running means the process was started and was alive when this result was written; it says nothing about progress, waiting for input, or a later exit or failure. Do not report progress from this result alone. <mode-specific follow-up>`

With completion waking on every exit (`notifyOnExitEmptySuccess=true`, the default for chat channels), the follow-up reads:

> `Completion will wake this conversation automatically. The completion turn may not be allowed to message the user, so if only waiting remains, report that the job is running without promising to report back and end this turn; do not keep polling. Use process (...) for follow-up.`

With silent empty successes (`notifyOnExitEmptySuccess=false`):

> `Use process (...) for follow-up. Completion wakes this conversation on output or failure; empty successful jobs are silent (tools.exec.notifyOnExitEmptySuccess=false). Arrange continuation or collect the result before ending the turn if empty success matters. The completion turn may not be allowed to message the user, so do not promise the user updates unless you poll this session until it finishes and report the outcome yourself.`

With `tools.exec.notifyOnExit=false`:

> `Use process (...) for follow-up. Automatic completion wake is disabled (tools.exec.notifyOnExit=false). If the task needs this result, use poll with a timeout to collect it before ending the turn, unless another continuation is already arranged. Without a completion wake, do not promise the user updates unless you poll this session until it finishes and report the outcome yourself.`

Each clause is checked against the code. "The completion turn may not be allowed to message the user" holds whenever a wake is queued: `buildExecEventPrompt` in `src/infra/heartbeat-events-filter.ts` still tells the completion turn "user delivery is disabled for this run" when `canRelayToUser` is false, and `heartbeat-runner-execution.ts` computes that at wake time from heartbeat visibility (`showAlerts`) and the delivery route. In the every-exit mode #161780 tells the agent to end the turn and stop polling, so that mode drops the promise outright ("without promising to report back") instead of offering polling as the way to back one. The other two modes already ask the agent to collect the result when it matters, so the promise rule there keeps the poll-to-the-end condition. The "what running proves" sentences name no tool and sit before the follow-up, so the trailing follow-up sentence stays adapter-owned:

- base exec uses `process`
- sandbox exec uses `sandbox_process`
- Gateway exec uses `gateway_process` when exposed
- Gateway exec without process follow-up tells the model to rerun in the foreground
- remote-node exec says background follow-up is unavailable and to wait for completion

### Overlap with #158884 and #161780

#158884 (merged 2026-09-26) appends a no-wake warning to the follow-up route when `notifyOnExit=false`. The previous head of this PR chose its own wake clause by `notifyOnExit` and left that warning alone.

#161780 (merged 2026-10-02) then made the follow-up conditional on `notifyOnExitEmptySuccess` as well. Stacked on the previous head, the every-exit mode would have said "you may be woken with a completion event ... do not promise the user updates unless you poll this session until it finishes" and, a sentence later, "Completion will wake this conversation automatically ... end this turn; do not keep polling". Those pull in opposite directions.

This head removes the separate wake clause. The delivery caveat and the promise rule now live inside each of #161780's three branches and agree with that branch's instruction, so they also reach the structured `details.followUp`. The "what running proves" sentences stay in the visible text only, before the follow-up. #161780's own sentences are unchanged except for the inserted caveat in the every-exit branch, where "report that the job is running" gains "without promising to report back".

On current `main`, `qa-lab`'s mock provider regex still matches only the pre-#161780 running text, which no mode emits any more. This PR's regex matches the caution followed by any single-line follow-up that contains the `Use process (...)` route, so it covers all three modes.

### How I expect this to help, and what it cannot do

This is an instruction in a tool result. A model can ignore it, and I could not make a model reproduce the original failure in a replay, so I cannot show a before/after in behavior, only in what the model is told. What I can say:

- On 2026-04-27 the agent read "Command still running" over Telegram and answered "Started. I'll report back". On current `main` that is the every-exit mode, which now tells the agent to report that the job is running and end the turn. The new text adds, at that exact point, that it must not promise to report back. In the other modes an agent that follows it has two honest moves: keep polling in the same turn and report when done, which is delivered because it is a reply to the user; or say "launched, ask me or I'll check", which makes no promise it cannot keep. Either avoids the wait I had.
- The misleading input is gone. Today's text reads as confirmation; the new text states the constraint where the decision is made.
- On the same day, 4 of the 64 background commands with a recorded exit in that session ended with a non-zero code, so a "started" relayed from a running result is wrong often enough to matter.

What it does not do: it does not make the agent keep a promise, and it does not change why the completion turns were silenced. That is the delivery-routing topic linked above and is out of scope here.

## User Impact

There is no API, field, or control-flow change. The "what running proves" sentences appear only in the visible text of the `status: running` exec result. The delivery caveat and promise rule are part of the mode-specific follow-up, so they appear in that text and in the structured `details.followUp` string, next to the wake wording they qualify. Subsequent process results are unchanged.

## Real Behavior Proof

I reran the behavior proof against exact head `0eac408a0ac213770c0147d82bbb09aa5fb34468`, rebased onto upstream `main` at `1a331439952556d653b14973fe294e158d1106bd`.

The harness is a `tsx` script that imports `createExecTool`, `createProcessTool`, and `waitForExecScope` from the checked-out `src/` and runs them unmodified. It spawns a real OS child with `background: true`, immediately reads its log, and then polls its terminal outcome. It uses no exec or process mocks.

The child waits 500 ms before printing `WORK_STARTED` and exiting with code 7.

The recording below is one asciinema 3.2.1 session from the earlier head `d85e6cac`, before #158884 landed: it runs the same harness twice, first in a checkout of upstream `main` at that head's base commit `8adb6ebf5f`, then in the PR checkout. `git log` shows the head before each run. On the base commit the running result has no caution while the immediate log is already empty and the child later exits 7; on the PR head the same result carries the caution before the unchanged follow-up sentence. The host I used for this revision has no asciinema or agg, so the recording was not redone; the transcripts further down are from the current head and show the wording that replaced the recorded one. Final frame of the rendered recording:

![Before/after terminal recording: on main the running result reads Command still running, Use process for follow-up; on the PR head the same result adds the new text. Both runs show an empty immediate log, then WORK_STARTED and exit code 7](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/martinfrancois/openclaw/assets/pr-120414-proof/proof-before-after-v3-final-frame.png)

- [proof-before-after-v3.gif](https://github.com/martinfrancois/openclaw/blob/assets/pr-120414-proof/proof-before-after-v3.gif?raw=true): the full rendered recording (agg 1.9.0).
- [proof-before-after-v3.cast](https://github.com/martinfrancois/openclaw/blob/assets/pr-120414-proof/proof-before-after-v3.cast): the asciinema recording itself.
- [proof.mts](https://github.com/martinfrancois/openclaw/blob/assets/pr-120414-proof/proof.mts) and [proof-driver.sh](https://github.com/martinfrancois/openclaw/blob/assets/pr-120414-proof/proof-driver.sh): the harness, with a [README](https://github.com/martinfrancois/openclaw/blob/assets/pr-120414-proof/README.md).

Redacted stdout transcripts of the same harness on the current head, one per notification mode. The harness now reads `notifyOnExit` and `notifyOnExitEmptySuccess` from the environment; everything else is unchanged.

Every-exit mode (the default for chat channels):

```text
head: 0eac408a0ac213770c0147d82bbb09aa5fb34468
node: v24.20.0
notifyOnExit: true notifyOnExitEmptySuccess: true
exec: Command still running (session <session-id>, pid <pid>). Running means the process was started and was alive when this result was written; it says nothing about progress, waiting for input, or a later exit or failure. Do not report progress from this result alone. Completion will wake this conversation automatically. The completion turn may not be allowed to message the user, so if only waiting remains, report that the job is running without promising to report back and end this turn; do not keep polling. Use process (list/poll/log/write/send-keys/submit/paste/kill/clear/remove) for follow-up.
immediate-log: (no output yet)
immediate-status: running
terminal-output:
WORK_STARTED

Process exited with code 7.
terminal-status: completed
terminal-exit-code: 7
```

Silent empty success:

```text
head: 0eac408a0ac213770c0147d82bbb09aa5fb34468
node: v24.20.0
notifyOnExit: true notifyOnExitEmptySuccess: false
exec: Command still running (session <session-id>, pid <pid>). Running means the process was started and was alive when this result was written; it says nothing about progress, waiting for input, or a later exit or failure. Do not report progress from this result alone. Use process (list/poll/log/write/send-keys/submit/paste/kill/clear/remove) for follow-up. Completion wakes this conversation on output or failure; empty successful jobs are silent (tools.exec.notifyOnExitEmptySuccess=false). Arrange continuation or collect the result before ending the turn if empty success matters. The completion turn may not be allowed to message the user, so do not promise the user updates unless you poll this session until it finishes and report the outcome yourself.
immediate-log: (no output yet)
immediate-status: running
terminal-output:
WORK_STARTED

Process exited with code 7.
terminal-status: completed
terminal-exit-code: 7
```

Wake disabled, with #158884's sentence also repeated by the `log` result:

```text
head: 0eac408a0ac213770c0147d82bbb09aa5fb34468
node: v24.20.0
notifyOnExit: false notifyOnExitEmptySuccess: false
exec: Command still running (session <session-id>, pid <pid>). Running means the process was started and was alive when this result was written; it says nothing about progress, waiting for input, or a later exit or failure. Do not report progress from this result alone. Use process (list/poll/log/write/send-keys/submit/paste/kill/clear/remove) for follow-up. Automatic completion wake is disabled (tools.exec.notifyOnExit=false). If the task needs this result, use poll with a timeout to collect it before ending the turn, unless another continuation is already arranged. Without a completion wake, do not promise the user updates unless you poll this session until it finishes and report the outcome yourself.
immediate-log: (no output yet)

Automatic completion wake is disabled (tools.exec.notifyOnExit=false). If the task needs this result, use poll with a timeout to collect it before ending the turn, unless another continuation is already arranged.
immediate-status: running
terminal-output:
WORK_STARTED

Process exited with code 7.
terminal-status: completed
terminal-exit-code: 7
```

This demonstrates the boundary on the current PR head: session liveness is visible before any evidence that the command reached its work, it says nothing about eventual success, and the delivery caveat matches the configured notification mode.

On this same head:

- `bash-tools.exec-background-followup.test.ts` drives a real `createExecTool` background process in each of the three notification modes on the file's current seeded-session harness. It asserts the visible text carries the running caution right before the structured follow-up, that the delivery caveat appears exactly when a wake is queued, that the every-exit mode drops the promise and the other two keep the poll-to-the-end rule, and that only the disabled mode carries #158884's sentence. With `bash-tools.exec-run.ts` reset to `main`, 3 of its 10 cases fail. The elapsed-yield-window path is no longer driven separately: `main` removed that coverage in #166762, and both start paths build the running result from the same per-run follow-up text.
- A case in `dynamic-tool-build.sandbox.test.ts` asserts the complete model-visible sandbox output. The existing `node_exec` case in `dynamic-tool-build.test.ts` asserts the complete remote-node output.
- `qa-lab`'s mock OpenAI provider parses the running text to drive its progress scenarios. `server.progress.test.ts` uses the every-exit text as `RUNNING_OUTPUT` and `server.tool-routing.test.ts` uses the silent-empty-success text, so both shapes (route last, route first) are parsed. With the regex reset to `main`, 6 of the 32 cases in those two files fail.
- Focused run on this head: 132 tests across the five touched test files pass.
- `node scripts/check-changed.mjs --base upstream/main` on this head: 38 of 41 lanes pass (format, lint, typecheck of core and extensions and both test sets, the mock factory ratchet, the other ratchets). The three that fail are `main`'s own at `6e4883fc`: the max-lines suppression ratchet names three `ui/src/pages` files this PR never touches, the core tsgo graph boundary counts 723 core test roots against an advisory 720 (this head adds no test file), and the dead export scan lists four files, none of them touched here. The first two were also verified to fail identically on a pristine checkout of the earlier base `a4182c6c`.
- Exact-head GitHub CI passed on this head: [run 39196328499](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/actions/runs/39196328499), with `openclaw/ci-gate`, dependency review and security review all green.

## Codex App-Server Contract Review

I inspected the direct sibling Codex source required by `AGENTS.md`, pinned to the version the rebased plugin declares: `@openai/codex` `0.162.0`, tag `rust-v0.162.0`, commit [`c1382380de69521303b416720a52f42d51af6248`](https://github.com/openai/codex/commit/c1382380de69521303b416720a52f42d51af6248).

- Codex app-server v2 accepts dynamic-tool text as an `InputText { text }` content item: [`app-server-protocol/src/protocol/v2/item.rs#L1675-L1692`](https://github.com/openai/codex/blob/c1382380de69521303b416720a52f42d51af6248/codex-rs/app-server-protocol/src/protocol/v2/item.rs#L1675-L1692).
- The app server decodes those items and submits them unchanged as `Op::DynamicToolResponse`: [`app-server/src/dynamic_tools.rs#L18-L58`](https://github.com/openai/codex/blob/c1382380de69521303b416720a52f42d51af6248/codex-rs/app-server/src/dynamic_tools.rs#L18-L58).
- Codex core maps every content item into the model's function-tool output without rewriting its text: [`core/src/tools/handlers/dynamic.rs#L153-L164`](https://github.com/openai/codex/blob/c1382380de69521303b416720a52f42d51af6248/codex-rs/core/src/tools/handlers/dynamic.rs#L153-L164).
- Codex's integration test confirms that the exact `InputText` reaches the follow-up `function_call_output`: [`app-server/tests/suite/v2/dynamic_tools.rs#L341-L582`](https://github.com/openai/codex/blob/c1382380de69521303b416720a52f42d51af6248/codex-rs/app-server/tests/suite/v2/dynamic_tools.rs#L341-L582).

On the OpenClaw side, the patch preserves the exact trailing `Use process (...)` literal. The sandbox projection rewrites only that suffix to `sandbox_process` in [`shell-dynamic-tools.ts`](https://github.com/martinfrancois/openclaw/blob/7c16cc2abf757c477b046c00346160269285ff86/extensions/codex/src/app-server/shell-dynamic-tools.ts#L102-L121). The node alias and the Gateway projection in the [same file](https://github.com/martinfrancois/openclaw/blob/7c16cc2abf757c477b046c00346160269285ff86/extensions/codex/src/app-server/shell-dynamic-tools.ts#L42-L88) replace the same suffix with their available or unavailable next step, the Gateway one through the shared projection in [`exec-tool-target-pinning.ts`](https://github.com/martinfrancois/openclaw/blob/7c16cc2abf757c477b046c00346160269285ff86/src/agents/exec-tool-target-pinning.ts#L81-L115).

## Evidence

- `git diff --check` and `oxfmt --check` pass on the tree.
- `node scripts/check-changed.mjs --base upstream/main` on this head: every lane passes except three that are `main`'s own (details above).
- The core real-process test owns the exec result.
- The Codex sandbox rewrite case and the existing `node_exec` case own the complete adapter output.
- The `qa-lab` mock provider is the one consumer that parses the running text; its regex and fixture are updated in the same commit.
- Production changes: three string constants, the three follow-up branches, and one template line in `bash-tools.exec-run.ts`; one regex in `qa-lab`'s `mock-openai-tool-routing.ts`; one note in `docs/tools/exec.md`.
- `CHANGELOG.md` remains untouched.
- The previous head `da456ec3` passed exact-head CI ([run 36861733565](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/actions/runs/36861733565)). This head is rebased onto `1a331439` to take in #161780; the rebase conflicted in `bash-tools.exec-run.ts` and its test, resolved as described above.
- This head is rebased onto `6e4883fc` (#176802); earlier rebases in this series went onto `a4182c6c` (#176397), `3307a081` (#176780) and `6ec77340` (#176838), each one picking up a `main`-side fix for a test this PR does not touch. `main` moved the follow-up text into the run body with #169645 so it reads the per-run wake capture state; the wording change moved with it and the three branches are otherwise unchanged. `main` rewrote the follow-up test file around a seeded session store and removed the old route test in #166762, so the three-mode assertions now run on that harness. `dynamic-tool-build.sandbox.test.ts` did not exist at the previous base; the sandbox case moved there and the sibling file is gone.
- Earlier heads of this PR carried a shorter caution ("Running means only that the session is alive, not that the command's work started or succeeded; do not report progress based on this result alone."). It was replaced because it read as denying that a process had started, which is not what the running result means, and because it said nothing about the promise that caused the harm in the transcript.

## AI Disclosure

This pull request is AI-assisted. Claude prepared the original change and tests. Hermes prepared an earlier exact-head behavior proof and dependency inspection. Codex prepared an earlier rebase, review fix, and cross-surface test refresh. Claude prepared the earlier rebase onto `main`, the `qa-lab` consumer update, the sibling test file, the Codex 0.154.0 and 0.162.0 source inspections, the recorded before/after proof, the transcript excerpt from my own OpenClaw session logs, the reconciliations with #158884 and #161780, the rebases onto `a4182c6c`, `3307a081`, `6ec77340` and `6e4883fc` with the test port, the three-mode test, the docs note, the rerun transcripts, and this description. The author remains responsible for the submitted change.

prs.title: refactor(levanto): isolate prepared Decision execution
prs.body:
## What Problem This Solves

Sage Decision protocol mapping and HTTP execution share the plugin registration owner.

## User Impact

No user-visible behavior or configuration change. Part 19 of the Decision refactor stack, based on [part 18](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/pull/188259).

## Why This Change Was Made

Separate Sage guarded HTTP execution from registration and prepared route projection. Preserve route preparation before awaited image inspection, renewed admission at dispatch, native redirect behavior, credential reflection handling and awaited release before cleanup.

No new public SDK surface, configuration or dependency. Existing registered-provider and host-admission tests remain.

This deliberately revisits the consolidation in https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/pull/177839 for this maintainer-directed Decision refactor. When an active session transcript changes during the first background memory refresh started by `memory_search`, that refresh can finish with the session source still dirty. prs.title: docs(codex): RFC for recovering pending provider-review linkage
prs.body:
Related: https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/issues/178923

Builds on merged prevention PR https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/pull/179054.

## What Problem This Solves

An earlier failed acknowledgment can leave an existing conversation bound to a replacement native thread while its pending provider review still identifies the original; the normal review UI then rejects continuation with `Provider review no longer matches the native thread`.

## User Impact

**RFC/design only, not a working recovery fix.** This draft does not restore affected conversations or change runtime behavior. It proposes verifying current authority, restoring the original link through canonical ownership, and then requiring a separate normal acknowledgment with all existing safety checks intact.

## Why This Change Was Made

PR #179054 prevents new replacements but explicitly does not repair an already-mismatched binding. This draft records the recovery contract, a data-only native policy comparator, and an already-mismatched regression specification. It implements no recovery endpoint, authority issuer, binding/review mutation, or acknowledgment path.

The OpenClaw coordinator and native broker remain unimplemented. Confirmation of the provider's ownership/configuration guarantees remains a dependency: Codex 0.160.0 exposes useful policy fields, but matching those fields does not establish exclusive native ownership or a configuration generation valid through canonical commit. If existing native semantics cannot supply that guarantee, provider support is required. Unknown evidence must refuse recovery.

Consistency repair must preserve the pending review and cannot approve continuation, fabricate ownership, spoof a channel sender, bypass catalog/current-policy checks, or replay held input.

## Evidence

- **23 supporting offline checks passed** for the data comparator and scenario fixture (22 data-comparison checks and one fixture consistency check).
- **31 actual recovery acceptance scenarios are specified but unexecuted**, including recovery of an already-mismatched state, authorization failures, changed policy/catalog/review, concurrency, idempotence, partial/uncertain recovery, rollback/crash disposition, and separate normal acknowledgment.
- No successful recovery, live provider acceptance, full Gateway/native integration, repository Vitest/build/typecheck or CI result is claimed.
- Local proposal diff syntax and full-content privacy scans passed. Only generic fixture identities and public source references are included.

Before this can become a recovery fix, implement and validate the coordinator/native broker and catalog preparation, resolve the provider-guarantee dependency, and prove the already-mismatched regression fails on prevention-only #179054 and passes on the implementation. This RFC should not close an existing-mismatch recovery report.

## What Problem This Solves

Guest workspace preparation can remain queued behind another reconciliation operation after its run is cancelled. Execution admission is already closed, but setup does not settle until the current holder releases the workspace.

## User Impact

The change lets cancellation reach queued initial preparation while the independent holder finishes normally. Ordinary holder release still permits preparation to succeed. Accepted command and file-write cleanup retains its existing workspace lifetime.

## Why This Change Was Made

The current sandbox context and reconciliation owners already accept cancellation. The attempt caller was leaving out its existing run abort signal when resolving sandbox context. This one-line production change completes that caller path and preserves the current warm-workspace reuse implementation. No new API, state, configuration, lock or timeout is introduced.

The exact integration target `9f14244a6067e9ca0e22d1a2b8c5150e9cb7c693` still reproduces the defect through a registered guest session, real admitted-run authority and an independently held reconciliation lease. Cancellation stayed pending for the full 2,001 ms observation interval, then rejected with its original reason after holder release. prs.title: fix(ui): keep the original filename when downloading a PDF from the native viewer
prs.body:
Closes #187543

## What Problem This Solves

When you download a PDF from the native viewer's toolbar in the Control UI sidebar, the file used to save with a random UUID name (e.g. `57384738-0f0c-4235-ae6f-d93b180ee80d.pdf`) instead of the original filename. Now the download keeps the original filename.

- Problem: The sidebar PDF preview fetched the attachment bytes, rewrote them into an anonymous `Blob`, and pointed the iframe at a `blob:` URL. A blob URL cannot carry a filename, so the browser's native PDF viewer fell back to the blob's UUID as the download name — even though the underlying `assistant-media` HTTP response already returned the correct `Content-Disposition: attachment; filename=...`.
- Solution: For same-origin `src` attachments, load the real HTTP URL directly in the iframe (after the existing bounded-size check), so the native viewer reads the original filename from the response header.
- What changed: `ui/src/pages/chat/components/chat-pdf-preview.tsx` renders `<iframe src={props.src}>` for the `src` path (keeping the existing 16MB bounded-read validation); the `file` path (guest/local blobs) is unchanged and still uses the worker/blob preview.
- What did NOT change: the 16MB preview-limit boundary, the media-ticket authorization chain, reader continuity across ticket refresh, and the fallback `unavailable()` card.

## Why This Change Was Made

Browsers can only get a download filename from the HTTP `Content-Disposition` header; no amount of naming on a blob URL can attach one, so the only reliable fix is for the iframe to load the real URL. The `src` and `file` props are mutually exclusive upstream, so keeping the blob path for `file` costs nothing and avoids touching guest-session behavior. We keep the bounded-read fetch as a validation gate (ok + 16MB), rendering the direct iframe only on success.

- Best fix: Load the real HTTP URL in the iframe; it is the only way the native viewer can see the original filename.
- Alternative: `new File(...)` naming or a `#fragment` hint — both are ignored by the native viewer for Save; rejected.
- Risk / non-goals: guest/local `file` blob path and the 16MB boundary are unchanged (covered by the unit matrix); same-origin `src` downloads verified interactively in real Chromium below.

## User Impact

Downloading a PDF from the Control UI sidebar now saves with the original filename (e.g. `r75-monthly-report.pdf`) instead of a UUID. No behavior change for guest/local `file` attachments.

## Evidence

The browser-level test now asserts the PDF iframe is pointed at the real attachment URL (which returns the `Content-Disposition` filename) instead of a `blob:` URL:

```ts
// chat-pdf-preview.browser.test.ts — "keeps the source URL"
expect(frame.getAttribute("src")).toBe(
  "/__openclaw__/assistant-media?mediaTicket=pdf-preview",
);
```

Before this change the same assertion matched `/^blob:/`, i.e. the iframe was fed an anonymous blob and the native viewer had no filename to use for Save.

The component unit tests (12 pass) cover the full matrix: direct `src` renders the real URL, no `createObjectURL` is called on the `src` path, the 16MB limit still falls back to `unavailable()`, ticket refresh preserves the already-loaded viewer (reader continuity, no re-mount), and the `file`/blob path is unchanged:

```
 Test Files  1 passed (1)
      Tests  12 passed (12)
```

Real-browser click-through (real Chromium + real HTTP server, current head): the fixed component's exact DOM — `<iframe src="/__openclaw__/assistant-media?mediaTicket=pdf-preview" referrerpolicy="no-referrer">` — is loaded against a live server returning the PDF with `Content-Disposition: attachment; filename="quarterly-report.pdf"`. The browser's real download event reports the original filename, while the pre-fix blob control produces a UUID:

```
AFTER (fixed: real HTTP src)
  iframe src                = /__openclaw__/assistant-media?mediaTicket=pdf-preview  (not blob:)
  server response           = 200 application/pdf, Content-Disposition: attachment; filename="quarterly-report.pdf"
  download suggestedFilename = quarterly-report.pdf        <- original filename preserved

BEFORE control (pre-fix: anonymous blob src)
  iframe src                = blob:null/d14f23d7-4665-4af4-ba08-bf5b84192943
  (blob URLs carry no Content-Disposition, so the native viewer derives a UUID name — the reported bug)
```

The src-assertion browser test additionally confirms the component emits this iframe DOM in real Chromium.


CI type-check fix (current head `6f6cbad`): `readPreviewSource` was declared to return `Promise<ArrayBuffer | undefined>`, but every falsy path in its body throws (unavailable file, non-ok response, over-limit), so it never returns `undefined`. The narrower `Promise<ArrayBuffer>` matches the true behavior and satisfies the `readBounded` memo's `bytes: ArrayBuffer` expectation (fixes `chat-pdf-preview.tsx` TS2769). The 12 unit tests still pass; this is a type annotation only — runtime behavior is unchanged.

prs.title: fix(macos): key Agent Events rows by globally unique id
prs.body:
## What Problem This Solves

The macOS Agent Events window (`Debug → Open Agent Events…`) keys its rows by `ControlAgentEvent.seq`, but `seq` is a per-run counter that the Gateway restarts at 1 for every run (`src/infra/agent-events.ts`). The window buffers up to 400 events spanning many runs, so ids 1, 2, 3… repeat. SwiftUI treats duplicate identifiers as the same element, so rows from different runs are reused and earlier runs lose theirs. The type already exposes a globally unique `id` (`"\(runId)-\(seq)"`).

Fixes #187608.

## Why This Change Was Made

`apps/macos/Sources/OpenClaw/AgentEventsWindow.swift:21` passes `id: \.id` instead of `id: \.seq` to `ForEach`. That is the only production change, and it is what the issue's Expected section names. The store, the event type, and the Gateway's sequence allocation stay untouched: per-run `seq` is correct for ordering events inside one run.

The regression test sits at that consumer boundary instead of the model. `AgentEventsWindowRowIdentityTests.keys rows by the globally unique event id` (same file as the store tests) reads the built body of the shipped window and pins the identity `ForEach` receives: `ForEach<ReversedCollection<Array<ControlAgentEvent>>, String, …>`. `String` is `ControlAgentEvent.id`; a `seq`-keyed window hands SwiftUI `Int`. It fails on `main` and passes with the fix.

## User Impact

Opening the debug Agent Events window after more than one agent run shows a stable, correctly attributed list: every row keeps its own identity instead of sharing one with an unrelated run. The window is debug-only, so no default user flow changes, and there is no config, storage, or protocol change.

## Evidence

**Real rendering on macOS.** The `agent-rows-proof.yml` workflow on `macos-latest` builds the package, boots the shipped `AgentEventsWindow` in a real `NSHostingView` with the real `AgentEventStore`, reads the AppKit accessibility tree, and records the window bitmap. Two runs append one event each (`seq=1` for both), then four each:

prs.title: fix(macos): don't check Off in Thinking/Verbose menu for sessions inheriting the agent default
prs.body:
Fixes #187607

## What Problem This Solves

In the macOS status-bar menu, a session that has not set its own Thinking/Verbose level inherits the agent default. The menu previously manufactured an "Off" checkmark for such sessions, misrepresenting the effective level.

## Why This Change Was Made

`StatusMenuSessions.swift` had two places that fell back a `nil` override to `"off"` when building or updating the Thinking/Verbose submenus. A `nil` value means "inherit the agent default", not "off", so this produced an incorrect check.

## User Impact

Sessions inheriting the agent default now show no item selected in their Thinking/Verbose submenus instead of a misleading "Off" check. Explicitly configured sessions are unaffected.

## Evidence

This is a macOS-only AppKit change. A new regression test in `apps/macos/Tests/OpenClawIPCTests/StatusMenuSummariesTests.swift` exercises the exact reported symptom: it builds the session submenu from a fixture whose session has no `thinkingLevel`/`verboseLevel`, then asserts neither the Thinking (`session.thinking`) nor the Verbose (`session.verbose`) submenu has any item checked. The fixture path goes through `configureSessionItem` → `buildPreferenceMenu` (fresh menu) and is the same path used by `updatePreferenceMenu`. Before this change the fixture session would have had "Off" checked; after it, no item is selected.

Transparency note: this host is Linux, which cannot compile or run the Swift test suite, and the CI `macos-swift` job does not run on ordinary `pull_request` events (the CI manifest short-circuits `run_macos_swift` to false for `pull_request`), so no live `swift test` output is available for this PR. The regression test above is authored to assert the exact reported symptom and is expected to pass under `swift test` on a macOS runner, but it has not been executed in this environment.

prs.title: chore: investigate Windows node exec pending in Code Mode (#176315)
prs.body:
Related: #176315

> **Investigation placeholder — intentionally draft, not ready for review or merge.** No implementation patch exists yet. The root cause and current-main reproduction remain unproven; no native Windows before/after result or passing regression is claimed.

## What Problem This Solves

A Windows-node command submitted through Code Mode can remain pending without returning native output, an exit status, or an actionable failure, even when discovery and native Codex session listing succeed.

## User Impact

The intended outcome is for remote Windows commands to return their actual output and exit status, or a truthful denial, timeout, cancellation, or unknown-outcome result. There is no delivered behavior change yet. Authorization and unknown-outcome safeguards must remain intact; uncertain requests must not be replayed automatically.

## Why This Change Was Made

Issue #176315 reports this failure with a Linux Gateway and native Windows node running OpenClaw 2026.10.4. The failing owner has not been identified, so this draft deliberately does not propose a speculative repair.

The next step is one bounded, harmless absolute-path `codex.exe --version` probe in an isolated paired environment, using normal supported approvals. Correlate the Code Mode bridge request with exec entry, preparation, approval disposition, node invocation, native process completion, terminal-result acceptance, and Code Mode continuation. Only then select the smallest fix at the responsible boundary.

## Evidence

**Completed investigation — source analysis, not native execution:**

- Read the report and complete comments, traced the execution and result-return owners, and compared release `383c124cc32f` with inspected main `76985e4c31c4`.
- The release sets `bridgeDispatchStarted` before `runBridgeRequest`; it does not establish that exec or a Windows process started. [Release source](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/blob/383c124cc32ffee3f8e56f549b88da94d269a4af/src/agents/code-mode-state.ts#L570-L573).
- Last confirmed incident boundary: an outstanding Code Mode `bridge:callValue`. First unconfirmed boundary: entry into the nested exec implementation and node-target resolution. Later execution and return stages remain unconfirmed for that request.
- Compared #168523 (headless approval delivery), #104798 (bare-name allowlist precheck), PR #166140 (open at the October 29 inspection) (Windows shell-wrapper policy), and merged PRs #175949 and #128440 (Code Mode lifecycle repairs). Similar symptoms do not establish a shared cause or prove that this report is fixed.

**Required before this can become an implementation PR:**

- [ ] Verify actual Gateway/node builds, Node versions, transport, capabilities, and effective approval policy in the isolated test environment.
- [ ] Capture the bounded native Windows failure and its first stalled boundary; reconcile the request before any control or retry.
- [ ] Compare the equivalent supported direct node-exec path with Code Mode, keeping policy and command equivalent.
- [ ] Add a regression that fails on the base and passes with the owner-correct repair.
- [ ] Capture native Windows before/after stdout and exit delivery; verify relevant denial, error, cancellation, and disconnect cases.
- [ ] Complete targeted tests, typecheck, lint/format, and independent review; replace this draft's pending statements with exact results.

Native Windows access and an isolated paired Gateway were unavailable in the investigating session. No implementation tests were run, and no production service, approval policy, or unrelated session was changed.

Reported by @ceo633 in [#176315](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/issues/176315).

- Implementation and verification: pending; no implementation session or patch exists yet.

prs.title: perf(plugins): avoid repeated registry index work
prs.body:
Related: https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/issues/188252

## What Problem This Solves

Cold provider-registry indexing reads and normalizes each canonical ID twice, then builds temporary arrays and a set to combine its aliases.

## User Impact

No intended behavior change. Canonical IDs, aliases, hook aliases, registry order, current-call eligibility and mutation invalidation retain their existing contracts.

## Why This Change Was Made

Reuse the normalized ID and append references directly to the existing index. Rows arrive in order, so comparing the last stored position prevents duplicate references within a row while preserving colliding providers. No cache, API, package or option is added. The production diff is +10/-8 lines; tests are unchanged.

## Acceptance Rule Before Measurement

Use the existing committed provider-registry selection/model-normalization workload at the pinned base and exact head, with cold registry generations and identical inputs/results. Measure canonical ID reads and normalization work; expected cold reads are 2P to P for P provider rows, while unrelated warm reads remain zero. Temporary reference-set construction is removed from the row loop. Preserve ordered lookup results, eligibility changes and registration/rollback/copy invalidation.

This is operation-count evidence, not a latency, RSS or allocation-byte claim. Timing comparisons, if collected, require at least five interleaved baseline/head pairs with load and spread recorded. Do not infer speed from a cold/warm imbalance.

## Evidence

- The existing committed warm-normalization case passed on both source bounds under explicit Node workers with maintained Vitest V8 precise coverage (`callCount: true`). Each arm creates the same two-provider cold registry and performs the same four lookups.

| Workload metric | Base | Head |
| --- | ---: | ---: |
| Total provider-ID normalizer calls | 14 | 12 |
| Index lookups | 4 | 4 |
| Cold row-loop executions | 2 | 2 |
| Per-row temporary reference-set statement executions | 2 | 0 (statement removed) |
| Unrelated metadata reads during warm lookups | 0 | 0 |

The stable outputs and existing warm-read assertion passed in both arms. Coverage attributes the two removed normalizer calls to reuse of the two canonical row IDs. Set counts come from the executed construction statement, not allocation-byte measurement. Profiling used identical committed inputs and isolated cold registry generations; no latency, RSS or allocated-byte improvement is inferred from the two diagnostic wall times.

- Three complete selection, runtime-hook provenance and thinking-policy suites passed: 58 tests in 24.70 seconds. These include alias/ID collisions, current-call eligibility, registration/rollback/copy invalidation and generation replacement.
- Targeted lint and production-core types passed in 3.00s and 9.42s. Formatting, syntax, whitespace and normal signed hooks passed.
- Fresh independent full-range review of the exact commit found no actionable correctness or security findings. No source changed after review; temporary profile overlays were restored and verified clean.
- Broad current-head PR CI remains required before landing. No live provider or performance timing claim is made.

prs.title: perf(ui): reduce work when opening large slash menus
prs.body:
## What Problem This Solves

Large slash-command menus do unnecessary per-option rendering work, and chat micro-interactions lacked a repeatable cross-engine census.

## User Impact

Slash menus retain their appearance and keyboard behavior while using less main-thread CPU. The new opt-in benchmark covers 20 chat action flows with 400-message transcripts, 1,000 sessions, 200 plugin commands, and 50 mentionable people.

## Why This Change Was Made

The menu constructs a reactive SVG subtree for every option even though the artwork is immutable. The renderer now reuses the existing icon-mask helper: a 253-option menu now creates zero SVG elements rather than 253. The existing 12 px size, 1.5 stroke, menu classes, lazy boundary, and content owner remain. No new application state, cache owner, dependency, or CSS request.

The harness verifies the actual UI effects: full copied text, rewind/edit/resubmit, failed-send retry/discard, fork destination, filtered mention selection, transcript search and restored focus, decoded pasted/dropped images, tool disclosure, terminal lifetime, split panes, and keyboard session selection. Settled messages expose rewind/fork rather than direct edit/delete/retry; mobile split creation is unavailable and explicitly skipped.

## Evidence

Twenty paired runs per cell reduce task CPU by 8.8–12.1% across Chromium desktop/mobile at 1×/4×. CPU p95 improves in every cell and the A/A CPU controls remain near flat. All 360 repeated observations retained surviving transcript row nodes (zero replacements); menu option SVG counts were consistently 253 on base/A/A and zero on head. Several absolute frame/long-task targets and the existing mobile composer shift remain unmet; the tables retain them.

Acceptance rule set before measurement: ten serial interleaved pairs, extended to twenty on the loaded host; a CPU gain of at least 5%, no material affected-metric regression, and A/A controls. Chromium uses main-thread thread-tick CPU. WebKit wall time is untraced; its separate Inspector timeline reports elapsed attribution, never CPU utilization. These are renderer measurements with synthetic Gateway responses, not live Gateway/provider latency.

The row-mutation probe observes only the active transcript, excluding composer/menu mutations. Earlier broad-observer timings were discarded. Input timing is native event-handler entry to next rAF callback, excluding input queueing and that frame’s subsequent layout/paint; it is not INP.

### Repeated slash-menu workload

On the baseline at mobile 4×, expanding completed work left tool rows outside the virtualizer window and the tool-toggle setup timed out. The shared setup now verifies expansion and scrolls the work header back into view before locating the nested controls. prs.title: fix(models): keep the model list when one plugin-owned provider lacks a credential
prs.body:
## Problem

`models.list` fails as a whole when one plugin-owned provider (`authScope: "plugin"`) has no live credential. Ambient credential discovery calls the provider's plugin-owned auth for every synthetic-auth provider, and that call throws `Plugin-owned auth for provider "<id>" is unavailable: live credential or no-auth evidence is missing`. The error escapes the catalog run, so no models come back for any provider.

Observed on a live install: after a restart, every `models.list` failed with this error for `typesafe`. A Particle key added through the add-provider dialog then showed no models. Particle itself was fine: it is enabled by default and its models come from its manifest catalog. The request never returned a list.

#188541 scoped the dialog warning to per-provider listing outcomes. It does not cover this case, because no outcomes come back when the request throws.

## Fix

`resolveAmbientAgentCredentialsForDiscovery` and `prepareAmbientAgentCredentialsForDiscovery` now skip a provider whose plugin-owned auth is unavailable (`ProviderAuthError` `missing-provider-auth` for that same provider). Other errors still propagate. Catalog availability already reports such a provider per model as `missing-auth` (`model-catalog-decisions.ts`), so the provider shows as unavailable instead of hiding every other provider.

## User impact

One misconfigured or credential-less plugin provider no longer empties the model picker and Models page for everyone. Its own models show as unavailable.

## Proof

- New test in `src/agents/model-auth.plugin-scope.test.ts`: with a plugin-owned provider and no active credential, both discovery functions return without that provider instead of throwing. It fails on `main` with the same error the live install logged.
- `pnpm test src/agents/model-auth.plugin-scope.test.ts --maxWorkers=1`: 35 tests pass, about 20 s wall time.
- Related suites pass: agent model discovery auth, external CLI discovery, synthetic auth discovery, `models.list` provider outcomes, prepared runtime sources, catalog worker pool.
- `pnpm check:changed` passes.

No overlap with Pash/Sarah changes.

## Merge danger

Two-way door: a revert fully undoes it. No state, config or contract change. Blast radius: model catalog discovery for installs with plugin-owned providers.

prs.title: perf(ui): defer hidden long-tail page rendering and add route census
prs.body:
Draft while repeated performance qualification and final three-surface captures finish. Source checks and independent review passed; this is not ready to merge.

## What Problem This Solves

Large Skills and settings inventories do rendering work for rows and editors that are not visible. Apps discovery also inserts a long catalog above the platform cards after the page appears, moving those cards thousands of pixels.

## User Impact

Skills uses the existing keyed catalog window; closed configuration objects create their descendants on first opening and retain editors afterward so drafts survive. Plugin Settings contains offscreen rows. Secrets shares one locale-aware date formatter per table and mounts row menus on first use. Apps reserves a bounded, scrollable discovery region while leaving unavailable catalogs collapsed. The shared catalog initially mounts 24 natural-flow cards, extending that prefix when needed to preserve the focused card and next row before measurement. Existing tags, selectors, navigation, domain owners, and lazy routes stay intact.

## Why This Change Was Made

The new reusable page census extends the existing Chromium/WebKit harness to all 56 canonical route IDs: 49 measured pages, two redirects, and five explicit active-owner exclusions. The synthetic Gateway-shaped inventories cover first visit after boot, a primary action, and departure at desktop/mobile, Chromium 1×/4× and WebKit. The fixes address the largest observed rendering costs rather than add another state or caching owner.

## Evidence

One-pair census runs rank costs; serial interleaved base/head/base-control runs qualify the changed owners. The shared host is noisy, so the qualification records renderer task CPU, structural counts, median/p95, and A/A controls. These are browser-rendering measurements, not live Gateway or provider latency.

| Proof | Result |
| --- | --- |
| Configuration browser regression | 24 passed; initially closed descendants absent, opened editor drafts retained |
| Catalog and Skills focused unit tests | 33 passed |
| Grid and Skills browser proof | 21 passed across Chromium/WebKit; keyboard traversal, final rows, notices, details and filtering |
| Secrets tests | 3 passed |
| Apps layout regression | Original CSS fails desktop/mobile; fixed CSS passes 2 Chromium + 2 WebKit cases, with final-row reachability and unavailable-catalog collapse |
| UI and scripts typecheck; scoped lint/format | Passed |
| Final build and production Knip | Passed for candidate `2270d99ae0a` |
| Independent local reviews | No actionable P0–P2 findings |
| Solid refactor checklist | In the four changed TSX renderers, each counted pattern stays 0 → 0: rendering controllers, effects/render effects, untrack, direct listeners, DOM queries, string-class composition, flush, and owner APIs |
| Strict asset check | Passed; measured raw-CSS cap adjustment below |
| Full route census | 1,764 untraced + 588 traced measurements passed; final Apps/Skills/Plugins refresh pending |
| Changed-owner qualification | PENDING |

Earlier-checkpoint mobile 4× Secrets qualification used 20 interleaved base/head/A/A triplets: renderer task median 1,253.23 → 1,131.23 ms; p95 1,547.59 → 1,315.44 ms. The paired CPU median was −12.34%; candidate versus A/A control was −14.72%, faster in all 20 pairs. The control itself varied, so this is not a precise wall-latency claim. That same earlier run found no demonstrated change in Plugins overview: task medians 685.21 → 688.07 ms, control 686.98 ms. Final-candidate timing verdicts remain pending until the new immutable-bundle census and qualification finish.

### Assets and size

| Surface | Base | Final build |
| --- | ---: | ---: |
| Startup JS gzip | 88,758 B | 88,749 B |
| Startup JS raw | 277,716 B | 277,716 B |
| Startup JS requests | 3 | 3 |
| Startup CSS gzip | 33,568 B | 33,568 B |
| Startup CSS requests | 1 | 1 |
| Total CSS gzip | 309,033 B | 309,163 B |
| Total CSS raw | 1,598,079 B | 1,598,572 B |
| Affected production UI LOC | 3,438 | 3,486 |
| Tests/config LOC | 1,049 | 1,325 |
| Benchmark/tooling LOC | 1,640 | 3,464 |
| Docs/baseline LOC | 786 | 809 |

The 9 B startup gzip difference from the original base is build variance; raw bytes and request counts are unchanged. The startup baseline retains the previous measured 88,753 B; the final build is 4 B lower, also within variance. Total CSS adds 130 B gzip and 493 B raw for containment and Apps layout stability. The raw-CSS ceiling is the measured 1,598,572 B plus its existing 64 B margin (1,598,636 B); the gzip ceiling is unchanged. This uses the campaign's allowance for measured rendering improvements. LOC counts cover every changed file against `bdb7d4ad4afb` through final candidate `2270d99ae0a`; reports and evidence artifacts are excluded from the commit.

Comparing the previous Apps bundle with the final 24-card bundle, all 134 emitted CSS groups and 2,470 of 2,472 JS groups match after normalizing emitted asset hashes and exact build identity. The two differences are the grid-containing `plugin-card` chunk and generated service-worker metadata. No JS/CSS logical groups were added or removed. This bounds the proof that must be refreshed to the shared grid's Apps/Skills/Plugins consumers; it does not turn older timing results into final-head measurements.

### Visual proof and full tables

The unchanged Advanced and Secrets layouts are shown below. Final Apps/Skills/Plugins captures and links to the complete per-context phase tables are pending.

![Advanced settings before and after](https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/81bfbbf5-f767-43e0-8641-46673e20e389)

![Secrets editor before and after](https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/3c1b540f-5583-4de3-9bf6-4f8ba5d3b36c)

WebKit traced elapsed script/style/layout attribution is separate from untraced timings. Unsupported WebKit CPU, long-task and CLS metrics remain unavailable rather than zero.

### Remaining limits

The absolute targets remain explicit: longest task ≤50 ms at 1×/≤200 ms at 4×, zero CLS, and WebKit/Chromium ≤1.3× (browser-local readiness for visits/departures; driver-inclusive wall time for actions). A relative win does not imply the absolute target is met. Shared shell geometry, independent Systems telemetry arrival, and native-only actions are identified in the tables. Board, Usage, Chat, New Session/boot/readiness and Logs remain with their active owners. No lease or live service was used.

prs.title: fix(doctor): abort stalled recovery inventories and restore service
prs.body:
Related #187900 #178359

## What Problem This Solves

Standalone `doctor --fix` can leave its managed Gateway stopped while waiting forever for a plugin's pre-repair backup inventory.

## User Impact

A stalled read-only inventory now observes the existing ten-minute capture deadline. If the original-state capture fails, standalone Doctor refuses repair and restores the service it stopped, including suspended Windows task autostart, with backup and retry guidance. Fast preparation and the update driver's existing optional-capture policy are preserved.

## Why This Change Was Made

The capture timer previously only aborted a signal: plugin inventory did not observe it, and fresh shared-state snapshot preparation did not receive it. Capture failures also returned warnings that allowed standalone repair to proceed. This change propagates cancellation through fresh and reused inventories, keeps the deadline alive while waiting, and refuses unbacked standalone repair. Only the contractually read-only inventory callback is raced; admitted native capture work still settles before service restoration.

Mandatory capture also needs to preserve the orphan rows Doctor is supposed to repair. Under existing exclusive custody of a closed, checkpointed SQLite source, ordinary original capture now uses the existing private raw-copy producer and retains foreign-key findings with a warning. Physical quick checks still refuse corruption; explicit full verification, generic rollback, and durable journal/WAL acquisition retain strict checks. These original images carry no clean generation receipt or automatic restoration authority.

The reported Windows native stack remains unknown. Source also corrects the report's bracket: task suspension happens during stop preparation; `beginMutation()` only disables early recovery. The disabled task therefore does not independently prove that `prepareRepair()` had started. This PR fixes a deterministic never-settling inventory path, without claiming to fix synchronous or unkillable kernel I/O stalls.

## Evidence

- RED on the original owners: inventory cancellation never settles; managed preparation hangs on timeout and permits repair after capture failure. The fast control passes.
- GREEN: focused regression proves timeout/failure refuse preparation, restore task autostart, restart the fake managed service, and verify health; fast preparation remains successful. Late inventory results cannot admit later resources.
- Landlock + Bubblewrap host-contained production `prepareRepair()` proof: a 33,607,680-byte synthetic agent database and all 13 declared plugin payloads were captured, sealed, and verified in 9.665 s of test time (49.90 s wrapper including cold test compilation). No live Gateway, service units, containers, or operator state were used.
- 135 unique focused tests pass across the changed owners and affected siblings. The corrected backup owner passes 37/37 (86.18 s wrapper); all 15 schema-flow consumer cases pass and verify that original capture retains the damaged rows; reuse passes 9/9 (93.29 s wrapper), including native cancellation settlement. Targeted noEmit types, formatting, and diff checks pass. Targeted lint passed before the final malformed-callback guard and archive correction; exact-head CI supplies final broad lint/build proof. No full local product build or published-driver upgrade was run; the earlier lint wrapper automatically prepared SDK declarations.
- First-head CI run 41167390016 exposed four schema-flow failures caused by this PR's mandatory capture. The correction identifies the installation in those standalone fixtures and preserves relational evidence before repair; physical corruption still fails capture. Final-head CI results are recorded below.
- Fresh independent shared autoreview, Codex P0–P2, complete staged candidate against `c993c8f2a51a`: scoped-clean, zero findings (final source verification complete). The index-only orphan-repair finding from the preceding review was addressed by staging the correction with the refusal. Platform-specific native stalls were not reproduced by review.
- Simplification: existing cancellation, snapshot, and recovery owners; no new manager, schema, or public configuration. Production growth +64 lines; net regression growth +216 lines, exactly allocated for inventory cancellation/late results, managed-service failure/fast controls, and original-image integrity. The growth in the backup owner is needed to preserve damaged original data while refusing unsafe repair.

prs.title: fix(dns): publish CoreDNS config atomically so failed writes keep the operator's files
prs.body:
## What Problem This Solves

Fixes #184888. `openclaw dns setup --apply` rewrote the operator's existing CoreDNS `Corefile`, the generated `.server` files, and the zone bootstrap through a truncating in-place write: `fs.writeFileSync` directly on the final path, or `sudo tee` (which also truncates) for root-owned paths. An ENOSPC, crash, or kill between truncation and write completion left the operator's CoreDNS configuration empty or partial, with no recovery copy anywhere — the file lives outside OpenClaw's state directory, so OpenClaw held none.

## User Impact

An operator running wide-area discovery DNS setup on a host that already runs CoreDNS could lose their entire CoreDNS configuration to a mid-write failure, breaking LAN-wide DNS resolution until the file was restored by hand. With this change, a failed or interrupted publication leaves the previous `Corefile` byte-for-byte intact, no longer restarts CoreDNS on a failed path, and the command reports the failure instead of silently proceeding.

## Why This Approach

Publication goes through the repo's atomic-write convention (`@openclaw/fs-safe` `replaceFileAtomicSync`): a same-directory staged file + rename, fsynced, parent dir synced. Root-owned paths fall back to a privileged staged publish. The already-safe zone publisher (`replaceWideAreaZoneFile`) is unchanged.

### Review findings, addressed one by one

Round 1 (reviewed head `5b0061eb`):

- **[P2] Resolve file symlinks before invoking the atomic publisher** — fixed. `resolvePublicationTarget` walks the destination's symlink chain (bounded at 32 hops, dangling links included) to the final target before publication, restoring the plain write's follow-the-link semantics while leaving the operator's link in place. A dangling link resolves to its missing target, which the plain write would have created. Regressions: `publishes through a symlinked Corefile to its managed target`, `creates a dangling Corefile link's target like the plain write did`.
- **[P2] Preserve ownership on the ordinary atomic path** — fixed. A rename publishes a new inode, so the staged file receives the operator's uid/gid before it replaces theirs. Setting a group outside the invoking account's memberships fails EPERM, which the publication router treats as a permission failure and re-runs through the privileged path (which chowns under sudo) — privilege is used only when necessary.
- **[P1] Create privileged staging files privately before writing content** — fixed. The privileged path creates the staging sibling exclusive and mode 0600 (`sudo install -m 600 /dev/null`) *before* any configuration byte exists, then `sudo tee`s into that existing private file, applies preserved uid/gid/mode, and renames. An interrupted publication can no longer leave restricted configuration readable by other local accounts.
- **[P2] Respect the operator's umask for newly created files** — fixed. Both publishers create fresh files with `0666 & ~process.umask()` (the plain write's contract) instead of a hardcoded 0644.
- **[P2] Narrow the mocked tee destination before writing it** — fixed in `5401ceca`: the destination element is guarded before `writeFileSync`.

Round 2 (reviewed head `5048abb1`):

- **[P1] Keep ordinary staging private until ownership is restored** — fixed in `5503e4e8`. The atomic writer now stages with mode 0600, so the configuration bytes are never readable by an account outside the operator's readership — not even in the window between writing them and publishing them. The operator's uid/gid and final mode are restored on the staged file immediately before the rename, so the published file still carries the operator's group. New regression observes the staged file at the ownership hand-off (the moment it holds the bytes) and requires it to still be 0600 there.
- **[P2] Flush privileged staging before publishing it** — fixed in `5503e4e8`. The privileged path flushes the staged file (`sudo sync`) before the rename and the parent directory after it, matching the ordinary publisher's durability: a crash after the rename cannot leave the published name pointing at missing or incomplete content. The regression asserts the flush order too.
- **[P2] Match the actual sudo tee command in the regression** — fixed in `5503e4e8`. The regression matched `" sudo tee "` against a joined command string that never carries that prefix, so the ordering assertion could not hold on any POSIX run. It now matches the structured executable and argument fields.
- **[medium] Verify staging confidentiality across the ownership transition** — the mechanism is fixed in `5503e4e8` (staging is 0600 from creation; the operator's group is applied only after the bytes are staged and immediately before the rename). The new regression asserts the staged file is still 0600 at the ownership hand-off, which is exactly the point where the bytes exist and the operator's group has not yet been applied.
- **Low-value test scaffolding** — the privileged simulator is no longer unused: `publishes through the privileged path when ownership hand-off is refused` forces a real POSIX refusal (a group the invoking account cannot set, modeled by an EPERM chown that unprivileged CI cannot arrange) into the privileged path end to end, asserting the private-staging order (`install -m 600` before `tee`), the flush before the rename, restored metadata (mode 0640), staging cleanup, and the published content.
- **Data-model compatibility** — this change touches no config, state, or database schema. The compatibility surface is the operator's on-disk CoreDNS configuration, and the regressions pin it: an existing Corefile keeps its mode, ownership, and group; a symlinked Corefile keeps its link and updates its managed target; a dangling link still creates its target; fresh files keep umask-sensitive creation; the zone publisher is untouched. The already-safe zone publisher and its boundary tests are unchanged.

## Evidence

- Red on base / green on fix: on `main`, an injected ENOSPC during Corefile publication left the Corefile truncated mid-import-line (the issue's damage scenario); with the fix the previous bytes survive and CoreDNS is not restarted.
- POSIX regressions (this PR's CI ubuntu + macOS shards): mode preservation (0640 stays 0640), private staging until the ownership hand-off, symlinked-Corefile publication to the managed target, dangling-link target creation, and the forced-privileged-path publication.
- Windows host note: the development host cannot execute the POSIX-only regressions locally — Windows has no POSIX mode semantics, so `fchmod` on the staged file fails with EPERM and the whole command routes to the privileged path on this host, and NTFS drops the group/other bits the mode assertions check. Those regressions are therefore verified in this PR's CI; the platform-neutral suite passes locally (7 passed, 5 POSIX-skipped).
- Checks: `pnpm vitest run src/cli/dns-cli.test.ts src/infra/widearea-dns.test.ts src/infra/widearea-dns.boundary.test.ts` (22 passed on the main-platform shards; 2 POSIX-only zone tests skip on Windows), `oxfmt --check`, `oxlint`, `tsgo:core`, the cli test-typecheck config, and both ratchets (assertion-safety baseline shrunk shrink-only, test-lines within ceiling) — all clean locally; the full matrix runs in CI.

Environment limitation, stated plainly: no macOS host is available here (WSL disk image broken, Docker daemon down), so shipped-CLI traces come from this PR's CI runs (ubuntu + macOS shards) of the real CLI registration harness rather than a local macOS terminal recording. If a maintainer wants a specific live trace (for example the `sudo brew services restart coredns` interaction or a second local account reading the staged sibling), I can try to arrange it, but the in-repo CI coverage above exercises every publication path the command owns.

prs.title: fix(cron): scheduled runs fail after a tool error the model recovered from
prs.body:
## What Problem This Solves

Fixes: a scheduled run whose tool call fails, and which then keeps working and ends with `NO_REPLY`, is recorded as failed with a synthetic "⚠️ <Tool> failed" result. Repeated recovered runs count toward the failure streak and can trigger failure alerts, owner repair requests and auto-disable for a job that is working.

## User Impact

User impact: a scheduled job that recovers from a tool error and deliberately stays quiet records `ok`, the same as a chat turn. Runtime failures still fail the run: aborts, provider and runtime errors, timeouts, denied commands and delivery failures keep their existing fatal paths.

## Why This Change Was Made

`buildEmbeddedRunPayloads` respected an intentional `NO_REPLY` after a tool error everywhere except scheduled runs, where it appended a tool-failure warning instead (unless a message-tool send was proven). The cron outcome then treated that warning as fatal. Code was overriding the model's own judgement of a run it had already finished.

This matches the direction of #170267: run status comes from structured runtime results, not from inferring task failure. That PR stopped treating the model's blocker prose as failure; this one stops treating a tool error the model recovered from as failure. The cron exclusion (`isCronTrigger`) is removed, so `NO_REPLY` is respected the same way in all runs. Aborted runs still report the tool failure.

## Evidence

- Production: an hourly stock check failed `view_image` on a screenshot, continued, wrote its report and ended with `NO_REPLY`; the run was recorded as error "⚠️ View Image failed".
- New cron regression in `run.meta-error-status.test.ts`: a failed `view_image` followed by a silent final on an announce job records `ok` through the real outcome path.
- New QA scenario `cron-recovered-tool-error` (mock-openai, real Gateway): the model reads a missing file, receives the tool error and ends with `NO_REPLY`. Two runs of an owned job and two runs of an unowned announce job all record `ok`, deliver nothing, send no failure alert and request no owner repair; both jobs keep `consecutiveErrors: 0`. The scenario also asserts the model received the failed read output in each run.
- QA suite on the PR head (mock-openai, `--concurrency 1`): `cron-recovered-tool-error`, `cron-blocked-outcome`, `cron-failed-tool-terminal-finalization` and `cron-send-then-continue` all pass (4/4). `cron-failure-repair-owner-conversation` fails identically on unmodified `main` ("the repair turn is not in the owner session transcript"); its job fails through a provider error, a path this change does not touch.
- Removed tests that encoded the old rule (scheduled `NO_REPLY` after a read failure must warn; invisible message-tool send still warns in cron). The aborted-run case is kept.
- Local: 322 tests across the payloads, cron isolated-agent, auto-reply and chat dispatch suites pass; oxfmt and oxlint are clean on changed files.

Net change in production code: the cron-only branch and its two delivery-evidence imports are removed. The mock-openai scheduled-job planners now dispatch from one sibling module, so the oversized `server.ts` shrinks.

Fixes Gateway startup crash loops when a pre-v8 shared-state database retains OpenClaw’s worker-environment lookup index. Startup fails with `OpenClaw v7 worker placement schema has unsupported attached objects` before the listener binds.

Recognize that shipped index too; the existing migration rebuilds the table and canonical schema installation restores its indexes. Unknown attached objects still refuse migration.

The existing legacy Doctor regression now retains this index instead of dropping it during fixture setup. Simplification: reuse the existing migration owner and integration test; production +2/-1 lines, tests +1/-1 lines, no additional test cases or scaffolding.

prs.body:
## What Problem This Solves

Short Control UI actions were ranked by automation wall time, mixing WebKit input delivery and assertion waits with application work.

## User Impact

There is no user-visible UI change. Cross-engine reports now rank native-input-to-DOM-commit elapsed time while keeping driver and wall ratios visible.

## Why This Change Was Made

Related: #189013. The earlier ~260 ms cluster did not establish a shared timer. The harness now records the first trusted native action event, last observed DOM mutation/native value edit, and scenario/settle boundaries on one browser clock. Missing boundaries remain unranked. The report and JSON headline use application elapsed time.

This is a DOM-commit proxy, not CPU or paint latency. Focus work can precede the first action event; compound typing/navigation retains driver gaps between inputs. The probe adds a scenario-end RPC, so instrumented wall times must not be called speedups over old uninstrumented runs. Navigation/reload and memory measurements retain their existing probes.

## Evidence

| Check | Result |
| --- | --- |
| Both-engine native boundary contracts | 8/8 passed: mutations, native value-only edits, no input, untrusted input |
| All 22 cluster rows, pilot | 44/44 observations passed |
| Full paired census | Running: 20 Chromium/WebKit pairs per row plus interleaved A/A slots; final table will be added before landing |

Source maps lead to the existing virtual-window measurements. The traces do not establish a flush for every row, so no speculative batching was added. No product speedup is claimed.

prs.title: fix(doctor): avoid false Discord and LINE recovery warnings
prs.body:
Fixes #180960

## What Problem This Solves

Doctor and update recovery inventories report unknown migration coverage for Discord's disposable command cache and LINE's core-captured queue rows.

## User Impact

Operators no longer receive unnecessary backup guidance for these migrations. The disposable Discord cache adds no captured resources, and warnings for genuinely undeclared plugin resources remain intact. Older recovery copies are unchanged.

## Why This Change Was Made
