Reds 2 to 12 each change one line of this head's production code (one `perl` substitution each, every result exit 1; failing tests by name):

| # | Change | Failing tests |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 2 | slice budget counts `event_json.length` (string length) | budgets slices by decoded payload bytes |
| 3 | slice byte column put back to stored size, `coalesce(octet_length(event_zstd), octet_length(event_json))` | budgets slices by decoded payload bytes |
| 4 | the read after the batch transaction without `runWithSessionTranscriptReadFence` | fence (changed: true) |
| 5 | batch threshold set to the 2 MiB slice budget instead of `MAX_SNAPSHOT_BYTES` | incremental after the batch (changed: false, true) |
| 6 | the read after the batch transaction rethrows `SessionTranscriptColdError` | archived after the batch deferred it, cold |
| 7 | context version compare ignores `transcript_updated_at` | rereads when the transcript changes; incremental after the batch (changed: true) |
| 8 | batch head never reused | incremental after the batch (changed: false) |
| 9 | `JSON.parse` inside the slice's transaction | parses outside the read transaction; incremental after the batch (changed: false, true) |
| 10 | no slice budget (one slice) | one slice per transaction; rereads; budgets; incremental export; incremental after the batch (changed: false, true) |
| 11 | first slice ignores the head's `afterSeq` | incremental export; incremental after the batch (changed: false, true) |
| 12 | slice query ignores the head's `throughSeq` | fence (changed: false, true) |

The memory batch tests call `prepareSessionMemoryEntries` directly; the transactions they count include the engine-neutral read snapshot (`runSqliteReadSnapshotSync`) the batch runs in, and a mock around `readTranscriptStatsBatchFromDatabase` counts statistics reads (one when the batch head is reused, two when it is read again). The fence test anchors the admission at `entry-2` and appends two 2.5 MiB rows after it. The incremental test prepares a 3 MiB transcript (above the slice budget, within 4 MiB: one batch transaction), appends about 2 MiB so it passes 4 MiB, and prepares it again: batch transaction plus two, exactly one parsed payload, the earlier content kept, both untouched and with the update time bumped after the batch transaction. The budget test seeds two zstd rows and three plain rows of 250 CJK characters, sets the budget to the smallest decoded payload of those five rows, asserts each row's stored size (zstd) or string length (CJK) stays below it, and asserts each of the five ends its own slice.

With the change: 12 passed (above).

### Other checks

| Check | Result |
| --- | --- |
| `git diff --check` against the base | exit 0 |
| `pnpm exec oxfmt --check` on the six changed source and test files and the two changed scripts | exit 0 |
| type-aware oxlint (`node scripts/run-oxlint.mjs`) on the six changed source and test files | exit 0 |
| `pnpm tsgo:core`, `pnpm tsgo:test:src` | exit 0 |
| line-cap, SQLite dialect, SQLite worker and mock-export ratchets, `lint:kysely`, `check:import-cycles`, `check:madge-import-cycles` | exit 0 |
| `db:worker-inventory:check` | exit 1, identically on a clean worktree of the base (`worker-access-inventory.md is stale`); regenerating the inventory there and on this branch differs only in three line-count cells (`session-accessor.sqlite-read.ts` twice, `session-memory-entry.worker.ts` once) |
| `check:max-lines-ratchet` | exit 1 on three `ui/` files this diff does not touch (`chat-message.test.tsx`, `config-page-state.ts`, `sessions-page-state.ts`) |

### Measured test cost

`pnpm test src/config/sessions/session-accessor.sqlite-read-hold.test.ts --maxWorkers=1`: 8.27 s Vitest duration, 10.04 s for the shard (host load averages about 28); the twelve tests take 0.05 to 0.86 s each. The PostgreSQL file: 0.37 s and 0.04 s for its two tests. CI seconds not measured.

## Gaps

- `STATE_DATABASE_READ_ADMISSION_INVALIDATED` is not reproduced and not fixed here. On this base the harness's close no longer overlapped an export on either side, so this run does not exercise a close during an export; no read was refused as invalidated on either side (`invalidated=0`). The seal lifecycle is #162085 territory and is untouched.
- Shared-state WAL checkpoint starvation and shared-state write stalls (#161439, #163748) are a different database and are not addressed.
- Decompression stays inside each slice's transaction (the same SQL decode function as before), so only parsing and projection leave it. Readers are still open for most of a back-to-back export, which is why the `TRUNCATE` probe improves much less than passive checkpoint completion.
- The batch transaction still reads the export statistics over the whole session (`readTranscriptStatsBatchFromDatabase`, which walks every row) for every transcript it reads the head of, including the ones it leaves to the sliced read. The after side logged one `slow SQLite transaction hold` line for the batch transaction in the pair run (1155 ms, before the round 0 line, so the first export) and one in the worker-memory run (1075 ms); the PASSIVE arms logged none.
- Transcripts above the 4 MiB retention limit are no longer read from the batch's SQLite snapshot: each is read after the batch transaction from its own, later snapshot (internally consistent through the version check). Transcripts within the limit, the only ones the cache retains, still share the batch snapshot as on main. Main's batch already returned each transcript as its own entry, and #170404 states that later transcript notifications catch writes after the pass snapshot; I found no consumer that compares entries of one batch with each other, but I did not audit every caller of `buildSessionEntries`.
- Transcripts within the 4 MiB limit are still decoded, parsed and projected inside the batch transaction, as on main, for a group of up to eight sources (the group bound #170404 records); this change does not shorten that hold and I did not measure it.
- The slices are tied together by the transcript context version (rewrite generation, highest raw seq, `transcript_updated_at`), not by one SQLite snapshot, and the same token also decides whether the batch's head is reused. A writer that changed stored rows below the fence without changing any of those three could let one read combine rows from two states, or reuse a head that no longer describes them. Every rewrite path I read changes one of them (`rotateTranscriptGenerationInTransaction` or `touchTranscriptMutationInTransaction` in the transcript store and suffix paths), and `SessionManager` writes already rely on the same token; payload re-encoding (`createTranscriptPayloadUpdater`) changes the stored form, not the decoded event. I did not audit every writer.
- Any append to the same session between two slices changes the raw seq, so that read falls back to the whole-transcript read in one transaction, with the base path's hold. How often that happens for an actively written session under real traffic is not measured; the harness writer appends to a different session.
- The 2 MiB budget is a fixed constant. A slice holds at most 2 MiB of payload text plus the one row that crosses the budget (a compressed row decodes to at most 4 MiB by the table's `CHECK`; a plain `event_json` row has no size check). A large transcript takes about 300 short transactions per export on this fixture instead of one.
- Warm exports of the large session through the memory batch are slower after the change: 2.7%, 2.5% and 1.5% in the three memory sets; in the pair, 3.3% slower (rounds 1 to 3, 1170.3 against 1133.3 ms) and 3.1% slower over the exports of the 20 s probe (1204 against 1168 ms); in the worker-memory run, 1.1% slower (1176.3 against 1163.3 ms). The sliced side runs about 300 short transactions per export, each with a read-only borrow and a context-version read; I did not profile which part costs the difference.
- With exports running, the writer's p99 append latency is higher after the change in all three PASSIVE repetitions (9.7 to 11.1 ms against 5.7 to 7.0 ms), and its mean append count is 5.8% lower (see Evidence). I did not profile this either.
- Under the TRUNCATE probe the writer completed 24% fewer appends after the change (567 against 743) while 2.7 times as many TRUNCATE checkpoints completed; not measured separately.
- PostgreSQL is not sliced: large transcripts are read in one snapshot as on main. The PostgreSQL proof is a statement-level test, not a load run with concurrent writers.
- The cap was enforced by a footprint supervisor on macOS, not by a Linux cgroup, so page-cache accounting and reclaim under a cgroup are not exercised. The test host has 512 GiB, so only the process was capped, not the host.

<details>
<summary>Further gaps</summary>

- Per-sync work is still proportional to the whole transcript for large sessions: the memory session entry keeps an incremental projection only for transcripts up to 4 MiB (`MAX_SNAPSHOT_BYTES` in `session-memory-entry.worker.ts`), so this fixture's session is decoded whole on every export, and one session-entry worker serializes behind it.
- The fenced reader (`loadTranscriptReadSnapshotSync`, used by hydration, `SessionManager` open and reload, the incognito history worker, the bundled session-memory hook capture, `loadTranscriptEventsSync` and `prepareTranscriptCommit`) still decodes and parses a whole transcript inside one read transaction, as on main. #171467 is about the memory session index, its hold was never measured, and `prepareTranscriptCommit` calls it inside an outer transaction where slicing releases nothing; it belongs in a follow-up with its own measurement.
- Readers that decode inside a writer or other outer transaction (`loadTranscriptEventsFromDatabase` callers in message cut, parent session, recovery, transcript mirror and incognito lifecycle; `prepareTranscriptCommit`) and `inspectTranscriptEventsSync` (Doctor one-shot) keep their in-transaction decode. Their writers need the decode and the rows to share one authoritative snapshot, and moving it is a write-path change that this PR does not need.
- The checkpoint probes use their own connection with `busy_timeout = 0` (`TRUNCATE`) or every 250 ms (`PASSIVE`); they measure whether a reader snapshot is open, not how the production checkpoint owner schedules work.
- The fixture is synthetic (random-word text, one large session). Compression ratio and decode cost on real transcripts differ; absolute milliseconds and MiB will differ on other hosts.
- #160386 also proposes delta ingestion in Memory Core (index only the events after the last indexed seq). This PR does not do that and does not reduce the total decode work of an export; it only bounds how long a read snapshot is held.

</details>

auto_merge.commit_title: fix(sessions): long transcripts pin a database read snapshot while being decoded (#164442)
auto_merge.commit_message:
* fix(sessions): parse transcript slices after their read transaction

- Whole-transcript export snapshots and fenced reads run as slices of at
  most 2 MiB of payload, one short deferred read transaction each
- Each slice selects payload text through the existing SQL decode
  expression; JSON.parse and projection run after the transaction closes
- The slice budget counts decoded payload bytes (transcriptEventReadBytesSql)
- Later slices continue only while the transcript context version is
  unchanged; otherwise the transcript is read in one transaction as before
- Keeps the incremental export rules (previous projection, afterEventSeq,
  no read when unchanged); reset-boundary projection stays in one transaction
- The memory export batch transaction keeps every transcript within the
  worker's existing 4 MiB retained-snapshot limit; larger ones are read in
  slices after it, with the same fence admission, incremental projection and
  cold handling
- Moves the export head into session-accessor.sqlite-export-head.ts
- Lists both new runtime modules in the PR wrapper inventory
- A transcript above the budget keeps the export head its batch transaction
  read; its sliced read reuses that head while the transcript context version
  is unchanged and re-reads it otherwise

* simplify: drop fenced-read slicing and the single-caller slice wrapper

- loadTranscriptReadSnapshotSync is back to the base: the hydration and SessionManager reader is outside #171467 (memory session indexing) and moves to a follow-up
- readTranscriptExportSnapshotReadOnlySync calls readTranscriptEventsInSlices directly; readTranscriptEventsInChunks and its two type aliases are gone
- prepareSessionMemoryEntries keeps deferred batch heads in their own map, so prepared keeps its base type and the unreachable "head" probe is gone
- hold test: fenced-read cases and the single-entry batch test (covered by the entry-order test) removed

* fix(sessions): keep PostgreSQL transcript exports on one read

- readTranscriptExportSnapshotsFromDatabase ignores deferAboveBytes on PostgreSQL
- memory export batch keeps large PostgreSQL transcripts in its read-only snapshot
- single exports on PostgreSQL read every payload in their first transaction, as on the merge base
- PostgreSQL conformance test: one read-only BEGIN, no advisory lock, one payload query

* simplify(sessions): fold the payload slice loop into the export slice reader

- session-transcript-payload-chunk.ts is gone: its only importer was session-accessor.sqlite-export-slices.ts, and its generic Database/Head callbacks served the fenced-read caller removed in b2c78b04f0e
- readTranscriptExportInSlices reads the head and slices directly; the 2 MiB budget lives next to transcriptEventReadBytesSql in session-transcript-read-bytes.ts
- readTranscriptExportSnapshotsFromDatabase records the context version in deferred, so TranscriptExportBatchHead and the worker's own version read are gone, and exports that are not deferred (all PostgreSQL exports) no longer read the version
- hold test: 16 cases to 12; the hand-built batch-head case, the UTF-16 store variant, the in-batch cold case, the first-slice corrupt-row case and the medium-transcript case are dropped or folded into the cases that guard the same boundary
- PostgreSQL test: no budget mock; two 2.5 MiB rows already split a sliced read at the real budget

---------

prs.title: fix(github): open reconnect flow from active sessions
prs.body:
## What Problem This Solves

When an agent's managed GitHub OAuth credential expires, `github_identity_status` can diagnose it but cannot open the reconnect flow from the active session. The operator has to find the agent's Tools settings manually.

## Why This Change

- Add a capability-negotiated `screen` action, `github_identity_settings`, that opens the current agent's Tools settings only in the requesting Control UI.
- Keep OAuth handling in the existing masked UI; no token, code, or callback data enters model context.
- Derive tool listings from session-stable capabilities, while reconnect guidance and Gateway routing honor current-client capabilities and effective tool/action policy.
- Retain manual Settings guidance when the reconnect action is not callable.
- Regenerate the compiled Gateway validator from its schema so the new command passes actual dispatch.

## User Impact

An active session can diagnose an expired GitHub identity, open the reconnect surface, and verify recovery without exposing credentials or losing the session.

## Evidence

- Merged current main `797540497ae53253adb5fa0581c2171389919cad` into the PR; conflict-resolution head `b12b31f213c5f2bc9c57974c35e504882cf5618e`.
- Resolved tool-registration and UI capability conflicts while retaining main's GitHub publication preview support and native-mobile UI-command exclusion. Regenerated the compiled Gateway validator from the combined schemas.
- 118 focused tests passed: 101 across Gateway dispatch, tool registration, prompt-prefix stability, identity status, and screen tools; 16 UI handshake tests; 1 UI navigation test.
- Added iOS/Android handshake regressions. Both fail when the native-mobile capability gate is removed and pass with the resolution.
- Core and UI TypeScript checks, focused lint/format, canonical Gateway validator freshness, and `git diff --check` passed.
- Auto Review completed with no P0/P1 findings. Conflict repair retains existing owners and introduces no new production abstractions.
- Broad CI must run on this new head; prior-head results are not current-head CI evidence. Browser E2E was not rerun for this conflict-only repair.

## Limits

This opens the existing operator-owned reconnect flow. It does not authorize GitHub access automatically or move OAuth handling into the model.

## What Problem This Solves

## User Impact

Internal test runtime improves. Production behavior, payload sizes, and user-facing contracts are unchanged.

## Why This Change Was Made

<!--

Keep the body short. Leave file lists, internal acronyms, and root-cause walkthroughs
in the diff or optional <details>; include technical detail only when it explains

-->

Use labeled native `Buffer.equals` assertions and lossless hex snapshots for complete-byte comparisons, following the mechanism in #188777 and #188823. All test cases and real I/O/process boundaries remain.

## Evidence

<!--
Show the most useful proof that this change works. Screenshots, screencasts,
terminal output, focused tests, CI results, live observations, redacted logs,
and artifact links are all useful. For user-visible UI changes, follow the root
AGENTS.md "Product and validation" screenshot completion/landing gate; these other
forms of evidence do not replace the required screenshots in chat AND the PR.

Reviewers will inspect the code, tests, and CI. Use this section to make the
validation easy to understand, not to restate the diff.
Summarize what was checked and the result; note meaningful gaps. Link long output
or put it in optional <details>, keeping the useful evidence summary visible.
-->

Three serial before and three serial after runs per retained file used `timeout 900 /usr/bin/time -v pnpm test <file> --maxWorkers=1 --reporter=verbose`, with the same private frozen dependencies, runtime, host, temp directory and cache. These are local Linux results using the native test router and pinned Bun fork; no CI-time improvement is claimed.

| File | Wall median before → after | Vitest median before → after | Body median before → after | Numeric equality callbacks before → after |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| iMessage runtime | 23.10 → 14.96s | 19.67 → 12.17s | 5.896 → 0.211s | 4,194,404 → 0 |
| Knowledge attachments | 31.35 → 26.72s | 28.56 → 24.17s | 17.055 → 13.620s | 2,102,754 → 402 |
| MCP relay UI tunnel | 5.11 → 2.43s | 3.56 → 0.919s | 2.862 → 0.398s | 2,228,281 → 131,105 |
| Playback staging | 9.76 → 8.33s | 7.49 → 5.57s | 2.773 → 0.094s | 2,097,193 → 3 |

Google lazy voice is **NOCHANGE and restored**: median file wall regressed from 10.72s to 12.99s despite a cheaper test body. Cold first runs are retained. Knowledge's first after run overlapped source-mirror preparation and is retained as confounded; the comparable after set is runs 2, 3 and 4. No product flake or failed benchmark run was observed.

All 11 converted assertions reject changed tail bytes or truncated data. Separate instrumentation, restored afterward, counted actual Vitest numeric equality callbacks while returning `undefined`: 10,491,122 callbacks disappear per complete four-file pass. No product work is removed.

Focused validation passes: target files, four sibling files (`send.test.ts`, `attachment-file.test.ts`, `control-ui.test.ts`, `playback-transcode.test.ts`), scoped strict typecheck, extension and playback type-aware lint, format, diff, line-cap/max-lines, assertion-safety, test-line, timeout and mock ratchets. The exact extension lint gate passed with 0 warnings and 0 errors in a source-verified rootless container limited to 4 CPUs / 8 GiB; the container is removed. An initial scratch typecheck had a Node-type resolution setup error; correcting its installed-type path passed. Two mutation diagnostics initially surfaced sanitized protocol errors/fallback rather than the original assertion labels; catch-and-rethrow diagnostics confirmed the intended byte assertions, and all instrumentation was restored.

`pr-simplify` is complete. Complete-source isolated Codex P0–P2 autoreview of base `9a3535b28ec5de2e5b50451882a11183c9ae272c` → the local candidate returned machine status **scoped-clean**, zero findings, with 34 intact target/owner/helper/sibling files. Commit `351b8df60bc92dfdef9e8f8f3329823c0652d67e` contains the identical reviewed and tested patch. Parent source review and native landing are complete.

Native tracked test LF remains 6,315,921. The effective cap remains 6,347,916 (scalar 6,320,000 + 199 inherited allocations totaling 27,916), preserving 31,995 slack. Test LF delta **0**, effective-cap delta **0**, production LF delta **0**; no allocation or baseline edits. The diff is 19 insertions / 19 deletions across four test files.

<details>
<summary>Retained behavioral contracts and overlap check</summary>

- iMessage: account-cap rejection without RPC, allowed default-account delivery, real file staging/readback, exact delivery count/order, receipt and client/state cleanup.
- Knowledge: independent disk/download/Git originals, Unicode, chunk continuation, schema/JSON framing, restart/search, 9 MiB scan-budget fixture, replay/interruption/tamper/authority/link cases.
- MCP: complete upload plus tail and varied download bytes, safe headers/cookies, chunk sizing/terminal frames, grants/revocation, websocket assembly/copy bounds and cleanup. The smaller 64 KiB websocket byte assertion remains unchanged.
- Playback: every byte read from the real staged input at the ffmpeg boundary, source identity mutations, rendition publication/type, writer close and post-use native input removal.

Fresh exact-path/basename open-PR searches and actual returned PR file lists found no target overlap. #186117 touches adjacent iMessage owners, which this patch does not edit. No case, helper, seam, or production behavior was deleted.

</details>

<details>
<summary>Complete per-run wall, Vitest, body, import, CPU and RSS measurements</summary>

All times are seconds. Body is the sum of verbose case durations; import is the reported slowest top-10 inclusive import total, which includes transform/dependency work and is not an additive stage. CPU is user/system; RSS is KiB.

prs.title: fix(doctor): settle missing retained originals onto verified survivors
prs.body:
Closes #179957

## What Problem This Solves

Fixes: `doctor --session-sqlite recover` defers duplicate-archive settlement forever when the historical original path is already missing, even though a byte-verified surviving archive exists — regardless of which duplicate the recovery happens to visit first. Earlier revisions of this change reported settlement without redirecting the affected receipts and accepted interrupted disposal claims as settled; this head repairs all three.

## User Impact

Offline recovery now reconciles historical archive references whose originals vanished: retained receipts are redirected onto the verified surviving archive and a following inspection is clean, instead of reporting `restored=0 ... reason: doctor recover completed with remaining issues` on every run. In the linked report, 6,420 missing references all had surviving archives matching the receipt size and SHA-256. Interrupted disposal still surfaces its failure and completes on the next recovery, exactly as before.

## Why This Change Was Made

Settlement required every non-disposed original to exist on disk, so a vanished original with `disposal.state='retained'` — which has nothing left to retire — deferred its references forever. Settlement records such originals explicitly and redirects their retained receipts through the manifest coalescing owner before reporting `historical_duplicate_settled`, so no persisted reference keeps the vanished path.

Two further repairs complete the behavior:

- Survivor selection now requires the survivor's own file to be present. Previously the first retained duplicate group was always the settlement destination, so a group ordered [vanished original, present byte-identical copy] tried to verify the vanished file and still deferred forever.
- The vanished-original handling is restricted to retained receipts. Pending-disposal claims (original already moved into its `.cleanup-` claim, unlink interrupted) keep their verification, selection, claim retirement, and completion requirements: their interruption still reports `historical_transcript_deferred` and the next recovery retires the claim and completes the redirection.

The "Archive was recreated after disposal" guard, the identity-mismatch deferral, and the durable disposal progress / manifest redirection contract of #155194 are unchanged.

## Evidence

Real CLI proof on isolated state (`OPENCLAW_STATE_DIR`, no credentials, localhost only): two byte-identical retained duplicate archives recorded in the shipped manifest format, then one original's file removed as in the linked report. Both orderings were run with fresh state; `<state>` redacts the state directory.

- Base `d8053dd5` (survivor visited first): `openclaw doctor --session-sqlite recover --json` reports `historical_transcript_deferred` twice for the vanished `duplicate.jsonl.imported-1` ("artifact is unexpectedly missing; original retained.") plus one restore-path deferral (`ENOENT ... imported-1`), `totals.issues = 3`; both manifests keep referencing the vanished path; a following `dry-run --json` keeps `totals.issues = 1`. This is the every-run deferral from #179957. (Vanished-first ordering on base is covered by the regression below: it reports three `historical_transcript_deferred` issues.)
- This branch, survivor visited first: `recover --json` reports `historical_duplicate_settled` ("Retired 1 byte-identical duplicate archive(s); rollback references now use the verified surviving originals."); both manifests' `plannedMoves`/`completedMoves` now reference only `duplicate.jsonl.imported-2` with `disposal: retained`; the survivor's SHA-256 is identical before/after (`b9f12b14…`); `dry-run --json` reports `totals.issues = 0`.
- This branch, vanished original visited first (fresh state, `duplicate.jsonl.imported-2` removed): `recover --json` reports `historical_duplicate_settled`; zero manifests reference the vanished path; both manifests' planned/completed receipts point only at `duplicate.jsonl.imported-1` with `disposal: retained`; `dry-run --json` reports `totals.issues = 0`.

Latest-stable upgrade compatibility (v2026.10.6 → this branch), same isolation:

- The published `openclaw@2026.10.6` package (npm, `OpenClaw 2026.10.6 (fe06181)`, node 24.22.1) reads the same state: `doctor --session-sqlite dry-run --json` loads the existing receipts and settings (`openclaw.json` with agent entries) and reports the unresolved deferral (`historical_transcript_deferred`, `totals.issues = 1`) — the every-run symptom.
- Switching the state to this branch (built from the current head): `recover --json` reports `historical_duplicate_settled`; `dry-run --json` reports `totals.issues = 0`; a repeated `recover --json` is a no-op (`totals.issues = 0`, no issue codes) — clean repeat recovery.
- No persisted data regressed: `openclaw.json` is byte-identical before/after (SHA-256 `85cf6e6c…`), the surviving archive is byte-identical (SHA-256 `b9f12b14…`), and zero manifests reference the vanished `duplicate.jsonl.imported-1` afterwards.
- Schema/model unchanged: no migration-manifest version, receipt, or artifact-format change in this PR; the stable release and this branch read and write the same shipped formats.

Regression coverage (`node scripts/run-vitest.mjs <file> --run`, node 24.19.0):

- `doctor-session-sqlite-recovery-inventory.test.ts`: the duplicate settlement regression now covers both orderings ("survivor-ordered-first" and "vanished-original-ordered-first") through the real recovery inventory and doctor recover — each asserts settled, coalesced references, persisted planned/completed receipts no longer containing the missing path, unchanged survivor bytes, and a clean dry-run. The vanished-first case is red without the survivor-selection change (three `historical_transcript_deferred` instead of settled) and the interrupted-disposal (injected-unlink) case is green; it was the `checks-node-changed-2` failure on the original head.
- `doctor-session-sqlite.missing-history-settlement.test.ts`: the plugin-repair consumer of duplicate settlement now expects the vanished older original to redirect onto its byte-identical survivor (`historical_duplicate_settled`, no completed move keeps the vanished path) instead of the previous deferral warning; it was the `checks-node-changed-4` failure on the previous head and is red on `main` behavior.
- Neighbors stay green: all 8 cases in the recovery file, 2 cases in `doctor-session-sqlite.missing-history-settlement.test.ts`, 4 cases in `doctor-session-sqlite.duplicate-lookup.test.ts` (unchanged from `main`; its earlier mocked missing-original duplicate was dropped in favor of the stronger end-to-end regression), and 48 cases across `retirement-mutations`, `retirement-disposal`, and `receipt-retirement`. Targeted strict typecheck of the changed files and their imports passes with the shard's compiler options (`noUncheckedIndexedAccess`).

Not run locally: full commands suite and the sharded native `tsgo` lanes (the native checker needs a newer glibc than this host); PR CI covers both.

Inherited CI failures on the previous heads, present at current `main` tip and outside this PR's changed files: `check-test-types-core-3` failed on `ui/src/pages/chat/components/chat-details-output-intent.test.tsx` (`TS2353 artifactsLoading` — the prop was removed from `chat-outputs.tsx` by #180031 `24b180b712f` without updating this test, which still uses it at `main` tip), and `check-lint` fails on a `max-lines` warning in `extensions/codex/src/app-server/native-subagent-inventory.test.ts` (1132 lines at `main` tip; this PR touches no `extensions/` or `ui/` files). The changed-files format/lint check for this PR's files reports 0 warnings/0 errors.

prs.title: test(qa-lab): check replayed history against a plugin tool under a core name
prs.body:
Closes #168610
Related: #101866

## What Problem This Solves

There is no production-boundary test showing that a non-bundled plugin tool registered under a core tool name cannot get its managed media paths replayed into a later turn's history as if a trusted core tool had produced them.

## User Impact

No user-visible change. QA Lab gains a scenario that fails when a plugin borrows a core tool's media trust through replayed channel history, and a mock-provider directive that lets scenarios script exact tool calls.

## Why This Change Was Made

The grounding change in #101866 decides media trust when a tool result is written and checks it when history is replayed. Its review asks for proof with an actual plugin under a core name, through the real writer, ending at the final model request. Two pieces were missing:

- The mock OpenAI provider could not be told to call a named tool with chosen arguments. `QA tool plan: {"calls":[{"name":"<tool>","args":{...}}],"reply":"..."}` in the current request now does that: each call in order, then the reply, with `{{media:N}}` replaced by the first media path the Nth call's result carried (structured media, a `MEDIA:` line, or a POSIX or drive-rooted Windows path in plain text). A call that Code Mode runs counts once its `wait` settles it: each output is read through `readScenarioToolCompletion`, and while the latest is a `waiting` receipt the server's existing Code Mode handling issues the `wait`. Calls go through the Tool Search dispatcher when the tool is not declared directly. A step the request cannot call replies `BUG-QA-TOOL-PLAN-UNDECLARED <name>`. Only results after the plan's own user turn count, and a plan quoted in history never starts.
- A channel that merges session history into the next prompt. QA Channel does not set `sessionTranscript`; Crabline Telegram runs the real Telegram plugin, which does.

`telegram-plugin-core-name-media-history` installs a run-owned, non-bundled plugin that registers `music_generate` and returns one file under the managed media store. No music provider is configured, so the core tool of that name is absent and the plugin's tool is the one that runs; the scenario checks its output text in the provider log. Turn 1 calls it and replies with its path and an unmanaged control path. Turn 2 reads the conversation context in the provider request and requires the plugin path to be replaced by `[unverified media reference removed]` while the control path stays as written.

The directive joins the existing scripted-turn chain beside the cron planners, so `server.ts` does not grow under the line-cap ratchet.

## Evidence

<!-- remediation-2026-10-20:start -->
### October 20 integration

Pushed `ce1095ab83725303f10c0497a7bbe8a5a7da9705`, merging `main` `f629720edbb9f4b458adae30c7506c1dc5d1adc6` into the existing branch without conflicts. The lockfile changed with main. prs.title: fix(update): interrupted updates leave a build lock that blocks the next update
prs.body:
## What Problem This Solves

Fixes: an update that is stopped or killed can leave `.artifacts/dist-artifacts.lock` behind, and the next update then fails with `source-artifact-ownership` and asks the operator to run `rm -rf`.

## User Impact

A lock from a dead owner now clears on the first attempt, with a warning in the run report and no manual step. Old-format lock records recover too. A signalled update now drains, releases the lock and exits 143 instead of being SIGKILLed after 2 seconds.

When a live process really holds the lock, the update waits up to 60 seconds with progress every 30 seconds, keeps building its candidate in the private worktree, and checks again before stopping the Gateway, for up to one step timeout (30 minutes by default). If the holder outlasts both waits, the update still ends with `source-artifact-ownership` before changing anything, and the current version keeps serving. Going ahead would put two writers on one dist.

The installed updater must contain this fix before it takes effect.

## Why This Change Was Made

Two defects combined. Both respawn launchers give a child 1 second, send a second SIGTERM, then SIGKILL after another second, while the update's signal handler needs about 50 seconds at that stage. If the kill lands before the lock is released, the lock is stranded. `staleRecovery: "fail-closed"` then meant nothing could reclaim it without `rm -rf`.

The launcher now gives `update` up to 35 minutes to drain. A new census in `scripts/lib/dist-artifact-owner-census.mts` lets a retained lock be replaced only after it shows no process can still write for that owner, and a failed observation never counts as proof of death. Lock records now carry start time, process group, host and a token that descendants inherit, so a reused PID isn't mistaken for the owner.

The census is 435 lines, so it's worth reviewing closely. Its limits:
- For old records with no token, it treats a process as a survivor if it is orphaned, younger than the record, and working in the checkout. A false positive costs a bounded wait.
- Records from another host count as held for 24 hours, then recover with a warning.
- Where `ps` can't run on macOS or other non-Linux Unix, recovery checks only the owner and child claims, and warns. Linux reads `/proc`.
- On Windows a reused PID counts as live. An orphan under a Linux subreaper with no visible token can be missed.

Other launcher commands, including `doctor`, keep the 2-second limit.

## Evidence

From the real incident: `kill -TERM` on an update in preflight ended it within 2 seconds with shell status 137 and left the lock. The next update failed on it.

Real CLI at the same update stage, under a guard denying `launchctl` and live paths:

| | Result |
| --- | --- |
| Base | SIGTERM gives returncode -9 after 2.04 s |
| This branch | 143 after 49.92 s, lock directory empty |

The stranded lock itself did not reproduce through the real CLI, which released it before the kill on base. It reproduces with the real launcher around a lock-holding child, and with SIGKILL.

Red on base:
- `test/scripts/dist-artifact-lock.test.ts`: 15 failed, 7 passed, on an earlier version of the file.
- `src/process/respawn-child-runner.process.test.ts` base variant: SIGTERM gives `[null,'SIGKILL']`, expected `[143,null]`.

Green:
- 5 shards, 142 passed, 1 skipped (Linux-only), across the lock, ownership, preflight, launcher, `entry.respawn`, `node-runtime-recovery` and `update-command-execution-validation` suites.
- `test/scripts-update-gateway*`: 71 of 71 passed, using the path for when `ps` can't run.
- Linux container (`node:24.20.0-bookworm`) with real processes, with and without `ps`: a dead owner acquires, a live owner is busy, a surviving descendant is busy then acquires, and a reused PID acquires with the unrelated process left alive.

Real-process negative controls cover a live holder, a dead owner with a surviving descendant, and a PID reused by an unrelated process.

`codex-api-review` found 4 P1 issues across two passes, all fixed. A third pass was `scoped-clean` at P1 (0.83). It reviewed the commit before the last rebase, which changed no code, worked from the diff, and did not verify Windows.

Not verified:
- Windows paths have never run. BusyBox and Alpine weren't tested directly.
- A real update past `updater-runtime-retention`. Admission and activation are covered by execution tests, not a live run.
- The tests on this exact head. I rebased after they ran, and the movement touched no files this fix depends on.
- Project typecheck wrappers: `run-tsgo` refuses the global virtual store, so typecheck used raw `tsrs` filtered to touched files.

Known unrelated or unexplained:
- `update-command-service-publication` has 2 failures under the guard, identical on base. It did not run outside the guard.
- `tsdown-build` timed out once in a combined run and passed 91 of 91 alone.

prs.title: fix: stop GitHub publication from delaying cloud workspace settlement
prs.body:
Related: #188796

## What Problem This Solves

Fixes cloud workspace settlement waiting on GitHub network publication after the workspace has already been accepted.

## User Impact

Cloud sessions can finish syncing their changes and accept subsequent work without waiting for GitHub. The original publication receipt completes through the existing lifecycle sweep. No schema, credential, personal-confirmation, retained-disk, or durability-policy change.

## Why This Change Was Made

Capture both turn-bound and queued session requests under the accepting claim, preserving their immutable snapshots before handing publication to existing recovery. Queued requests can reuse an already-published, owned, correctly attributed exact snapshot without another push; unrelated head drift still refuses and preserves previously recorded effects. The existing remote-head reader moves into the recovery owner to keep the executor within its line limit.

## Evidence

- Hosted-review limitation: [ClawSweeper run 41144371719](https://github.com/openclaw/clawsweeper/actions/runs/41144371719) stopped before review at its input-safety gate, so it produced no verdict. Its redacted failure manifest reports two unverified findings and locates the first in the **base** blob `96b09cf5b0a75a94af05d93f8e03c1583d11ca1a`, `src/gateway/github-publication.test.ts:403` at `563ba501dced074d9d282fb3a4cb48cfc31bcf9e`. This is the existing diagnostic-redaction fixture, using a reserved test domain and fixture-marked data; this PR only changes a later test hunk. The second finding is not located by that manifest. Scanner-owner qualification is still needed; no exemption was added, no flagged value is reproduced, and local independent review/CI are not being represented as hosted-review success.
- Red/green handoff regression: the base performed 47 Git/GitHub commands where only the 14 pre-handoff commands were expected. The repaired handoff and claim-held sweep add none. Existing restart coverage still reports the result once.
- Real Git regression: three queued requests publish the accepted contents with one push and one PR, preserve later dirty-file edits, and retain frozen snapshots across preparation retries. The missing session snapshot and duplicate-request failures were reproduced before repair.
- Main publication suite: 22 passed; boundary suite: 34 passed. Runtime/history/personal coverage exposed one personal-head-drift receipt regression during development; it was repaired, and the final targeted head-drift and real-Git queue cases both passed. The subsequent observer extraction preserves the same command arguments, decoding, and authority-wrapped runner.
- Final targeted lint (7 files, 293 rules), formatting, Gateway-methods TypeScript check, and `git diff --check` passed.
- Canonical autoreview via the restricted OpenClaw engine, P0–P3: no actionable findings in the full candidate against `563ba501dced074d9d282fb3a4cb48cfc31bcf9e`. Reviewed snapshot is committed as `3359972b4dc49ce6f2605e5addd5b6b3ab2c61b3`.
- Test-line ratchet remains **1,026 lines over its inherited ceiling**. This change adds exactly 37 test lines and a matching 37-line allocation; both totals rise equally, and the shared baseline is unchanged. This is not claimed as a passing ratchet.

Proof ran in secretless, network-disabled Node 24.22.1 containers with real Git/SQLite and synthetic GitHub responses. The 23 optional PostgreSQL cases and live cloud/GitHub publication flow were not exercised. Exact-head [aggregate CI passed](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/actions/runs/41143173993/job/124364732824). The inherited local test-line debt above describes the pinned authoring base; the hosted merge-tree ratchet passed without changing this PR or raising its baseline. CI seconds are not yet available.

<details>
<summary>Test cost and simplification</summary>

- `pnpm test src/gateway/github-publication.test.ts --maxWorkers=1`: 27.58 seconds command-runner wall time.
- `pnpm test src/gateway/github-publication-boundaries.test.ts --maxWorkers=1`: 85.76 seconds, including cold worker compilation; the new real-Git scenario itself takes about 4.2 seconds. Real Git is necessary here: the old synthetic transport did not advance HEAD and could not expose queued-request snapshot reuse failures.
- Final targeted repair proof: 2 passed in 59.41 seconds, including worker compilation.
- Against the pinned base: production +111/−74 lines; tests +51/−14 lines; allocation +2 lines. The inline publication/report loop disappears; the existing writer and lifecycle sweep remain the only state and scheduling owners. Growth preserves the previously uncaptured session-request path and exact queued-request outcomes.

</details>

## Contributor credit

Adapted from Galin Iliev’s [S5 source commit](https://github.com/galiniliev/openclaw/commit/8c2d1d7a98f6299d6cc08126244efdd178d4c6f9), rederived on current main rather than importing the dependent commit wholesale.

prs.body:
## What Problem This Solves

The session-diff E2E intermittently crashes while checking syntax colors, obscuring genuine regressions in the diff sidebar. Related: #188734. This repairs the separately observed diff-sidebar failure.

## User Impact

No production or visual behavior changes. The existing diff-sidebar flow continues to verify file patches, gap expansion, syntax colors, change scopes, and view modes.

## Why This Change Was Made

The prior failure stack points to the test's `getComputedStyle(token.parentElement!)`, not production highlighting. Async highlighting can replace a span between Playwright's locator lookup and its evaluation. Query and measure connected spans in the same browser task, and poll for the actual highlighted-color outcome. The keyword-text and differing-color assertions remain intact; there is no catch, sleep, timeout increase, or production guard.

## Evidence

| Check | Result |
| --- | --- |
| Original assertion on unchanged production base `b39e2d09329c` | **7/20 failed** with the same detached-parent `getComputedStyle` error; 78.64 seconds |
| Original Linux failure | #188734 run [41133010054, UI 2/7](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/actions/runs/41133010054/job/124328950730), exact test and stack at lines 499–500 |
| Fixed assertion, original 137-file shard composition, four workers | **50/50 passed**; full run: 136 files passed, one pre-existing sibling failure (below); 682.84 seconds |
| `pnpm tsgo:ui` | Passed |
| Focused chat E2E test typecheck | Passed |
| Focused UI lint and format; `git diff --check` | Passed |
| PR CI test-line ratchet | Tested merge has 6,313,493 / 6,313,028; its captured main parent `9ef50cafa7` has 6,313,489 / 6,313,024. Same 465-line debt; checker and scalar baseline unchanged |
| Local base test-line ratchet | Base: 6,314,049 / 6,313,024; head: 6,314,053 / 6,313,028. Same 1,025-line pre-existing debt; exact +4 allocation |
| Independent Codex autoreview, P0–P2 | Clean final local snapshot against `b39e2d09329c`; no actionable findings |

The repeated proof runs headlessly on macOS using the same frozen production build for baseline and fix. Blacksmith Testbox queued after allocation, so the lease was stopped and the authorized local fallback used. No Linux replacement result is claimed. The 50 target iterations all passed. The one broader failure was `chat-outbox-migration`: “preserves qualified and global v3 Blobs through migration, reload, explicit retries and independent retirement” timed out at the initial-roster wait before migration assertions. Its exact focused replay using the unchanged base production build and unchanged outbox test source failed at the same wait (29.73 seconds). This existing readiness failure is retained, not reported as green. No new UI build, startup-budget run, screenshot, or production Knip run was performed for a test-only edit: production files, imports, styles, and emitted bytes are unchanged.

Touched E2E LOC: **699 → 703**. Production LOC delta: **0**. The test-line allocation is exactly **4**, preserving existing budget debt. Current main independently restores that headroom in #188780. No effects, state, listeners, cleanup, queries, or ownership changes in production.

## Initial CI and follow-up attribution

[CI attempt 1, run 41141443921](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/actions/runs/41141443921) finished with 37 successful jobs, 27 skipped jobs, two failed root jobs and the failed aggregate. Both real-Gateway shards and the diff test's UI shard passed. The failures are retained as failures:

- `checks-fast-baseline-ratchets`: the exact captured main parent and tested merge have the same 465-line debt, as recorded above. Main fixes this guard in #188780.
- `checks-ui-e2e (5/7)`: `Logs wheel reachability > keeps the newest log reachable after refresh in webkit (390 px)` times out at its **initial** newest-row wait, before the Refresh action. At failure, 2,000 entries were retained but rows 485–501 remained visible (`scrollTop=22468`, total height 89316, viewport 378), after 16 `logs.tail` reads. The diagnostic artifact reports no active tasks beyond the failed test.

prs.title: fix(memory): atomic append on sandbox bridge eliminates concurrent flush data loss
prs.body:
## What Problem This Solves

Two concurrent pre-compaction memory flushes for the same sandboxed agent workspace can both report a successful append while one flush's durable note is silently absent from the daily memory file.

`appendMemoryFlushContent`'s sandbox branch implemented "append" as an unlocked read → concatenate → whole-file `writeFile`. Both flushes read the same pre-image, and the later whole-file write clobbers the earlier note. Because the lost write happens immediately before compaction removes the source conversation detail, the dropped note is often the only persistent record of that content — and the caller still receives `appendOnly: true` success.

The non-sandbox path is unaffected: it delegates to `fs-safe` root `append()`.

## Why This Approach

The sandbox backend has no atomic append primitive. The Python mutation helper that used to live in this repository has moved into the external `@openclaw/fs-safe` package, whose guest protocol supports exactly `copy`, `rename`, `write`, `create`, `read`, `readdir`, `mkdirp`, and `remove` — no `append`. A bridge-level atomic append therefore cannot be implemented inside this repository, and a host-side `fs.appendFile` on the mounted path would bypass the pinned symlink/hardlink guards the sandbox exists to enforce.

This routes the sandbox append through the **same in-process file mutation queue ordinary `write`/`edit` already use**, keyed by the canonical sandbox queue key (`resolveSandboxFileMutationQueueKey`). Because that key is identical to the one `write`/`edit` compute for the same target, this serializes **append-vs-append**, **append-vs-write**, and **append-vs-edit**.

Scope is stated honestly: this closes the in-process race (multiple sessions/tools inside one gateway process sharing a sandbox workspace), matching the invariant `write`/`edit` already provide. It does **not** add cross-process locking. Cross-process correctness still needs a true atomic append primitive in the sandbox backend, which belongs in `@openclaw/fs-safe`.

This is the design from #117757, which a maintainer had repaired onto the canonical queue lane before it went stale.

## Evidence

### Failing test first (fix reverted)

```
$ npx vitest run src/agents/agent-tools.create-openclaw-coding-tools.test.ts \
    -t "serializes concurrent sandbox memory-flush appends"

 × createOpenClawCodingTools > serializes concurrent sandbox memory-flush appends instead of losing one
 FAIL  AssertionError: expected 'seed\ndurable-note-A' to be 'seed\ndurable-note-A\ndurable-note-B'
 Test Files  1 failed (1)
      Tests  1 failed | 65 skipped (66)
```

This is the reported data loss: both flushes returned success, `durable-note-B` is gone.

### Passing with the fix

```
$ npx vitest run src/agents/agent-tools.create-openclaw-coding-tools.test.ts \
    -t "serializes concurrent sandbox memory-flush appends"

 ✓ createOpenClawCodingTools > serializes concurrent sandbox memory-flush appends instead of losing one
 Test Files  1 passed (1)
      Tests  1 passed | 65 skipped (66)
```

The test holds the first append inside the bridge `writeFile` and asserts that a second append sharing the same queue does not reach the bridge write until the first commits. `writeFile` is only ever called inside the queued section, so more than one write call means serialization was bypassed.

### Regression suites

```
$ npx vitest run src/agents/agent-tools.create-openclaw-coding-tools.test.ts
 Test Files  1 passed (1)
      Tests  66 passed (66)

$ npx vitest run src/agents/agent-tools.memory-flush-append-write.test.ts
 Test Files  1 passed (1)
      Tests  5 passed (5)

$ npx vitest run src/agents/agent-tools.at-prefixed-remote-paths.test.ts
 Test Files  1 passed (1)
      Tests  1 passed | 1 skipped (2)
```

### Static checks

```
$ npx oxfmt --check --no-error-on-unmatched-pattern -- <2 changed files>
All matched files use the correct format.

$ npx oxlint --config .oxlintrc.json <2 changed files>
(no output — 0 warnings, 0 errors)
```

`npx tsc -p tsconfig.core.json --noEmit` reports zero errors in the two changed files. The pre-existing repository-wide `TS2883`/`TS4058`/`TS4094` vitest type-naming diagnostics are unchanged by this PR.

## What Changed

- **`src/agents/agent-tools.read.ts`** — the sandbox branch of `appendMemoryFlushContent` now computes the canonical sandbox queue key and wraps its read → concatenate → `writeFile` sequence in `withFileMutationQueueKeyResolution`. The non-sandbox branch is untouched. Dead tail code that the sandbox path never reached was removed.
  - Also restores the caller-authority recheck immediately before `mkdirp`. The queued append awaits sandbox stat/read before it mutates, so a receipt revoked while that read is in flight must not be able to create the parent directory before the write is rejected. The pre-refactor implementation checked here; the queue refactor had collapsed the two checks into one after the directory creation.
- **`src/agents/agent-tools.create-openclaw-coding-tools.test.ts`** — adds the concurrency regression test.

Two files, source + test. No sandbox bridge files are modified.

## Related Issue

Fixes #117741

## Not Claimed

- Cross-process serialization. Two gateway processes sharing one sandbox workspace can still race; that needs an atomic append primitive in `@openclaw/fs-safe`.
- Docker container and live provider-driven compaction were not exercised end-to-end; the production tool constructor, memory-flush wrapper, mutation queue, and a real filesystem-backed sandbox bridge were.

prs.title: fix(memory): preserve concurrent sandbox flush notes
prs.body:
## What Problem This Solves

Fixes lost memory notes when concurrent memory flushes append to the same sandbox workspace file.

Supersedes #131604, thanks @michielhdoteth.

Related: #117741

## User Impact

Concurrent flushes within one Gateway process retain every appended note. Cross-process writers remain outside this guarantee; the sandbox backend has no atomic append primitive. No configuration or migration is required.

## Why This Change Was Made

The sandbox append read and rewrote the entire file without joining the existing write/edit mutation queue. The fix serializes that operation using the bridge's physical file identity, preserving path safety and the authority check immediately before writing.

Consolidating duplicated source-execution scopes and eliminating the intermediate write-content variable keeps production LOC at **-1**. The real bridge regression adds 30 test lines, with an exact 30-line allocation because existing tests did not exercise concurrent memory flushes.

## Evidence

- **Red on main `38fd51c52ab11ce75810ac7917bef4fc2b11010c`:** four separate memory-flush tools all reported success, but the real sandbox bridge persisted only `seed` and `note-D`, losing the other three notes. The affected main source remained unchanged at publication.
- **Green after:** all 8 tests in `fs-bridge.backend.e2e.test.ts` pass, including the same concurrent-append reproduction. This runs the production bridge with a local shell/Python backend and real files, without Docker or a model. New case: 434 ms; full cold file wall time: 42.43 s (most time was compilation). The exact-head [CI run](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/actions/runs/41149547274) passed (8 min 19 s overall).
- **Consumer checks:** 245 passing tests across 12 core consumer files, plus 75 passing tests and one existing skip across gateway files, Codex filesystem streaming/composition, and OpenShell backend consumers: **328 passing tests across 18 files overall**. Additional checks ran in rootless containers capped at four CPUs and 8 GiB.
- Core and affected `agents-tools` test typechecks, targeted lint, formatting, test-line ratchet, and `git diff --check` passed. The typecheck's existing state-logging root-budget advisory is unrelated.
- **Autoreview:** Codex engine, P0–P2, `scoped-clean` with no actionable findings on the production/test local snapshot against the main SHA above (diff SHA-256 `a69aa006a290400e7d167303caf0214b3272df2af772e6e40c46a47949a85a11`). Review could not execute tests in its sandbox; the tests above ran separately. Local ClawSweeper is unavailable on this host; one hosted review was requested and is in progress.
- The contributor head was read with GitHub view/diff and was never checked out, installed, or executed. This implementation and regression were written on a branch based on main. Contributor credit is preserved in the commit trailer.
- Live model-driven compaction was not exercised; the regression proves the actual memory-flush writer and sandbox bridge boundary directly. The Team Gateway was not modified or restarted.

prs.title: fix(update): leftover runtimes and database snapshots are never reclaimed on hosts running a Gateway
prs.body:
## What Problem This Solves

Fixes: update runtimes, preflight worktrees, admission repos and full database snapshots piling up after updates on any host that runs a Gateway or node service, because cleanup treats every running OpenClaw process as using every artifact.

## User Impact

Later updates now reclaim prior-run artifacts nothing uses. On the host that reported this, leftovers included three directories of 21-22 GB, each a full copy of the agent and state databases, plus several GB of retained runtimes dating back two weeks, on a machine where update disk admission is already tight.

Cleanup can't fail an update. Failures become warnings in the run report, and removal renames first and continues in the background.

Verified Git activation now removes restorable database snapshots, as package updates already do. This reduces how many rollback copies stay on disk.

The installed updater must contain this fix before it takes effect. `openclaw update cleanup --dry-run` still doesn't list these snapshots and Doctor doesn't sweep them, so only the next update reclaims them.

## Why This Change Was Made

`classifyProcessArtifactCustody` returned a holder with no paths for any OpenClaw process, and the caller only narrowed to the directory when paths were present. A host running a Gateway could therefore never reclaim anything. An artifact now counts as held only by its live owning run, or by a process actually using that path through argv, cwd, executable or a mapped file.

Retained runtimes hard-link into the checkout, so `lsof`-style mapped paths report a false holder. A mapped file with other hard links on macOS no longer counts as use. A copied file does.

Git transactions never removed their database snapshots. For older copies, the sweep decides from the run that captured them:

| Situation | Decision |
| --- | --- |
| Run succeeded, or never activated | Remove |
| Run in progress, or any update recovery pending | Keep |
| Failed after activating | Keep until a later success and 7 days after the failure |
| Kept for manual recovery | Keep 7 days |
| No run records it, and it holds this state's database at its archive path | Keep until 7 days old |
| No run records it, and it belongs to another state directory | Keep until that state directory's next update |
| Process census fails | Keep, regardless of age |

Runtimes and worktrees with no owner record are removed once 24 hours old and unused. New runs record an owner, so the next sweep removes theirs straight away.

Tradeoffs, since this deletes database copies:
- A copy from a state directory that never updates again, or whose path is spelled differently, is kept forever.
- A failed run's snapshot whose capture receipt was compacted out of history falls to the 7-day age rule.
- A process running JS from a runtime with no argv, cwd or uniquely mapped file evidence goes undetected.
- Each scratch directory gains a small owner-record file, deleted along with the directory.
- Inspection can overrun its 10-second budget by one census, so the docs say "about 10 seconds".
- An early disk refusal never reaches this sweep, and `gitArtifactStorageRoot` redirects aren't swept.

## Evidence

Red on base:
- A brand-new empty runtime directory listed 37 "holder" PIDs with 0 files open inside it. A fake OpenClaw process counted and a plain `node -e` process did not, so identity decided the result, not use.
- A runtime stayed retained after its holder exited.
- A verified Git update kept its database snapshot.
- Another state directory's snapshot was deleted by age before the P1 fix (`ENOENT` on the copy).
- With the hard-link rule disabled, the hard-link negative control failed.

Green:
- Full focused set: 339 tests passed across 18 files, before a one-line logging change and the last rebase.
- Final tree: 51 tests passed across 4 files, covering custody, process, earlier-artifacts and retention.
- Consumer tests (74 passed) ran earlier in the work and were not rerun after later commits. The Windows installer script test in that set skipped on macOS.

Real-process tests cover an unused runtime reclaimed while an unrelated OpenClaw process runs, a runtime kept for argv, cwd or a mapped file, reclaim after a real SIGTERM of the claim code, PID reuse not protecting a dead run's artifact, and a removal failure producing a warning while the update continues. One test retries the sweep up to 5 times, with no sleeps, because a real census can fail on a busy host.

A test also caught a safety bug during this work: a transient census failure could delete an old runtime still in use. One unreadable process no longer fails the census, and a failed census now keeps the artifact.

`codex-api-review` found real issues across its passes, all fixed: ignored container holders, a Windows assumption in a test, run matching that could mistake a later run's cleanup report for the capture run, and the other-state snapshot P1 above. The final pass was `scoped-clean` at P0-P2 on the final diff. It worked from the diff and didn't run code.

Not verified:
- A real `openclaw update` or an upgrade from the latest stable, because an update was running on the test host.
- Real Windows, including whether an in-use tree refuses the rename the design relies on there.
- A real Linux host or container. Linux mappings were tested with mocks.
- SIGTERM through the CLI signal path. The test killed a real child process with no handlers.
- Whether info-level removal lines print in the terminal by default. A removal may only show in the log file and `--json`.
- Project lint and typecheck wrappers: `run-oxlint` and `run-tsgo` refuse the global virtual store, so type-aware lint and boundary guards need CI. `tsrs` on the infra project showed one error in `packages/ai/src/transports/openai-responses-websocket.ts`, a file this PR doesn't touch.

prs.title: fix(exec): dollar amounts in agent messages are corrupted when exec text uses $<digit> in double quotes
prs.body:
Closes #179890

## What Problem This Solves

Fixes: dollar amounts in agent-sent messages are silently corrupted ("$900" becomes "00") when an `exec` command passes the text in double quotes.

## User Impact

User impact: exec commands that would deliver a corrupted dollar amount are refused before they run. The refusal shows the text as written next to what the shell would deliver, and how to fix it (single quotes, `\$`, or a quoted heredoc), so the agent retries correctly instead of sending the wrong amount to a customer. It can be disabled with `OPENCLAW_EXEC_DOLLAR_GUARD=off`.

**Open question for maintainers:** this is default-on and uses an environment switch. If you'd prefer it opt-in, or shipped as a plugin on the existing `before_tool_call` hook instead of in core, I'm happy to rework it that way. Tell me which shape you want.

## Why This Change Was Made

`runBeforeToolCallHook` checks `exec` command text for a `$<digit>` that the shell would expand, before any plugin or approval policy runs. Codex-native shell commands reach the same policy through the PreToolUse native hook relay. Relay planning now counts the guard as a before-tool-call policy and keeps `exec` in the PreToolUse matcher, so native commands are covered even with no other policy installed.

The scanner is deliberately conservative. It only flags an expansion it can show would be empty:
- It honours single quotes, `\$`, `$'...'`, quoted heredoc delimiters, `${...}`, `$((...))` and comments.
- It recurses into `$(...)`, including substitutions inside unquoted heredoc bodies, with their own quoting.
- It ignores `$0` (the shell or script name) unless it reads as money (`$0.50`).
- It stays out of commands that define functions or set positional parameters (`set --`, `shift`, `getopts`), where `$1.00` may be intended.
- It fails open on anything it cannot parse.

Code-mode `exec` (JavaScript) is excluded.

## Evidence

- `src/agents/shell-dollar-expansion-guard.test.ts` (35 tests): the hazard shapes, every safe quoting form, `$0`, populated positional parameters, heredoc command substitution, `bash -lc` unwrapping, fail-open, and the `runBeforeToolCallHook` veto, allow and disable cases. The `$0`, positional-parameter and heredoc-substitution cases fail on the previous revision and pass now.
- `src/agents/harness/native-hook-relay.dollar-guard.test.ts` (6 tests): Codex `Bash` and `exec_command` are denied and single-quoted amounts pass. Relay planning enables PreToolUse for `exec` with no other policy and keeps it in a relay scoped to other tools; these planning cases fail without the relay change.
- The existing `agent-tools.before-tool-call*` and `native-hook-relay*` unit suites pass. `native-hook-relay.participants` and `native-hook-relay.remote-http` fail identically on `main` without this change in my environment.
- `pnpm tsgo:core`, oxlint and oxfmt are clean.
- Replayed against 391 unique `$`-bearing exec commands from a production deployment: 18 were flagged, all genuine expansion bugs, with no false positives.
- Still to add: a gateway trace of a real agent refusing and retrying. I'll attach it before asking for re-review.

prs.title: improve: keep unchanged sandbox workspaces warm between turns
prs.body:
## What Problem This Solves

Consecutive sandboxed turns pause and resume an unchanged workspace and spend unnecessary time resolving the same file paths before dispatching the model.

## User Impact

Unchanged turns keep the existing sandbox running while the workspace owner checks both copies. Host/guest edits, interrupted reads, pending reconciliation, and crash recovery retain the paused reconciliation path. No configuration or SQLite schema migration is required.

## Why This Change Was Made

The existing reconciliation lease owns the decision. A probe stops on changed content before preparing CAS packs; only unchanged observations are accepted. Acceptance failures and lost authority propagate rather than retrying an uncertain write. Fresh identity and containment checks remain, including protection against same-size edits with restored mtime.

The unchanged-file realpath check now uses `realpathSync.native` inside the existing computation worker, removing one asynchronous pool round trip per file. The production call chain was audited: manifest requests dispatch through the workspace compute pool, and the inline path requires worker context established by the worker entry point. No new synchronous filesystem work runs on the Gateway main thread.

Production delta: +101/−33, net +68 lines across four files. The added path reuses existing state, authority, and recovery owners; there is no new cache, watcher, or schema. Simplification review retained the paused fallback because fingerprint observations cannot fence guest writes arriving before quiescence.

## Evidence

The original unchanged-reuse regression fails on the baseline and passes here. On a synthetic btrfs fixture with 62,000 files and 1.102 GB total per projection, all 15 real Gateway mutation turns passed: five host edits, five guest edits, and five guest deletions, verifying both copies after each turn. Focused tests separately cover restored-mtime edits and pending-conflict reopen/recovery. Final scanner/fingerprint/projection selection: 92 passed, 2 filesystem skips; preparation and fixture checks also passed. On the original candidate, targeted typechecks and full `check:changed` passed.

Codex autoreview covered the implementation through P2 with no actionable findings. Initial head `7ef82ca871dbeeca9104953f61461e494789dcaf` passed exact-head CI. During landing, #188728 introduced a conflict in the reuse caller by adding cancellation propagation. Integration head `1f88fb5b7586ec900756782243a8fe7d2da8522c` preserves that signal through the specialized reuse owner into the existing store lease. The production change from the measured candidate is only signal forwarding; benchmark and scanner code are unchanged.

After integration, projection/store/preparation tests passed: 85 passed, 2 filesystem skips, including the new cancellation regression. The pending-conflict test was extracted into the existing helper to keep the owning suite below its line cap; all five targeted reuse/failure/recovery cases passed afterward. Codex reviewed the final integrated implementation through P2 with no actionable findings. The test-line allocation is 141 lines for warm reuse, edits/deletions, cancellation/authority/acceptance failures, and pending-conflict restart recovery.

### Work counts and timing limits

The warm candidate records zero quiesce/resume operations. Both revisions reuse a running container with zero actual starts/replacements and one mount snapshot per warm turn. These counts are the verified benefit; absolute latency qualification is deferred to production by explicit maintainer decision.

Local timing protocol: one active session, two exact subscribers, a real built Gateway and sandbox read/exec tools, loopback inference fixture, 4 CPU / 12 GiB topology. Baseline `e8e02333cd64c8df71bed4c35221fada414642f1` versus that base plus this production patch; identical committed benchmark tooling. Counterbalance A→B→B→A has 10 warm samples per revision. Cold existing-runtime turns are separate (only 2 matched samples/revision).

| Warm metric | Baseline p50 / p95 ms | Candidate p50 / p95 ms |
| --- | ---: | ---: |
| Overall workspace-sandbox | 4,613 / 6,806 | 3,917 / 8,907 |
| Synchronize canonical | 2,284 / 3,955 | 1,774 / 5,067 |
| Synchronize projection | 1,923 / 3,540 | 1,484 / 3,111 |
| Quiesce | 92 / 796 | 0 / 0 |
| Resume | 82 / 454 | 0 / 0 |
| Container provisioning/validation | 157 / 979 | 607 / 1,350 |
| Process CPU | 11,623 / 14,827 | 10,147 / 15,957 |
| Main-thread CPU | 749 / 1,186 | 1,067 / 1,376 |

These are descriptive, not a proven causal speedup. The initial A/A gate passed (6,280→6,616 ms), but the closing unchanged-baseline control fell to 3,395 ms; process CPU drifted −27.5%. The original local 20% gain/stability rule therefore did not pass. The maintainer explicitly accepts that noisy/inconclusive result for this bounded, correctness-verified change and requires production follow-through. Sparse tail and CPU increases are retained, not relabeled green. Synchronization phase timers cover probes on the fast path; observation acceptance remains in the overall span. Do not sum overlapping phases or their independent percentiles.

Container timing audit: 85.7% of the mean backend increase is in the existing mount snapshot (one inspect plus one `exec cat /proc/self/mountinfo`). Provisioning residual median is 16.99→17.17 ms and registry timings are effectively unchanged. There are no added validation calls or changed timing boundaries. Retained diagnostics cannot distinguish ambient contention from a scheduling effect of omitting pause/resume; no evidence-supported code fix was identified. Production monitoring retains this uncertainty.

The committed measurement entry point is `scripts/perf/transcript-broadcast-measure.ts`, run with `--turn-start-phases --diagnostics --prep-trace --stress-tools --runs 1 --rounds 6 --clients 2 --exact-clients 2 --cold-session-rounds 0 --sandbox-turn-timeout-ms 600000` against the prepared synthetic btrfs state and each built entry. Dirty proof uses `--rounds 15 --turn-start-workspace-mutations`. Production timeouts are unchanged. Full registry population and production hardware were not reproduced; controlled dirty-path timing and candidate fresh admission remain uncovered. An isolated Testbox attempt could not run because its kernel lacks btrfs; the lease was stopped.

### Production proof after deployment

Compare the existing per-run `managed worktree preparation` phase timings and overall `workspace-sandbox` stage against the preceding deployed revision. Report sample counts and p50/p90/max for reused same-session turns, with stopped-runtime/fresh admission separated and comparable workspace size/concurrency where available. Verify that unchanged runs omit quiesce/resume, inspect container-validation tails, and check synchronization/recovery errors. This PR authorizes no deployment; production observations follow the deployment owner.

A reliable filesystem change signal to remove full-tree probes is a separate follow-up, not part of this PR.

Prior-head CI passed on `7ef82ca871dbeeca9104953f61461e494789dcaf`: [run 41145463744](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/actions/runs/41145463744), including `openclaw/ci-gate`. The automatically triggered GitHub Codex code review also completed on that head with no findings. The integration run [41148134797](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/actions/runs/41148134797) failed only the two jobs that enforce formatting, both pointing to the reuse call after signal forwarding. Canonical formatting is corrected in final head `79588c933a3b648e499d8fa49e3fab850ae2d7d1`; its targeted `format:check` passed and Codex reviewed the formatting-only diff with no findings. Final exact-head CI passed on `79588c933a3b648e499d8fa49e3fab850ae2d7d1`: [run 41149249553](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/actions/runs/41149249553), with no failing jobs. Ordinary pinned-head landing; no admin exception.

The complete local `check:changed` run passed every check except an inherited unused export, `prepareClientPluginNodeCapabilities`. Neither that module nor its Knip inputs changed here; main already fixes it in [#188839](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/pull/188839), commit `4a393be419f30ecfd65972fe3ea1416c6f707316`. The local failure is retained rather than relabeled green. No admin exception has been used.

prs.title: feat(automations): preview impact before changing default models
prs.body:
Related: #188761

## What Problem This Solves

Changing a default model can leave existing automations blocked by model policy or account/runtime compatibility, with no warning at the point of change.

## User Impact

Models and Agents settings show automation impact before changing the primary model, and ask for confirmation when enabled jobs have blockers or unknown compatibility. CLI and agent callers can inspect the same read-only result. Existing model overrides, account ownership, permissions, schedules, and expired work are not changed.

This is an advisory metadata preview, not proof that upstream inference, fallback attempts, tools, or delivery will succeed. Missing personal/native observations remain explicitly unknown. CLI `models set` reports unavailable assessment as unknown and preserves its existing offline save behavior.

## Why This Change Was Made

One cron-owned assessment reuses scheduled model selection, account-route availability, and runtime checks. UI callers use it before autosave/config writes; `automations model-impact` and the model-facing `model_impact` action expose the same result and recovery guidance. This is the agreed preview-and-guidance first stage; bulk editing automation overrides is intentionally deferred. No migration or new configuration option is required.

## Evidence

- Real isolated Gateway + browser: cancellation preserved the config hash and job records; acceptance changed only the global primary. No WebSocket interception, synthetic credentials, scheduler disabled; 2 tests passed (50.11 s wall including fixture/compiler startup; new case 4.805 s).
- Mock browser coverage: global and agent model changes, blocked unchanged selections, cancellation and stale intent; 2 passed (27.66 s including UI build). Models owner/presentation: 52 passed (4.50 s); agent model/activation: 14 passed (3.05 s).
- Integrated tool, CLI, command, auth-login caller and prompt-prefix coverage: 213 passed across 8 files (104.66 s wall). Separate schema suite: 45 passed. Final tool argument/line-limit cleanup: 58 passed (43.38 s cold wall).
- Cron assessment: 6 passed; registered-handler visibility/read-only proof: 1 passed. Existing account propagation (32), catalog decisions (23), method discovery/admission (41) passed. Domain/handler cold per-file wall times were 47.99/50.75 s; test execution 0.476/2.309 s.
- Independent local autoreview of the full candidate against `b39e2d09329cc81b09cf55980a2506623236ea59`, P0–P2: one private-current-session visibility finding reproduced red, fixed, and re-reviewed with no actionable findings. The repaired handler + tool replay passed 59 tests (52.08 s). Later equivalent argument-reading cleanup was checked by the final tool replay.
- Runtime/UI build passed (5m16.6s phases). Production core/UI and relevant test typechecks, scoped lint, i18n/controller checks, generated protocol checks, documentation formatting, whitespace, and production/full-tree unused-file scans passed.
- Test-line ratchet remains red on **1,025 pre-existing excess lines** at the pinned base. This change records exactly **1,306 net regression-test LF lines** in its separate allocation; the shared scalar is unchanged. Added coverage protects selection/account policy, visibility, CLI/tool transport, and UI cancellation/config-only acceptance. No test or guard was weakened.
- CI seconds: not yet available. No upstream inference/credential-acceptance, WebKit, or live scheduled-run claim. The original settings screenshot is pre-selection; real-Gateway captures demonstrate the new interaction, not a clean baseline runtime comparison.

<details><summary>Scope and simplification</summary>

One shared read-only assessment serves the UI/CLI/tool callers. Existing account/runtime mismatch and catalog auth-ref decisions are shared with execution/catalog consumers instead of copied. No new persisted state, migrations, fallback engine, or bulk-edit workflow. Most generated churn is validator renumbering. Non-generated production/docs growth is approximately 1.4k lines across these consumers; test growth is the exact allocation above.

</details>

### Before

<details><summary>Actual isolated Gateway interaction</summary>

The real Gateway produced the inherited-provider incompatibility; cancel preserved config/jobs and accept changed only the default.

![Real Gateway automation compatibility warning](https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/1263c1df-f37a-4c8d-a432-275a3b7c8d68)

</details>
