prs.title: fix(agents): keep a finished Claude CLI turn that outgrew its stream budget
prs.body:
## What Problem This Solves

A Claude CLI run that **finished its work** is reported as a failed run, and its completion is dropped.

`src/agents/cli-output-stream-limits.ts` defines one constant, `8 * 1024 * 1024`, and uses it for two different jobs:

```ts
maxTurnRawChars: CLI_STREAM_JSON_DEFAULT_MAX_TURN_RAW_CHARS,   // cumulative per-run odometer
maxPendingLineChars: CLI_STREAM_JSON_DEFAULT_MAX_TURN_RAW_CHARS, // genuine per-line memory bound
```

`maxPendingLineChars` is a real memory bound — it caps one un-newlined line held in `lineBuffer.pending`. `maxTurnRawChars` is not: it is an odometer over a stream whose partial-message deltas and tool results are discarded the moment they are assembled. Under `--include-partial-messages --verbose`, 8 MiB of cumulative stream-json is ordinary for a long agentic turn, not pathological.

When the odometer trips, `accountClaudeJsonlLine()` sets `parseErrorText`, `handleJsonlLine()` early-returns for every later line, and the terminal `result` record — which arrives **last**, and carries the finished answer — is never seen. `getOutput()` then returns empty text with an `errorText`, and `execute-process.ts:355` raises a `format` `FailoverError`, which the gateway classifies `status=400` / `chain_exhausted`.

Observed on a 23-minute run (`claude-opus-5-5`, 1,404,065 ms) that had already written its 81 KB report to disk:

```
cli terminal failure: provider=claude-cli model=claude-opus-5-5 ...
  error=CLI JSONL output exceeded 8388608 characters; refusing to parse output.
lane task error ... FailoverError
model_fallback_decision reason=format status=400 chain_exhausted
```

The session was marked `failed` and its `completionTarget=parent` completion never reached the requester. Ten runs have been destroyed this way since Sep 1 across five different lanes.

The same cliff exists on `maxTurnLines` (20,000): whichever odometer trips first abandons the turn identically, so fixing only the character budget would just move the failure.

## What Changed

**Cumulative turn budgets stop the parser from *assembling*; they no longer abandon the *turn*.** Once `maxTurnRawChars` or `maxTurnLines` is spent on the Claude stream-json path, the parser retains nothing further and decodes each remaining line only far enough to recognize the records that still change the turn's outcome: the terminal `result`, attributed progress for an outstanding Agent call, and the tool result that settles one.

- If the terminal result arrives, the run **is not failed**: `getErrorText()` returns `null`, `getOutput()` returns the finished answer and session continuity, and a new `getOutputTruncationText()` reports the truncation. `execute-process.ts` logs it as `cli stream truncated: provider=… ` instead of throwing.
- If it never arrives, the turn's outcome is genuinely unknowable and the **existing error is unchanged** — byte-identical text, same `format` failover. The guard is not removed.
- `maxPendingLineChars` is untouched and stays fatal. It is the one limit that bounds a single allocation.

New module `src/agents/cli-output-stream-budget.ts` owns the budget accounting, the ordinary-frame accountant, the post-budget watcher, the terminal-result event dispatcher and terminal reply selection, keeping `cli-output-stream.ts` inside the repo's 700-line file budget (same reason `cli-output-stream-limits.ts` exists).

**Truncated turns keep the reply text they already assembled.** A tool-split reply streams as pre-tool text, a tool call, then a closing message that the terminal envelope restates. Because a spent budget stops assembly before that closing message, the envelope alone would erase the pre-tool half. `resolveCliTerminalReplyText` keeps the preserved candidate as a bounded prefix while a tool split still connects it to the answer, and joins it to the envelope with the normal message separator. A draft with no tool split stays superseded exactly as on an unbudgeted turn, so recovery never resurrects a superseded draft.

**A truncated turn keeps its recovery clock alive (review round 20).** Waiting for the terminal result is only safe if the run survives long enough to produce it. While a parsed tool is active, `execute-process.ts:145-156` routes every stdout chunk to `observeOutput(false)` — the transport allowance — and `diagnostic-owned-activity.ts:97-104` makes even `observeOutput(true)` inert whenever `activeTools.size > 0`. So the blocked-tool clock can be advanced by exactly two things: `observeAttributedAgentProgress`, fed only from `onAttributedSubagentProgress`, and the tool result that clears the active tool. The first revision of this watcher dispatched neither — its `line.includes("result")` prefilter dropped an attributed child frame such as `{"type":"assistant","parent_tool_use_id":…}` before any decode, and it routed only `type === "result"` records onward, so the top-level `tool_result` that settles a foreground `Agent` call never reached `onToolResult`. With an Agent tool outstanding at exhaustion, `lastProgressAgeMs` grew unbounded for the rest of the turn, and past the 15-minute `BLOCKED_TOOL_CALL_ABORT_FLOOR_MS` floor `diagnostic.ts:327-336` can abort the still-working run before the result this recovery waits for.

The watcher now admits a non-null `parent_tool_use_id`, dispatches attributed child progress, and settles outstanding tool calls. Settlement is deliberately **bounded**: new `dispatchClaudeCliOutstandingToolSettlement` emits a result only for a call already in `tracker.startedIds` and has no start path at all, so that set stays frozen after assembly stops and neither the tool-split state nor the synthetic-no-response condition that terminal reply selection reads can move.

Two details that look incidental and are not:

- **It is a sibling of `dispatchClaudeCliStreamingToolEvent`, not a mode on it.** The first revision of this round added a `settleOutstandingOnly` flag to the shared dispatcher. `git merge-tree --write-tree --name-only upstream/main HEAD` then reported a *new* conflicted file, `src/agents/cli-output-events.ts`, because upstream is actively reworking the exact hunks the flag touched (`onToolInputDelta`, the `content_block_start` and `content_block_delta` branches). Appending a sibling in a region upstream has not touched keeps this PR's conflict set byte-identical to the reviewed base. The two jobs also genuinely differ — the streaming dispatcher starts calls and tracks streamed tool input; settlement must do neither.
- **The prefilter tests for a string value, not the bare key.** 51 of the 65 frames in `test/fixtures/cli/claude-2.1-subagent-forwarding.jsonl` carry `"parent_tool_use_id":null`, so `line.includes("parent_tool_use_id")` would hand nearly every post-budget line to the JSON decoder the prefilter exists to avoid. `/"parent_tool_use_id"\s*:\s*"/` admits only real child records. This is a cost refinement, not a behavior change — both forms behave identically, which is why no test pins it; the measurement is below.

### Why this approach, and not the alternatives

The issue listed four candidate fixes. Three of them do not meet the bar, which is that *a run that reached a terminal result must not be reported as failed*:

- **Count only assembled events, not partial-message deltas.** Changes the constant's meaning depending on which CLI flags a backend was launched with, and only moves the cliff: a long enough run still trips it and still loses a finished result. It also does not touch the `maxTurnLines` cliff at all.
- **Scale or configure the cap per backend / run kind.** Contradicts the limits file's own stated invariant ("the limits are process constants, not per-backend configuration"), adds config surface, and again only moves the cliff — any finite odometer eventually fails a finished run.
- **Stop buffering; stream-parse and discard deltas once assembled.** The right long-term direction, but a rewrite of the parser's assembly model (`assistantText`, `preserveFrom`/`segmentStart` boundary tracking, `preferStreamedClaudeTextOverResult`) for a defect whose whole cost is a mis-classification at the end of the run.

The chosen approach is the smallest change that removes the cliff entirely rather than relocating it, keeps every real memory bound, and leaves the failure path intact for the case where the turn outcome really is unknown.

A fourth alternative was considered and rejected in round 20: simply routing every admitted post-budget record through the parser's full semantic handler. It is the obvious reading of the review finding, and it is measurably wrong — see the controls below.

## Evidence

### Real behavior proof

`scripts/proof-cli-stream-turn-budget.ts` drives the production `createCliJsonlStreamingParser` exactly as `execute-process.ts` does — raw chunks through `push()`, then `finish()`, then `getErrorText()`/`getOutput()`. Nothing in the parser, its record decoding, its budget accounting or its output assembly is stubbed; only the `claude` subprocess edge is synthesized, using the stream-json shapes the CLI emits under `--include-partial-messages --verbose`.

```
$ pnpm tsx scripts/proof-cli-stream-turn-budget.ts
[recovered-raw] streamed 8495402 chars past the budget, recovered "Report written to ~/reports/theseus-research/context-epidemiology.md"; truncation: CLI JSONL output exceeded 8388608 characters; stopped assembling output and kept watching for the terminal result.
[recovered-lines] streamed 20001 chars past the budget, recovered "Report written to ~/reports/theseus-research/context-epidemiology.md"; truncation: CLI JSONL output exceeded 20000 lines; stopped assembling output and kept watching for the terminal result.
[tool-split-silent] 20001 frames/chars spent between the tool call and the result; recovered 77 chars, both halves present
[tool-split-commentary] 8495402 frames/chars spent between the tool call and the result; recovered 1806 chars, both halves present
[superseded-draft] draft correctly superseded by the envelope
[discounted-output-seen] interrupted run still reports "hello"
[unknowable-raw] still fails as designed: CLI JSONL output exceeded 8388608 characters; refusing to parse output.
[semantic-progress-after-budget] 3 attributed child frames advanced the blocked-tool clock, the Agent tool settled, ordinary output resumed advancing it, and the reply is unchanged
[settled-media-normalized] 4300000 echoed base64 chars omitted at the parser boundary; settled result is 176 chars
[retention-flat] streamed 33626977 post-budget bytes; heap delta -17216840 bytes; 0 new assistant deltas
All runtime assertions passed.
```

The two `tool-split` scenarios are the reply-loss case directly: pre-tool text, a tool call, the budget spent, then the closing message and an envelope that restates only that message. They assert both halves survive. `superseded-draft` is their guard — the same shape with no tool split, where the envelope must still win.

`semantic-progress-after-budget` is new in round 20 and covers the recovery clock. It wires the exact callbacks `execute-process.ts` wires (`onToolUseStart`, `onToolResult`, `onAttributedSubagentProgress`) and asserts, in order, that three attributed child frames each advance semantic progress while the Agent call is outstanding, that a result for a call this stream never started does **not** settle it, that the real result does, that ordinary output advances progress again afterwards, and that none of it changes the recovered reply. Two predicates it cannot run for real are restated with their source lines so the restatement is checkable: `activeParsedTools` mirrors `execute-events.ts:240-277`, and the progress arithmetic mirrors `diagnostic-owned-activity.ts:97-127` (the real diagnostic owner needs a live registration). With the round-20 source hunks reverted and the harness kept, this scenario is the only one that fails, with `0 of 3 attributed child frames advanced semantic progress`.

`settled-media-normalized` is new in the second commit of round 20 and closes a regression the first one introduced. A Read or MCP image call can start before exhaustion and return after it, so its result settles through the post-budget path; `normalizeClaudeCliStreamJsonRecord` strips Claude's echoed base64 **in place**, which is why the pre-budget path gets it for free as a side effect of character accounting. The watcher now applies the same normalization to every record it decodes before any dispatch. A `tool_result` carrying 4,300,000 base64 characters reaches `onToolResult` as a **176-character** record with `omitted: true` and the decoded byte count.

`retention-flat` also answers the cost question for round 20's wider record admission. Measured over five runs each on this host, the whole harness takes a median **0.78 s** at this head against **0.77 s** with the round-20 source reverted — and this head runs one extra scenario. The post-budget path's added work is within measurement noise on a 33 MiB post-budget stream.

`retention-flat` is the answer to the obvious objection, that recovering the run weakens a memory bound. It pushes **32 MiB of realistic frames after the budget is already spent** and asserts both that zero new assistant deltas are assembled and that the heap grows by less than a quarter of the bytes streamed. Measured heap delta is negative (the transient frames are collected); retention past the budget stays flat because the only records ever acted on are the terminal result, attributed child progress, and a tool result for a call already started — none of which is retained.

The harness is registered in `config/knip.config.ts` `repositoryScriptEntries`, and the file is present in the tree at the PR head, so `check-dependencies` stays green.

**Limit of this proof, stated plainly:** it does not spawn `claude` and does not go through `executeCliProcess`. An end-to-end trace through a real Claude CLI process is not something this fork can produce on demand — it needs a ~20-minute agentic turn that naturally exceeds 8 MiB of stream-json, which is not reproducible to order. The 23-minute production failure quoted above is the real-world observation; everything after it is parser-level.

### Regression tests

All regressions live in `src/agents/cli-output-framing.test.ts`. Base-fail/head-pass is measured by reverting only the source files and re-running, with the tests kept in place.

Round 20 — source hunks in `cli-output-stream.ts`, `cli-output-stream-budget.ts` and `cli-output-events.ts` reverted:

| Test | Source reverted | At this head |
|---|---|---|
| `dispatches attributed Agent progress after the budget stops assembly` (new) | **fail** | pass |
| `settles the outstanding tool after the budget stops assembly` (new) | **fail** | pass |
| `starts no new tool call and settles no unstarted call after the budget` (new guard) | pass | pass |
| `keeps post-budget tool-split reply text while the outstanding tool settles` (new guard) | pass | pass |
| `omits echoed binary from a tool result that settles after the budget` (new, second commit) | n/a — pins the second commit | pass |

Measured: **2 failed / 29 passed, exit 1** with the first commit's source reverted; **31 passed, exit 0** at that head. The two failures are separate `it` blocks, so neither masks the other. The second commit adds the 32nd case; removing only its one-line normalizer call fails that case alone — **1 failed / 31 passed, exit 1**, with the raw base64 visible in the dispatched delta.

Two further controls say why the *shape* of the fix matters, not just its presence:

| Control | Result |
|---|---|
| Route every admitted post-budget record through the parser's full semantic handler | **1 failed / 30 passed, exit 1** — a post-budget `tool_use` starts a new call (`['Agent','Grep']`), unfreezing the `startedIds` set reply selection reads. The proof also fails its *first* scenario: `recovered-raw: 1 assistant delta(s) were assembled after the budget was spent` |
| The same, and drop the line prefilter too ("just resume handling") | **3 failed / 28 passed, exit 1** — both budget kinds assemble a post-budget delta (`['dropped']`), breaking this PR's own truncation contract |

Each control was re-measured against the shipped structure, not against the first revision of it.

Round 10 — the earlier round's measurement, reproduced for continuity (it was taken against `bf578b0edd8` with two source files reverted, and its counts do not describe the current head):

| Test | At `bf578b0edd8` | Then |
|---|---|---|
| `counts actual blank Claude frames without invoking hooks or inventing a finish frame` (exists on `origin/main`) | **fail** | pass |
| `keeps a finished Claude turn that outgrew the line-count budget instead of failing it` | **fail** | pass |
| `keeps pre-budget tool-split text when the budget is spent before the closing message` | **fail** | pass |
| `reports assembled built-in partial deltas when no result envelope arrives` | **fail** | pass |
| `reports assembled hook-handled text when no result envelope arrives` | **fail** | pass |
| `lets a post-budget result supersede a draft with no outstanding tool split` (guard) | pass | pass |

Measured then: **5 failed / 22 passed** with the source reverted, **0 failed / 27 passed**. No test that exists on `origin/main` has been deleted or weakened in either round.

### Validation gate

Run from the topic worktree at head `e9d7a0512d7` (both round-20 commits were gated independently):

| Gate | Result |
|---|---|
| `pnpm check:changed` | **exit 0 — 45 lane headers** |
| `pnpm deadcode:unused-files` | exit 0 — production **and** full-tree scans, 0 entries each |
| `node scripts/run-vitest.mjs run` over the five `cli-output-*` suites | exit 0 — 117 passed, 0 failed |
| `pnpm tsx scripts/proof-cli-stream-turn-budget.ts` | exit 0, 10/10 scenarios, all assertions passed |
| `git diff --check` | clean |

Round 20 hit the `check:line-cap-ratchet` lane again: wiring the tool tracker into the watcher took `cli-output-stream.ts` to 701 counted lines against its cap of 700. Nothing was trimmed or suppressed — `createTerminalResultEventDispatcher`, branch-owned code, moved into the existing sibling module, which puts the file back under cap.

A previous revision of this body claimed `check:line-cap-ratchet` was blocked by the local toolchain's git 2.34.1. That claim was withdrawn in round 10 and stays withdrawn: the lane runs under git 2.55, and in both rounds it caught real over-cap growth introduced by the round's own work.

The PR is `CONFLICTING` against current `main`, in `src/agents/cli-output-stream.ts` only — measured with `git merge-tree --write-tree --name-only upstream/main <ref>`, which reports the same single-file conflict set at the reviewed base `1167f68387b` and at this head, so round 20 neither added to it nor resolved it. (It did briefly add to it; see the sibling-not-a-flag note above.) The fork's `main` is well behind upstream; resolving that is a fork-sync decision and is deliberately not done here.

*Written by Tank (Claude), an AI agent operated by Eddie Abrams (zeroaltitude).*

prs.title: fix(agents): keep Claude CLI replies after many large tool results
prs.body:
Related: #150132, #153545

## What Problem This Solves

Fixes: a Claude CLI turn loses its final reply with `CLI JSONL output exceeded 8388608 characters` when the model runs enough tools with large output to push more than 8 MiB of tool results through stdout.

## User Impact

User impact: tool-heavy Claude CLI turns (many large `Bash` or file reads) now deliver their final reply instead of failing at the turn budget. Per-line (8 MiB) and frame (20,000) limits and the turn timeout are unchanged.

## Why This Change Was Made

#153545 stopped charging partial-message envelopes, but tool results still count in full. Claude Code writes each result as a `user` record and echoes the payload twice (`message.content` and `tool_use_result`). The parser hands those payloads to `onToolResult` and keeps only the tool ID, so they spend the budget without being retained.

Tool-result-only `user` records are now charged for the line minus a lower bound of each payload's wire size. Strings and structure re-encode minimally; every number counts as one character, so wire forms that re-encode longer (`1e20` becomes 21 digits) can never shrink the charge. IDs, metadata, unknown fields, and whitespace padding are always charged in full, with a 32-character floor, and each record still counts as a frame. Mixed `user` records and payloads too deep to re-serialize keep full raw accounting.

<details>
<summary>Changes since the last review</summary>

- Rebased onto `main` @ `d4e933a29`. `main` reworked `cli-output-stream.ts` in the meantime; the rebase applied cleanly.
- `cli-output-stream.ts` was at the 700-line cap on `main`. The parser now picks the single decoded record once and passes it to the partial-message, tool-result, and media-normalization measurements. Behavior is unchanged.
- Added real behavior proof through the shipped `claude-cli` backend (below).

</details>

## Evidence

### Real behavior proof (shipped claude-cli backend)

One `openclaw agent exec` turn through the bundled Anthropic plugin's `claude-cli` backend (`agentRuntime: { id: "claude-cli" }`), built from this repo. Claude Code `2.1.288`, model `claude-haiku-5-5`, Node 24, macOS. Each build ran with its own temporary `OPENCLAW_HOME`, state directory, and config. The config only sets the model and its runtime:

```json
{
  "agents": {
    "defaults": {
      "model": "anthropic/claude-haiku-5-5",
      "models": { "anthropic/claude-haiku-5-5": { "agentRuntime": { "id": "claude-cli" } } },
      "timeoutSeconds": 1800
    }
  }
}
```

```sh
openclaw agent exec --config openclaw.json --cwd work --message-file work/prompt.txt --timeout 1800 --json
```

`work/prompt.txt`:

```
This is a load test of tool-output streaming. Run the shell command `./fill.sh N` for every N from 1 to 72, one tool call per N (you may issue several calls in parallel in one message). The output is filler text; do not read, analyse or summarise it, and do not run any other command. After all 72 calls have run, reply with exactly the word DONE and nothing else.
```

`work/fill.sh` prints 120,000 characters (1,500 lines of 79 `=`):

```sh
awk 'BEGIN { s = sprintf("%79s", ""); gsub(/ /, "=", s); for (i = 0; i < 1500; i++) print s }'
```

It is the same scenario as the capture below, adapted to the shipped backend. On normal turns the backend disables native `Bash`, so the model runs OpenClaw's `exec` through the MCP bridge. Claude Code shows the model a 2 KB preview of each large MCP result and echoes the full output in `tool_use_result`. Random base64 is not used here: as an MCP result, it exceeds Claude Code's MCP token limit and is replaced by a short error, so no large payload reaches stdout. Claude Code's session transcript for the PR run records 72 tool-result records of 124,577 characters each (8,969,544 in total).

| Build | Exit | `status` | Tool calls | Final reply |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `main` @ `d4e933a29` | 1 | `error`: `CLI JSONL output exceeded 8388608 characters; refusing to parse output.` | 67 of 72 completed; OpenClaw then stopped the CLI and the other 5 were rejected | lost (`final: ""`, no payloads) |

prs.title: feat(backup): recover local Gateway state with PostgreSQL agents
prs.body:
Related: #178971

## What Problem This Solves

Recover a replacement Gateway's local identity and PostgreSQL store pointers while its agent history remains in the existing central stores.

## User Impact

Proposes `openclaw backup local create --output <archive> --json` and `openclaw backup local restore <archive> --json`. The private archive contains the SQLite global database, its matched device/client credentials and configured PostgreSQL anchors. It excludes PostgreSQL records, configuration, workspaces and provider secrets managed through external SecretRefs.

Restore requires a stopped Gateway, original configured paths and fresh database targets. This remains a **draft awaiting maintainer acceptance of the storage/public CLI design in #178971**.

## Why This Change Was Made

Existing full backups export PostgreSQL history and restore fresh namespaces. Replacing a Gateway that will reconnect to the same central stores needs its native global/client pair and original UUID/schema pointers instead. A global-only snapshot cannot restore that pair.

This reuses native updater capture/restore, custody and matched-client receipt owners. The local profile applies the existing global snapshot sanitizer, including removal of pending outbound delivery intent: an older checkpoint must not resend messages acknowledged after capture. Ordinary full-backup rollback behavior is unchanged.

Restore reads configuration without observing or initializing database targets. Under native custody, it validates images, the global/client pair and anchor identities, creates missing private parent directories durably, then prepares and publishes images. A genuinely empty replacement state root is covered.

The archive is a per-database recovery point, not a distributed atomic snapshot. Anchors created after capture require a newer checkpoint; this does not discover namespaces after every local pointer is lost.

## Evidence

Current upstream head: `3426d311496` merges `origin/main` at `0ded0ed7a8c` to clear the `config/test-lines-baseline.txt` conflict; it changes none of this PR's files. The live proof below ran on the previous head `d553602eda5a5887ba1c5f326e0a34a7db63cb42` (merge of `origin/main` plus the ratchet fixes; `openclaw --version` of that full build reports `2026.10.8 (d553602)`), whose PR-owned sources are identical to the current head.

Live proof on this exact head, run with the built CLI against real PostgreSQL 16 and a real model provider:

1. **Source Gateway with a PostgreSQL agent store** completes a real model turn (`TANGERINE-4471` stored; reply `OK`). The agent namespace `proof_agent_c285…` holds 48 tables; the local tree holds the SQLite global/client pair and the agent anchor.
2. **Pending outbound delivery present at capture**: one `delivery_queue_entries` row is enqueued through the runtime's own storage owner before `backup local create` runs against the live Gateway (3 images, 206 KiB archive).
3. **Refusals before publication**: restore while the source Gateway still owns the state, and restore over existing database targets, both fail with `Local checkpoint restore requires fresh database targets: …` and change nothing.
4. **Replacement root**: the departed state directory is moved aside, an empty directory is created at the original path with the host-managed config kept outside it, and `backup local restore` publishes exactly the global, client and anchor databases.
5. **No delivery replay**: the departed global database still holds its 1 pending row (source acknowledges after capture); the restored global database holds 0; the replacement Gateway log has no delivery recovery activity.
6. **Same PostgreSQL identity**: the restored anchor row is byte-identical (`store_id c285d948-…`, schema `proof_agent_c285d94839f24786`); no new namespace is created. Doctor reports `Agent data: … effective=postgres (configured); observed=postgres`.
7. **Recovery turn**: the replacement Gateway lists the prior session from PostgreSQL and answers the recall turn with `TANGERINE-4471`.
8. **Data-model compatibility**: the released `openclaw@2026.10.8` (dc2523e) creates an all-SQLite installation and runs a turn (`MARIGOLD-2287`); this head refuses to serve its schema 25 until `doctor --fix` upgrades it to 38 with pre-migration backups, then serves it and answers the recall turn with `MARIGOLD-2287`. The released CLI does not accept the `database` key, so no released installation can hold PostgreSQL agent anchors; this head refuses `backup local create` on that layout with the documented message.

Native regressions: `src/infra/local-checkpoint.proof.test.ts` (capture with a pending delivery, source acknowledgement, cold-root restore, recovery without a second send, forged paths and anchor mismatch), `src/infra/sqlite-snapshot.prepared-volume.test.ts`, the no-replace copy cases in `src/infra/sqlite-file-copy.test.ts`, and the `backup local` dispatch rows in `src/cli/program/register.agent.test.ts` pass on this head, as do core types, test types, and the test-lines, assertion-safety and mock-exports ratchets against `origin/main`.

prs.body:
## What Problem This Solves

Readiness audits cannot distinguish an editable static Chat composer from a hydrated editor, or visible live transcript rows from an owner that is ready while its rows remain hidden.

## User Impact

There is no user-visible rendering change. The cold-load benchmark gains additive observations for editable composer eligibility and visible live transcript readiness, while every existing metric keeps its meaning and collection window.

## Why This Change Was Made

`firstUsableComposerMs` and `firstUsableComposerKind` observe the static Chat editor, active hydrated Chat editor, or New Session editor when visible, enabled, writable, and outside an inert subtree. `firstLiveTranscript` reuses the warm probe's existing row visibility and owner-readiness observations. The original `firstEnabledComposerMs`, `firstTranscript`, `catchupApplied`, and sampler lifetime are unchanged.

These are DOM-readiness observations. They do not prove compositor paint, click occlusion, send admission, or key-to-paint latency; missing observations remain null/absent, and old captures are not relabeled.

## Evidence

| Check | Result |
| --- | --- |
| Regression on base `4d2a9f8bb4c47da0daae7fd820cab33fa450ef7b` | New test failed at the missing `firstLiveTranscript` assertion, after the existing transcript and catch-up assertions passed. |
| Changed browser-test file | 10/10 passed after fixture consolidation (685 ms Vitest, 3.34 s command), including caught-up rows that are still hidden before reveal; one run on each source revision. |
| UI, scripts, and UI-test type leaves | All passed. |
| Targeted scripts/UI-test lint, four-file formatting, diff check | All passed. |
| Independent P2 reviews | Original four-file patch scoped clean with complete eligibility/handoff/visibility owners; fresh fixture-only correction also scoped clean, no findings. |
| Test-line ratchet against exact base | Passed with net −1 test line; no baseline/allocation change. |
| Built static Chat → loading frame → hydrated Chat | Native typing preserved the exact draft and focus, accepted continued typing, and sent zero messages. The new composer metric reported `static` while the legacy hydrated marker was still null. |
| Built visible Chat transcript | The actual warm probe recorded the live marker after visible rows and owner readiness; ordering followed the existing transcript and catch-up markers. |
| Built New Session | Reported `new`, with no static editor; native typing produced the exact draft, the owner's Start action changed from disabled to enabled, and zero messages were sent. |

The browser qualification used a synthetic Gateway and reused production bundle `c0c068e1ecd9ec78a75ad6847e032f4d0f5b1241`, after verifying the affected input/handoff/owner sources matched the patch base. It imported the actual patched warm probe and extracted the exact patched presentation callback. This was a behavior qualification on a busy 32-CPU host, not a timing cohort or warm-cache adoption proof. One New Session driver assertion initially compared text content with an icon-only button's accessible label; the corrected New-only run checked the actual submit control's enabled state. The successful Chat case was not rerun.

The first PR CI run (`41139734015`) rejected the original +44 test lines at the test-line ratchet. The repair consolidates repeated iframe setup in this same test file, preserving all ten cases, assertions, frame waits, and cleanup. Benchmark/probe bytes are unchanged from that tested head, so the built calibration evidence above is reused. No baseline or allocation was raised.

No startup modules, product rendering, or dependencies changed; no UI build or visual-change screenshot was needed for this diagnostic-only patch. No lease was allocated.

prs.title: fix(discord): thread replies and bindings stop working when a slow channel stop overlaps a restart
prs.body:
Related to #177691. Reviewed snapshots through `206f11bc8903`.

## What Problem This Solves

Discord thread replies and bindings can stop working when a restart overtakes an older task that is still stopping. Each start gets its own binding manager, so the old task's late stop cannot tear down the replacement's manager.

Two paths reproduced on main snapshot `7e81872cbbc`. In round 1, a startup held at `/gateway/bot` resumed late, failed with `Plugin service scheduler is closed`, and stopped the shared manager from its `finally`. In round 2, a slow bind made two replacement starts wait on the old stop. Read-only logpoints observed the mechanism in one run. An aborted start's cleanup stopped the manager that the other start had reused. The account broke in 3 of 4 main runs, including holds before and during the create. Of the three broken runs, only the logpoints run had the inspector attached. The other two match it by symptom only.

Only the narrow config-reload race was exercised. Recovery on a later provider start and other restart entries are read from code, not tested.

## User Impact

A late stop leaves replies working in old bound, newly bound and unbound guild threads. New binds are approved and written to SQLite.

- The old adapter is unregistered at handover. It cannot resurface after the newest owner stops and block session listings for other channels.
- Both native creates check ownership before sending, including direct subagent auto-bind. No built Gateway run measured the subagent path. A bind caught before its create is refused, and no webhook create POST is sent. Built Gateways measured this at `3fe8a885`, `2ae50585` and `206f11bc8903`, the last against real Discord, but not at `900208f1`. In round 2 the approver saw only the deferred update at both snapshots, with the approval prompt unchanged and no error text.
- An accepted thread or webhook create is still published. No built Gateway accepted a thread create. An accepted thread gets no follow-up webhook from the retired manager, so replies use bot sends without the persona. The retired manager sends no intro. This fallback has test and driver coverage, not real Discord proof. No run has shown a webhook-delivered reply.
- A bind settled by the replaced manager keeps that manager's idle timeout, max age and persist flag. The replacement's limits apply only to binds it creates.
- A replaced manager clears its sweep timer at its next tick, even if provider cleanup hangs, so it stops scanning.

A replacement registers without waiting for the old provider to stop. Binding work the old manager already queued, such as an accepted create, settles before queued work on the replacement runs. This includes async session-wide unbinds, idle timeout and max-age updates, inbound activity touches, startup cleanup of stale ACP bindings, and the replacement's own stop. It does not wait for the old manager's stop or the rest of its sweep. Each REST attempt keeps its 15 s timeout and a rate limited request is retried at most three times. Queueing, rate limit delays and persistence mean the total wait has no fixed cap. Deprecated synchronous unbind and duration setters skip the queue and can still overtake the create.

## Why This Change Was Made

`2ae50585` removes manager reuse across starts. Stop removes the account entry and token only for the current manager. #169226 merged the same reuse removal for Feishu.

- `68fb31d6` retires the predecessor's adapter by identity across loaders and guards both native creates.
- `3fe8a885` publishes a native create accepted before replacement, while still refusing new creates by a retired manager. This preserves #153508's accepted-write settlement without granting permission for later sends.
- `900208f1` copies the predecessor's queued-work promise without awaiting it at registration. Async session mutations and replacement stop wait for it, restoring #156627's ordering without joining the old stop.
- `206f11bc8903` makes retired sweepers clear themselves before checking pending work. Cancellation lags at most one 120 s interval.

## Evidence

### Tests

For reviewed snapshots through `206f11bc8903`, all 12 required gates passed. The 19 Discord monitor files passed 182 tests and the 7 binding-consumer files passed 145. Type checks, formatting, typed lint and four ratchets passed.

- The original 3 restart cases fail with main's manager. Creation cases catch old-stop token cleanup and stale adapters resurfacing. The latter fails at `2ae50585` and passes with main's manager and the fix.
- The direct-create cases fail at `2ae50585`. Accepted thread and webhook settlement cases fail with that manager and `68fb31d6`, then pass at `3fe8a885` and `900208f1`.
- The session-wide unbind, idle and max-age cases hold a create across two replacements. All 3 fail with `3fe8a885` and pass at `900208f1`. Wrong-fix controls catch partial inheritance and waiting at registration.
- Two new restart cases hold voice cleanup across two replacements, idle and pending. Both fail at `900208f1`. Guards that skip scans but keep the timer, or check pending work first, fail.

### Built Gateway proof

Rounds 1 to 3 used isolated built Gateways, a Discord stand-in, fake credentials and a local mock response server, not real Discord or model services. Synthesized interactions went only to the newest connected socket at injection time. SQLite rows were checked during runs, not across Gateway restarts. These runs predate the timer commit.

Round 1 compared main `7e81872cbbc` with `2ae50585`. Two `channels.discord.historyLimit` edits about 3 s apart, with one `/gateway/bot` response held about 10 s, overran the 5 s stop grace. The shared edge shim rewrote the gateway URL in `/gateway/bot` and `resume_gateway_url` in READY, renumbered dispatch sequence numbers, and answered interaction callbacks itself. The exact scheduler throw site is inferred.

Main failed in all 4 runs. All 3 guild-thread turns tried after the late stop in the primary run got no reply and logged `SessionWorkStartChangedError`. New binds failed with a binding-owner error.

Round 2 built `3fe8a885` and passed the unchanged late-stop sequence. It also compared main and `2ae50585` on the slow-bind path. At both fix snapshots, refused creates wrote no row, replies kept working, and the pre-create hold sent no webhook create POST. Accepted settlement was unproven because the stand-in returned 404 to every native create.

Round 3 built `900208f1`. Its late-stop run matched round 2 in its outcome rows, but its first replacement start exited with `Skills discovery was retired before publication` and was auto-restarted. The hold lasted 16.1 s, against 10.1 s in round 2, because the harness waited for the usable replacement. The stand-in lacks the webhook create and execution routes, so the edge synthesized four HTTP 200 webhook-create responses with fake IDs and tokens. There was one in each accepted-create run, plus one in a no-reload control at `900208f1`. No webhook-execution response was used. By the edge code, other native REST calls passed unchanged, and the edge answered interaction calls as in round 1.

Each build had one run of this case. At `900208f1`, under a synthetic webhook-create success, the held bind was approved and its webhook ID and token were stored, with no simulated orphan. At `2ae50585`, the same synthetic success was refused, leaving no row and a simulated orphan. Main stored the row but stopped replying and logged 27 ownership-change errors.

Round 3 is PARTIAL for webhook replies. In the bound reply of the accepted run at `900208f1`, a bot send was used despite the stored webhook. The no-reload control, run at `900208f1` only, also used a bot send. The cause of that bot send is read from code, not measured. The reply's agent session key finds no binding row, so no thread id reaches the webhook path. Persona delivery and webhook reply POSTs remain unproven. The optional session-wide probe stopped before its held create, with a Gateway error that begins `Session key does not contain an agent id`. That probe was not run on main or `2ae50585`, so it is not known whether the failure predates this change. Those waits have regression-test coverage only. The separate predecessor socket leak repeated and is not fixed here.

### Live Discord proof

At `206f11bc8903` I ran a built Gateway with real Discord via a TLS proxy and real `gpt-5.6-luna`. A retired manager refused a bind before any webhook create request. A webhook create Discord accepted across a handover was stored by the original bind. L1 was inconclusive, and both attempts needed SIGKILL after a clean-shutdown log. The no-hold control, L2 and L3 each ran once. I ran no base. Details and limits are in https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/pull/178931#issuecomment-6509058680. L3 receipts are in https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/pull/178931#issuecomment-6512844287.

### Driver proof

At `206f11bc8903` I ran a scripted driver over the built modules, with a loopback Discord REST stand-in and no Gateway. A retired manager sent no create or intro. Limits are in https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/pull/178931#issuecomment-6511023964, and redacted receipts in https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/pull/178931#issuecomment-6511604213.

A second driver added a loopback Gateway stand-in and ran the built channel manager restart over the built provider. Two runs per case were reproduced twice by an independent rerun. After the replacement registered, the older task's startup `finally` stopped only its own manager, and the replacement then took a driver-issued bind and send. The Gateway lifecycle `finally` and a running provider's late stop are unproven. See https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/pull/178931#issuecomment-6512196949.

Fixes completed worktree writes keeping each other's disk postchecks blocked when free space reaches the safety reserve.

prs.title: feat(agents): preserve stores during controlled Gateway handoff
prs.body:
Related: #178748

## What Problem This Solves

An agent's identity and history should survive a change in where it runs. An operator may start an agent on a shared Gateway, then move it to a dedicated Gateway for capacity or isolation. Today there is no supported per-agent removal operation for that handoff: `agents.delete({ agentId, deleteFiles: false })` still requests session-store purging. Keeping files does not preserve sessions.

With PostgreSQL, the durable agent data can already stay in the same database. The missing operation releases the source Gateway's use of that store without deleting its contents.

## User Impact

An administrator can:

1. Stop routing new work to the source and wait for `agents.detach({ agentId })` to succeed.
2. Transfer the closed original anchor and required workspace files, keeping the agent ID and PostgreSQL namespace.
3. Use existing `agents.create` on the destination, verify retained identity/history, restore destination settings, then switch routing.

This enables planned capacity changes and maintenance without resetting the agent's history or copying its PostgreSQL rows. Workspace files remain a separate transfer responsibility. This is a new operator capability, with no claim of a current outage or regression.

## Why This Change Was Made

Changing `agents.delete` would weaken its cleanup contract. Editing the roster or copying an anchor alone bypasses admission closure, draining and restart recovery. Detach makes retention explicit while reusing those lifecycle owners.

The implementation records durable detach intent, drains work, closes database owners and retains the store/files. Recovery and destructive retries cannot convert a pending detach into deletion; offline CLI deletion refuses a pending detach, and `openclaw agents detach <id> --force --json` runs the same journaled lifecycle while the Gateway is stopped.

Core supplies the local lifecycle primitive; a controller or plugin orchestrates placement and routing. There is no database schema-version change, new adoption RPC or distributed ownership manager. Three unchanged session-policy constants move out of the method table to meet the repository's file limit.

## Scope and Compatibility

This is administrator-controlled sequential handoff. The controller owns exclusive assignment, routing, database permissions and file transfer. Source tombstones refuse ordinary writes after restart, but cannot prevent explicit source recreation or duplicate adoption.

Detach removes Gateway-local bindings, execution approvals and provenance; restore required destination settings explicitly. It retains cron jobs; the detached agent cannot execute them. Existing restrictions on the sole configured agent and shared/inherited credential owners remain. Local shared state and anchors can remain SQLite.

The new journal phases are a compatibility commitment: binaries without this change reject retained detach journals, including completed records, at the journal read sites (agent re-creation, deletion, recovery) while still starting and serving the remaining agents. Keep a compatible runtime while those records remain.

**Held-scheduler caveat (undecided).** The integration test's `held: true` and `held: offline CLI` cases, and one sentence in `docs/gateway/postgresql.md`, refer to a `cron.migration` RPC (hold / export / resume phases). That RPC exists only in a downstream scheduler-custody overlay, not in upstream OpenClaw, so those two cases fail on upstream with `unknown method: cron.migration`. The unheld path is what this PR proves. Whether to drop the held cases and that doc sentence, or to upstream a scheduler hold first, is an open decision for the author and maintainers; nothing in this revision changes code to paper over it.

## Evidence (exact head)

Head: `fcc6e8302b862be09ab72de1dfe0f8ffe9347318` (PR branch merged with upstream `main` `0661e52a19d`; the reviewed commits are unchanged, conflicts were resolved in the merge commit).

### Live two-Gateway handoff on this head (redacted transcript)

Setup: two real Gateway processes started from this head's source (`startGatewayServer` with a managed restart owner, as under the CLI supervisor), each with its own `HOME`, state directory, config, token and port; one PostgreSQL 16 database (`unaccent`, `pg_trgm`) shared through `database.families.agent.engine = "postgres"` with one schema prefix; SQLite shared state and anchors stay local. Every RPC is a separate client process; the scopes it requests are printed with each call. A third process is an upstream `main` checkout without this change (`54afe289085`), used as the no-PR build. Paths, tokens, the database password and the user name are redacted; nothing else is edited.

What the transcript shows, in order:

1. Source Gateway A creates `traveler` (PostgreSQL store, anchor records store UUID and namespace), a session and one transcript message.
2. Destination Gateway B's state directory is created and written by the no-PR build, then opened by this head: the pre-existing session and message load (existing-data check).
3. An `operator.write`-only caller is refused `agents.detach` (`FORBIDDEN`, missing `operator.admin`); roster and journal are untouched.
4. An administrator's `agents.detach` succeeds (`ok: true`, hot reload applied, no recovery restart). The roster drops `traveler`; the journal records `detach-retiring`, `deleteFiles: false`, `cleanupCompleted: true`; the anchor file, workspace file and PostgreSQL namespace are all still present.
5. Before restart the source refuses a `traveler` write; `keeper` is still listed and readable.
6. After restarting A, `sessions.create` for `traveler` is refused (`Unknown agent id`) and a write into the old session is refused (`deletion is in progress; new work is unavailable`); `keeper` still writes.
7. The closed anchor and workspace are copied to B (same agent id, same namespace recorded in the anchor).
8. B's `agents.create` admits the existing anchor; `chat.history` on B returns the **same session id and message** created on A; a new write on B lands (2 messages). The source still refuses `traveler` afterwards.
9. Offline CLI on the stopped source: a journal left in `detach-retiring` is completed by `openclaw agents detach --force --json` (`detached: true, storePreserved: true`; roster entry removed, workspace and state directories retained); a journal in `retiring` (pending destructive deletion) is **not** converted (`has a pending deletion; finish agents.delete before detaching`); with the Gateway running, the offline command refuses with `requires exclusive offline state ownership`, no mutation.
10. The no-PR build against the source state: its Gateway starts and lists `keeper`, but `agents.create traveler` and `agents.delete traveler` are refused with `Invalid agent deletion journal phase.`, and its journal reader reports the same error.

Not exercised live here: a replaced deletion lease racing a detach between two processes (covered at the journal-authority level by `src/state/agent-deletion-journal.fence.test.ts`, `changed before recovery`), the held-scheduler cases (see caveat), and a packaged v2026.10.5 upgrade.

prs.title: improve(cron): surface scheduled jobs blocked on a missing creator channel and guide recovery
prs.body:
Related: #162087

## What Problem This Solves

A capped automation created from a direct (DM) conversation before creator origins were recorded fails closed on every scheduled run: the account-scoped liveness check cannot resolve a channel from a DM owner key with no recorded origin, so it reports the (configured) account as unavailable. The only recovery today is recreating the job, which demotes it to broader `trusted` authority. The jobs are also undiscoverable: nothing surfaces which saved jobs are blocked, and the run error suggests re-adding the account even when the account is fine.

## User Impact

User impact: operators can now discover blocked jobs and recover them without demoting their authority. `openclaw automations status` reports a `reauthorizationRequired` count, each affected job's details and list entries flag `reauthorizationRequired: true`, and the run error names the real cause and the least-privilege recovery: re-save the job's tool cap from the creator's authenticated turn (which records a fresh origin via the existing reauthorization path), or recreate it from the intended account.

## Why This Change Was Made

This is the guided-recovery side of the failure mode recommended by the security review on #162087 ("require guided reauthorization: keep the fail-closed boundary and add a clear operator or creator recovery flow"). It does not change the boundary: the liveness guard still fails closed; the change only detects the exact blocked class, surfaces it, and makes the error accurate. The trigger-path origin threading is already merged (#176158) and is not touched here. The detection predicate mirrors the guard precisely (named account, unknown origin, non group/channel owner key), so it flags exactly the jobs that fail and no others.

## Evidence

Source head: `fe17c08e16d9c00d7e645e25480c39493028a791`, which merges main `0d38c2dfcbfb`.

### Shipped Gateway proof, October 26

I built the head (tree `8132c05bdac84fa711ae03d9bf8fafd50ab82dd9`) and its main parent `0d38c2dfcbfbb1ae2bec19a0a26973640390a5a8` (tree `40c5902ba2f3ece22bf6461af8bfe93ad3b34398`) on macOS arm64 with Node 24.22.1 and pnpm 12.15.0: `pnpm install --frozen-lockfile`, then `OPENCLAW_BUILD_PRIVATE_QA=1 node --import ./scripts/tsx.mjs scripts/build-all.mts qaRuntime`. Both exited 0. `dist/entry.js` SHA256 is `ae7797afd96e9a9fb60d6bf1ec8cb1a0ea9383307cf740a151ba0ac4015ad913` for the head and `a1454578a78ce6c7614a1113671823495c9ad187b78d4e161c0102e5046bc991` for main. Tracked source was unchanged before each run.

Each run used a fresh HOME, state and config and a loopback Gateway started with `node openclaw.mjs gateway run --bind loopback --allow-unconfigured`. The channel is the repository's `qa-channel` plugin on its local QA bus (`extensions/qa-lab`), with accounts `default` and a named `creatorbot`, `session.dmScope: "per-channel-peer"` and `commands.ownerAllowFrom: ["alice"]`. The model is `scripts/e2e/mock-openai-server.mjs` with scripted responses. Every operator step goes through the shipped CLI. The DM sender `alice` is synthetic; no Telegram or Discord account and no real provider were used.

The script:

1. `alice` DMs `creatorbot` and the scripted model calls `automations` `add` with `toolsAllow: ["read"]`. The Gateway stores cap `["read","skills_read"]`, account-mode policy, owner `agent:main:qa-channel:direct:dm:alice` on `creatorbot`, and creator origin `{"kind":"external","channel":"qa-channel"}`. The origin is store-private, so I read it from the job row with a read-only SQLite open rather than from a projection.
2. The operator reschedules the job from the CLI with `openclaw automations edit <id> --every 1m`. Remote management carries no creator source, so the stored origin becomes `{"kind":"unknown"}` while the cap, owner and account stay the same. The detector and the run guard normalize that to the same unknown origin as a job saved before origins were recorded. I did not reproduce an actual pre-origin row from an older release.
3. Discovery, rejection, same-cap re-save from an authenticated `alice` DM turn, then the next scheduled occurrence.

Head run, 18:03:55Z to 18:07:54Z, condensed from the run transcript (commands verbatim, JSON trimmed to the fields this PR changes, exit codes kept):

```text

           stored: toolsAllow ["read","skills_read"], mode account, accountId creatorbot, callerOrigin {"kind":"external","channel":"qa-channel"}
$ openclaw automations status                     "jobs": 2, "reauthorizationRequired": 0                      [exit 0]
$ openclaw automations edit <id> --every 1m       "everyMs": 60000, "reauthorizationRequired": true            [exit 0]
           stored: toolsAllow ["read","skills_read"], mode account, accountId creatorbot, callerOrigin {"kind":"unknown"}

18:06:04.154Z  scheduled run: "status": "error", "error": "Scheduled account \"creatorbot\" is unavailable: the job has no

$ openclaw automations run <id> --wait --wait-timeout 3m --poll-interval 2s

18:07:22.253Z  scheduled run: "status": "ok", "summary": "PROOF-178677-SCHEDULED-OK", "deliveryStatus": "delivered"
               qa-channel creatorbot -> dm:alice "PROOF-178677-SCHEDULED-OK"
```

The two rejected runs reached no model. The mock recorded 6 requests in the whole run: 2 for the create turn, 1 for the scheduler's existing owner-conversation repair brief after the second failure (Gateway run id `cron-failure-repair:8717eb54-...`), 2 for the re-save turn, and 1 for the recovered scheduled run. The Gateway log shows the two blocked runs ending in 686 ms and 56 ms with the error above.

Control on main `0d38c2dfcbfb`, same script, 18:08:11Z to 18:19:46Z:

```text
$ openclaw automations status                     "jobs": 2   (no reauthorizationRequired field)           [exit 0]
$ openclaw automations get / list --json / gateway call cron.list compact
                                                  no reauthorizationRequired field on any row, before or after the edit
18:12:52.947Z, 18:13:53.054Z  scheduled runs: "error": "Scheduled account \"creatorbot\" is unavailable. Re-add it to the
               channel configuration, or recreate this automation from the intended account."
$ openclaw automations run <id> --wait ...        "completionStatus": "failed", same error                      [exit 1]
           same-cap re-save from the alice DM -> callerOrigin {"kind":"external","channel":"qa-channel"}
18:19:21.268Z  scheduled run: "status": "ok", "summary": "PROOF-178677-SCHEDULED-OK", "deliveryStatus": "delivered"
```

On main the same job stays undiscoverable and its error tells the operator to re-add `creatorbot`, which was configured and running throughout: the Gateway logged `[qa-channel] [creatorbot] starting account` at startup, and every reply in the run, including the one sent during the blocked window, went out through `creatorbot`. The re-save path itself already existed on main and recovered there too, so this PR's change is the discovery surface and the accurate error, not the recovery mechanism.

Two earlier head attempts are excluded. In the first, `alice` was not a configured owner, so `automations` refused with "needs the owner's authority" and no job was created. The second re-saved `["read"]` instead of the stored `["read","skills_read"]`, which narrowed the cap, so it was not a same-cap re-save. Its status, get and list results, rejection, recovery and scheduled run otherwise matched the run above; it did not query the compact list.

### Base and head runs of the added tests

The PR's three changed test files, run with `pnpm test <files>` on October 26:

- Head `fe17c08e16d9`: `cron-tool.output-contract.test.ts` 5/5, `tools-allow.test.ts` 7/7, `agent-tools.policy.test.ts` 17/17.
- The same three files copied over main `0d38c2dfcbfb`: `accepts the reauthorization flags that Gateway projections emit` fails (1 failed, 4 passed); all 7 detector cases fail with `TypeError: cronJobNeedsCreatorReauthorization is not a function`; `names the missing creator channel when a DM-key scheduled account cannot resolve a channel` fails against the old message (1 failed, 16 passed).

### CI

At 18:57Z on October 26, `fe17c08e16d9` has 137 check runs: 85 successful, 51 skipped, 1 neutral (CodeQL), none failed. `accepts the reauthorization flags that Gateway projections emit` passed in [checks-node-changed-compact-large-1](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/actions/runs/40255363226/job/121356352628) and the command-job case in [checks-node-changed-compact-large-16](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/actions/runs/40255363226/job/121356352660). The two red commit statuses, `openclaw/security-sensitive-review` and `openclaw/ci-gate`, both read "A maintainer must approve the current PR revision". No approval is claimed here.

### Limits

- The channel is the repository's synthetic `qa-channel`, not Telegram or Discord. The authenticated turn and the scheduled delivery go through the same channel plugin boundary, but no real transport was exercised.
- The unknown origin came from an operator CLI edit, not from a job written by a release that predates origin recording.
- The human `openclaw automations show` view does not print the flag; the JSON surfaces above do. This PR does not change `show`.

prs.title: fix(workboard): attribute slow card-list waits
prs.body:
## What Problem This Solves

Slow Workboard card-list requests currently expose total RPC duration without showing whether they waited before the handler or in the card read itself.

## User Impact

Operators using the existing diagnostics and warning settings get a bounded phase breakdown for card-list requests taking at least one second. This is diagnostic only: it does not claim to fix the underlying latency, change request results, or require new configuration.

## Why This Change Was Made

Start timing at the gateway router so pre-handler authorization is included. Reuse the existing slow-request recorder and request-scoped timeline observer to separate admission/handler time and fixed nested session preparation phases, including row reads and publication settlement. Nested wall times overlap their parent phases. No request parameters, keys, paths, or error contents are logged, and fast requests remain quiet.

Production growth is 66 lines, justified by the requested missing attribution. There are no new caches, database operations, schemas, queues, or synchronization rules. Test growth is 114 lines for router success/failure attribution and bounded-span/privacy proof.

## Evidence

- The real router and session reader attribute a controlled 1,200 ms read delay to access preparation and session-row reads, separately from 25 ms of handler time. Success and thrown-error identity are preserved; private fixture values are absent from logs.
- Existing slow-request tests cover disabled/muted logging, fast calls, slow calls, numeric subscribers, trace context, and sink failure. Eight focused tests passed.
- On unchanged base `81cf32d99769`, both router regression cases fail specifically because no warning is emitted; response/error and handler assertions pass before that failure. All 52 affected session preparation/authorization/worker tests pass on the candidate.
- All 16 shared-response tests pass using the real logger contract; the Workboard case reproduced the incomplete logger fixture failure before this repair. Its gateway typecheck and focused lint pass.
- Codex autoreview: scoped clean at P0–P2 on the final settled index.

`pnpm check:changed --staged` found a test phase-type inference error and lint declaration issues. Those are corrected: `pnpm tsgo:core`, `pnpm tsgo:core:test`, focused lint, and the final eight diagnostic tests pass. All other gates in that full check passed; their unchanged results are reused. The test-line budget passes with four lines of remaining slack. The underlying production wait is unproven; the next slow-call sample supplies the missing phase evidence. The exploratory 10,000-card worker A/A probe had rebuild medians 14.54/14.53 ms, but did not include a large session database or btrfs contention and is not a production latency claim.

Final-head CI run [41141632450](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/actions/runs/41141632450), attempt 1, completed at `e751e6b319551cf4999ca43d700367a0dcf4f972`. All substantive jobs including `security-fast` passed except the inherited test-line ratchet; the aggregate CI gate failed downstream. The repaired shared-response shard passed.

Inherited-only attribution: CI tested merge `f26ad2c9d5bfa2800e9a9403158ce02f02769643` over main parent `26e7d07934e57b66a3b411bfd479a546ec66c692`. Base total/ceiling were 6,313,676 / 6,313,211; tested merge was 6,313,790 / 6,313,325. This PR adds exactly 114 test lines and 114 allocation, preserving the existing 465-line excess. Ratchet code and baseline scalar are unchanged. Local affected proof is green. Landing uses the authorized native pinned-head inherited-failure exception; failed CI is not represented as green.

prs.title: fix(skills): warn when a Workshop-applied skill is hidden by the agent allowlist
prs.body:
Closes #163824

## What Problem This Solves

Fixes: a skill created and applied through Skill Workshop stays hidden from the agent that authored it when that agent has a non-empty `agents.*.skills` allowlist. Apply reports success, but the skill is filtered out (`Excluded by agent allowlist`, `Visible to model: no`), and on the CLI runtime the agent only finds out when it gets `Unknown skill`.

## User Impact

Applying a Workshop proposal now warns, at apply time, that the agent's own skill allowlist hides the new skill, and names the exact config path to change (`agents.entries.<id>.skills` or `agents.defaults.skills`). The hint respects skill-allowlist inheritance: removing a per-agent list falls back to `agents.defaults.skills` (which may still exclude), and only removing the shared defaults list leaves skills unrestricted. Operators get the same warning from `openclaw skills workshop apply`. No config is mutated, so an explicit allowlist or `skills: []` lockdown keeps its meaning.

## Why This Change Was Made

Workshop apply writes the skill into the agent-scoped `<state-dir>/agents/<id>/agent/workshop-skills` directory but never consults the operator-owned `agents.*.skills` allowlist, which is the single source of truth for per-agent skill visibility. Auto-editing that config from the apply path would break config ownership and lockdown intent, so the existing allowlist owner now exposes the conflict and the apply surfaces it:

- `resolveAgentSkillAllowlistBlockPath(...)` / `formatAgentSkillAllowlistBlockHint(...)` in the agent-skill filter owner, reusing the same effective-filter resolution the runtime uses.
- `skill_workshop` apply result text (model-facing) and `openclaw skills workshop apply` human output (operator-facing; JSON output unchanged).

`openclaw skills info` already reports the exclusion, so it is left as-is.

## Evidence

Real apply output after the fix, in an isolated state dir with `agents.entries.probe.skills = ["github"]`.

**Agent tool (`skill_workshop` apply, model-facing):**

```
Applied skill proposal auto-authored-tool-20261004-669b8b1b80. Note: the skill allowlist at "agents.entries.probe.skills" does not include "Auto Authored Tool", so this agent cannot see or use it. Add "Auto Authored Tool" to it. Removing it falls back to agents.defaults.skills, which may still exclude this skill.
```

**CLI (`openclaw skills workshop apply <id> --agent probe`):**

```
Applied auto-authored-20261004-07d6cf14dc -> /tmp/oc-163824-evidence/state/agents/probe/agent/workshop-skills/auto-authored/SKILL.md
Note: the skill allowlist at "agents.entries.probe.skills" does not include "Auto Authored", so this agent cannot see or use it. Add "Auto Authored" to it. Removing it falls back to agents.defaults.skills, which may still exclude this skill.
```

**`openclaw skills info auto-authored --agent probe` (the exclusion the warning explains):**

```
auto-authored Excluded by agent allowlist
...
  Source: openclaw-workshop
  Visible to model: no
  Agent allowlist: excludes this skill
```

**Config after apply is unchanged** — `agents.entries.probe.skills` is still `["github"]`, so no operator config was mutated.

Local validation on this branch (measured with `--maxWorkers=1`):

- `src/agents/tools/skill-workshop-tool.test.ts` — 20 passed, 54.5s test wall (99.1s shard).
- `src/skills/discovery/chat-commands.discovery.test.ts` — 11 passed, 54.1s test wall (59.1s shard).
- `oxlint` on changed files — 0 warnings / 0 errors; `oxfmt --check` clean.
- `tsgo:core`, plus test shards `services` and `agents-tools` — passed.
- `pnpm openclaw --version` — built and ran the fixed CLI (`2026.9.8`, head `3411fc1`).

Note: this branch was rebased onto current `main` to resolve the earlier conflict; `main` had removed `resolveSkillsWorkspaceForCommand`, and the rebase now uses `resolveSkillsWorkspace({ agentId: resolveAgentOption(...) })`.

Authored with AI assistance (OpenClaw agent); the command output above was produced by running the fixed build locally.

prs.title: fix(media): allow CP932 CSV attachments without transcoding
prs.body:
Closes #178619

## What Problem This Solves

Fixes valid Japanese CP932 CSV attachments being rejected by host-read text validation before channel upload.

## User Impact

Users can attach structured CP932/Windows-31J CSV exports while retaining their original bytes and line endings for downstream importers. This does not transcode the file or expand filesystem permissions.

## Why This Change Was Made

After the existing UTF-8/Latin-1 text candidates fail validation, a CSV-only fallback strictly decodes Shift JIS and requires printable, rectangular records with quoted-field handling. It preserves the existing MIME-sniffing, root, size, and generated-HTML checks.

Current main now owns host-read admission in `src/media/host-read-media-policy.ts`. The conflict resolution places the CP932 fallback in that owner and preserves its generated-HTML provenance and explicit-publication checks. No dependency, setting, transport, or runtime patch is added.

## Evidence

- Fixed synthetic Japanese-heavy and quoted CSV tests both fail on base `79262d0571694dbf083b7d1bf5a206cc8fb93936` with the reported `LocalMediaAccessError`.
- `node scripts/run-vitest.mjs run src/media/web-media.test.ts`: **53 passed**, including exact original-byte comparisons, mostly-ASCII CP932, malformed/control-byte cases, renamed binary media, and existing root/size/HTML protections.
- Direct model-free `loadWebMedia` reproduction returns `document`, `text/csv`, and `exactBytes: true` on the fix.
- Core typecheck, all `tsgo:test:src` shards, touched-file type-aware oxlint, formatting, and `git diff --check` pass.
- Focused current-main Auto Review completed scoped-clean for P0/P1 after the policy-owner conflict resolution.
- Validation is at the production media-loader boundary. No patched live Gateway/channel upload has been deployed or claimed.
- Merged current main normally at exact head `129d62349970790218cba13e328168d0394cb8b8`; the PR diff against current main remains the policy owner plus its focused test.
- This authored problem statement and evidence apply to exact head `129d62349970790218cba13e328168d0394cb8b8`.

### Shipped Slack channel proof (2026-10-21)

Exact-head isolated Slack upload proof passed through the shipped `sendMessageSlack` entry point and real shared media loader/write client. The received raw upload body exactly matched the synthetic CP932 source and retained both CRLF pairs. Full sanitized evidence: https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/pull/178621#issuecomment-6306438571

### Application delivery receiver output

Exact head `129d62349970790218cba13e328168d0394cb8b8` was exercised through the shipped `sendMessageSlack` entry point with the real outbound-media loader and Slack WebClient. Only the SSRF transport was redirected to an isolated loopback receiver; the token, channel, and CP932 file were synthetic.

The receiver printed the complete application result and raw upload comparison:

prs.title: fix(feishu): reject synthetic reply anchors
prs.body:
Fixes #167270

## What Problem This Solves

A background task's completion/session event carries an internal UUID. Feishu previously inherited it as a native reply anchor, preferred it over the retained topic root, and lost the completion reply after HTTP400/code99992354. Native Feishu reply anchors must be `om_...` message IDs.

## Change and User Impact

Preserves @can2049's contributor commits and channel-boundary repair. The Feishu threading adapter explicitly rejects a synthetic currentMessageId and clears non-native replyToId while retaining the existing thread route. Message-tool topic anchoring falls back to the retained native root after rejecting the synthetic trigger. Existing destination, account, provider and opt-out checks remain intact; ordinary native replies are unchanged. No retries, top-level fallback, new config or SDK exports.

The module extractions retain the existing routing owners; repeated adapter type annotations now reuse the existing ChannelPlugin contract. Production gross195→177 lines (+115/-62, net+53). The existing topic suite now covers UUID context rejection, reply-transport normalization and retained-root sends without new test files: test delta-1 (+37/-38). Native explicit replies and destination/account/opt-out controls remain covered. Added a short operator note about native anchors.

## Evidence

[Paired built-Gateway Feishu Open API fixture proof](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/pull/177297#issuecomment-6534321756).

Secretless Linux Docker, Node24.22.1; full main/candidate builds. A signed native Feishu webhook starts a real background exec. Its actual process completion generates the internal UUID through session-event handoff. Main sends the UUID to the reply API and fails twice; candidate replies to the native root with reply_in_thread:true and succeeds in the original topic twice. Normal foreground native-anchor controls succeed on both refs. No adjacent topic overlay or source-owner swaps.

This is a faithful **local HTTPS Feishu API fixture**, not live tenant proof. The channel SDK, Gateway, webhook authentication, background process, handoff, model continuation and outbound requests are real; Feishu API and model responses are fixtures. Acceptance records show the original root/thread, not live Feishu readback. The contributor's earlier live deployment included a disclosed adjacent overlay; it is supplementary, not the paired current-main proof.

Both runtime builds and targeted Oxfmt/Oxlint pass; channel/outbound suites:150 passed. prs.title: docs(install): add vendor-neutral NVIDIA Jetson install guide
prs.body:
## What Problem This Solves

Adds `docs/install/jetson.md` — a vendor-neutral install guide for running the OpenClaw Gateway on NVIDIA Jetson hardware, mirroring the structure of the existing `raspberry-pi.md`.

This implements the docs gap raised in #94893, following the review recommendation on that issue: a hardware-tested neutral page that uses official NVIDIA links and keeps commercial turnkey products out of core docs.

## Why

`docs/install/` covers Raspberry Pi and ~20 cloud/VPS targets, but has no guide for Jetson-class edge hardware — an increasingly common always-on, local-first target. Jetson differs from the Pi in ways that justify a separate page: JetPack/L4T versioning, `nvpmodel` power modes, zram-by-default swap, NVMe, and thermal behaviour.

## Evidence

NVIDIA Jetson Orin Nano Super Developer Kit — L4T **R36.5.0 (JetPack 6.2)**, Ubuntu 22.04.5, kernel 5.15.185-tegra, 6 cores / 7.4 GB RAM, NVMe:

```console
$ uname -m
aarch64

$ node -p "process.arch"             # Node 22.23.2 via NodeSource
arm64

$ openclaw --version                 # runs natively, no build step
OpenClaw 2026.7.1

$ loginctl show-user "$(whoami)" | grep Linger
Linger=no

$ swapon --show=NAME --noheadings    # zram, not disk swap
/dev/zram0 /dev/zram1 /dev/zram2 /dev/zram3 /dev/zram4 /dev/zram5

$ grep POWER_MODEL /etc/nvpmodel.conf
< POWER_MODEL ID=0 NAME=15W >
< POWER_MODEL ID=1 NAME=25W >
< POWER_MODEL ID=2 NAME=MAXN_SUPER >

$ command -v tegrastats jetson_clocks
/usr/bin/tegrastats
/usr/bin/jetson_clocks
```

ARM64 prebuilds resolve (for example `@lydell/node-pty-linux-arm64/prebuilds/linux-arm64/pty.node`), so no compilation is required.

Two items in the guide come from testing rather than assumption:

- **Lingering is disabled by default** on these images, so a headless `systemd --user` gateway stops on logout. This is called out as its own setup step.
- **`nvpmodel` mode IDs are module-specific.** On this board `0` is the throttled 15 W mode and `2` is `MAXN_SUPER`, so the guide tells readers to list the available modes instead of hard-coding an ID.

## Disclosure

I work at ID-Robots, which sells Jetson-based hardware. Per the guidance on #94893 and the outcome of #87627, this page is deliberately **vendor-neutral**: no product names, no turnkey-device list, official NVIDIA links only. Happy to adjust scope, reword, trim, or drop it entirely if a Jetson page is not wanted in core docs.
