prs.title: feat(zerocode): steer the running turn when you send a message mid-turn
prs.body:
## Summary

- **Base branch:** `master` (all contributions)
- **What changed and why:**
  - #11132 added daemon `session/steer`; eligible ZeroCode Submit now offers plain text to the running turn when the queue is empty, preserving message order. Attachments, cancellation, approval prompts, and existing queued work retain their current paths.
  - An accepted steer appears after text already streamed, without starting another client turn. Acceptance confirms enqueueing, not consumption by the agent.
  - An explicit refusal or RPC error reply queues the text. A timeout restores it to the input with `zc-steer-unconfirmed`, without automatically resending it.
  - If a turn with an accepted steer ends `Cancelled` or `Failed`, `zc-steer-ended-early` warns that the text may not have been read. The flag resets at terminal settlement, fresh turn start, resync reset, and session reset. `Completed` does not show this warning.
- **Scope boundary:** `apps/zerocode` only. No daemon/runtime changes, Cargo files, CI, new key bindings or settings, attachment steering, or async key-action refactor. Inject continues to cancel the turn. The synchronous steer await can still pause the TUI for up to 5 seconds.
- **Blast radius:** ZeroCode's running-turn Submit path, client RPC wrapper, turn settlement, and localized info notices. Idle Submit and other daemon clients retain their behavior.
- **Linked issue(s):** Related #11132, Related #9487. Daemon steer-consumed/steer-dropped signaling remains follow-up work; no dedicated open issue was found in the issue search. No issue is closed by this PR.

### What this does, simply

When the agent is working, type a follow-up and press Enter to offer it to the same turn. Before, it waited in the client queue and started a separate turn. Only plain text with no earlier queued messages takes this path.

The agent can read a steer between steps. It cannot interrupt a single long tool call, such as a build, until that call returns. An explicit refusal sends the message to the queue. If delivery times out, the message returns to the input with a reminder to check before sending again.

If the turn is cancelled or fails after accepting a steer, an info notice says: “This turn ended early; a message you sent into it may not have been read. Check before sending it again.” The client cannot tell which accepted messages the daemon consumed. Some daemon drops still end as `Completed`, so this warning cannot detect them. Steered text can appear in the transcript yet be absent from session history after reload.

## Testing (required)

### How you can test (when useful)

- **Reviewer testing requested?** Yes. The cancel-after-steer case was captured live on head `46f3999a52` (https://github.com/zeroclaw-labs/zeroclaw/pull/11621#issuecomment-6514782111). The failed-after-steer ending and the steer timeout were also captured live on `46f3999a52`, using a local stub provider and a paused daemon (https://github.com/Audacity88/zeroclaw/blob/evidence-screenshots/pr-11621/live-46f3999a5/MANIFEST.txt). A steer during a long tool call was not captured live, because the stub provider makes no tool calls.
- **Interface(s) exercised:** `surface`: `tui`; messaging channel: N/A, this is the direct daemon TUI.
- **Setup / preconditions:** A current daemon with `session/steer` and ZeroCode built from the final repaired revision. Use a session with an empty queue and a multi-step task. A long tool call makes the cancel path easier to observe.
- **Steps to run:** Start “list the files in this repo one directory at a time”. While tools run, type “also count them” and press Enter. In a separate run, send that steer during a long tool call, then press Esc before it finishes. The failure state is covered by `chat::tests::an_accepted_steer_then_failed_turn_shows_delivery_notice`. It was also reproduced live: a stub provider returns HTTP 400 after the steer. For the timeout, pause the daemon (`kill -STOP`) for over 5 s while steering, then `kill -CONT` it. See https://github.com/Audacity88/zeroclaw/blob/evidence-screenshots/pr-11621/live-46f3999a5/MANIFEST.txt.
- **Expected on this branch (after):** On acceptance the message appears in the transcript, the queue stays empty, and no new client turn starts. Cancellation or failure shows the early-end delivery warning. Successful completion shows no such warning. Sending the next ordinary prompt clears the notice and starts with a clean accepted-steer flag. A timeout restores the input and warns without automatically queueing or resending.
- **Prior behavior on `master` (before):** The same mid-turn message waits in the client queue instead of steering the active turn. On the published pre-repair PR head, accepted steering followed by cancellation or failure leaves a sent-looking transcript row with no delivery warning.

### How I tested

- **CI checks relied on and why they cover this change:** [`CI Required Gate`](https://github.com/zeroclaw-labs/zeroclaw/actions/runs/40999201897) passed on the current head `46f3999a5`, including Format, Lint, Test, and Zerocode RPC Boundary.
- **Known CI coverage gap, if any:** Live transport is not covered by automated tests. Instead, the cancel-after-steer, failed-after-steer and steer-timeout cases were checked live (see Visual interface evidence). A long tool call was not exercised live.
- **Commands run and tail output:**

  Run on head `46f3999a5` (master merge `ef039234e` + `5a261d989` early-end notice + `46f3999a5` removal of the rendered evidence tests), Mac mini, `zc-cargo-narrow`, `-j2`, `--test-threads=2`:

  ```text
  cargo fmt --all -- --check                                  ok
  cargo clippy -p zerocode --all-targets -- -D warnings        ok
  cargo test -p zerocode
    zerocode (lib)       54 passed; 0 failed
    zerocode (bin)       1572 passed; 2 failed; 2 ignored
    terminal_disconnect  3 passed
  ```

  Both failures also fail on clean master `5a51398dd` on this machine and are not touched by this PR: `connection_tests::insecure_tls_prompt_preserves_default_sigint` and `app::tests::input_wait_returns_early_for_pending_transport_events` (timing-sensitive under load; failed 3/3 on master here).

  Focused tests in that run (all pass):

  - `client::session_method_tests::session_steer_sends_content_and_reads_accepted`
  - `chat::tests::steering_is_offered_only_for_a_plain_message_into_a_running_turn`
  - `chat::tests::a_steered_message_joins_the_running_turn_without_starting_one`
  - `chat::tests::a_steer_on_the_last_output_does_not_repeat_the_answer_at_completion`
  - `chat::tests::a_steer_timeout_is_not_treated_as_a_refusal`
  - `chat::tests::submit_during_a_running_turn_steers_and_falls_back_to_the_queue`
  - `chat::tests::an_unanswered_steer_returns_the_text_to_the_input_instead_of_queueing`
  - `chat::tests::an_accepted_steer_then_cancelled_turn_shows_delivery_notice`
  - `chat::tests::an_accepted_steer_then_failed_turn_shows_delivery_notice`
  - `chat::tests::an_accepted_steer_then_completed_turn_has_no_delivery_notice`
  - `chat::tests::a_turn_after_cancelled_steering_starts_without_delivery_uncertainty`

  The existing `i18n::tests::en_catalogue_parses` and `i18n::tests::argument_messages_format_in_all_builtin_catalogues` also remain relevant catalogue checks. New key presence and distinct translations were checked statically in all five locale sources; this is not a Fluent parser or runtime test.
- **Beyond CI, what did you manually verify?** Historical live acceptance run on experiment build [`20261015T062922Z-af67956b5e9d`](https://github.com/Audacity88/zeroclaw/tree/experiment/zerocode-builds/20261015T062922Z-af67956b5e9d), carrying this change and #11725 on dogfood base [`20261008T194402Z-0341618f9d69`](https://github.com/Audacity88/zeroclaw/tree/dogfood/zerocode-builds/20261008T194402Z-0341618f9d69). During a multi-step file-listing task, “also count them” appeared immediately in the transcript, no new turn started, and the agent acted on it at its next tool step. This is acceptance evidence on a stacked build, not a live test of this repair. The final-head cancel-after-steer run remains pending from Dan.
- **Visual interface evidence:** Real screenshots of the current head (46f3999a52): see comment https://github.com/zeroclaw-labs/zeroclaw/pull/11621#issuecomment-6514782111 (steer accepted into the running turn with an empty queue; Esc cancel showing the early-end delivery notice). Also on 46f3999a52: [S01 steer accepted](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Audacity88/zeroclaw/evidence-screenshots/pr-11621/live-46f3999a5/S01-failslow-steer-accepted.png), [S02 provider failure after the steer, with the early-end notice](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Audacity88/zeroclaw/evidence-screenshots/pr-11621/live-46f3999a5/S02-failed-after-steer-ended-early-notice.png), [S03 steer RPC timeout: text back in the input with `zc-steer-unconfirmed`](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Audacity88/zeroclaw/evidence-screenshots/pr-11621/live-46f3999a5/S03-steer-rpc-timeout-unconfirmed-text-back-in-input.png), and [S04 after the daemon resumes, the steer had arrived and the text was not resent](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Audacity88/zeroclaw/evidence-screenshots/pr-11621/live-46f3999a5/S04-after-resume-steer-had-arrived-text-still-in-input.png).
- **Tested revision, interface, and evidence path:** `46f3999a52`, ZeroCode Chat over local RPC, daemon and client from the same debug build, Terminal.app at 150×42.
- **Screenshot or exact-output evidence:** https://github.com/zeroclaw-labs/zeroclaw/pull/11621#issuecomment-6514782111: the steer shown inside the running turn with Queue (0), then Esc and the early-end delivery notice. Failed and timeout endings: https://github.com/Audacity88/zeroclaw/blob/evidence-screenshots/pr-11621/live-46f3999a5/ (S01 to S04, with MANIFEST and stub).
- **Action or changed state and observed result:** Covered by the lifecycle tests above: an accepted steer followed by a cancelled or failed turn shows the delivery notice; a completed turn and the next turn do not. The live capture above shows the cancelled case.
- **If any command was intentionally skipped, why:** Workspace-wide tests were skipped; the change is confined to `apps/zerocode`. No live capture of the repaired state was made.


## Security & Privacy Impact (required)

- New permissions, capabilities, or file system access scope? No. Existing daemon session authorization and steering admission apply.
- New external network calls? Yes. Eligible Submit sends `session/steer` over the existing authenticated daemon connection. It adds no destination or connection type, and refusal uses the existing queue.
- Secrets / tokens / credentials handling changed? No.
- PII, real identities, or personal data in diff, tests, fixtures, or docs? No. Test text is synthetic.
- Prompt injection or untrusted model-visible text introduced/changed? No new untrusted source. User-authored follow-ups use the daemon's existing steering admission instead of waiting for another turn.
- If any `Yes`, describe the risk and mitigation: The new RPC can time out after enqueueing. Unknown delivery returns the text to the input without automatic resend; accepted steering followed by cancellation/failure shows a caution. Session permissions and admission rules remain daemon-owned.

## Compatibility (required)

- Backward compatible? Yes. An older daemon that lacks `session/steer` returns an error, so the text queues as before. No wire schema or persisted data format changes.
- Config / env / CLI surface changed? No config, environment variable, command syntax, or key binding changes. TUI Enter behavior during eligible running turns changes as described above.
- Rust/MSRV/toolchain floor changed? No.
- If backward compatibility is `No` or either surface/floor question is `Yes`: exact upgrade steps for existing users: N/A - no configuration migration or toolchain upgrade is required. Update ZeroCode normally; localized catalogue updates are distributed through the existing locale fetch path.

## Rollback (required for medium/high-risk PRs)

This is `risk:medium` behavioral work. The low-risk default does not apply.

Medium/high-risk PRs must fill:

- **Fast rollback command/path:** Before merge, switch to the previously working ZeroCode binary. After squash merge, `git revert <merge-commit-of-this-PR>`, rebuild, and redeploy ZeroCode through the normal release path. The daemon and stored sessions need no rollback or migration; eligible mid-turn messages return to the client queue behavior.
- **Feature flags or config toggles:** None.
- **Observable failure symptoms:** A steered message appears in the transcript but is missing from session history after reload; cancellation/failure leaves no warning; duplicate execution after a timeout; duplicate final answers; or drawing, streamed updates, and key handling freeze for up to 5 seconds after Enter while awaiting steering. Completed-path daemon drops remain undetectable without consumed/dropped signaling.

## Supersede Attribution (required only when `Supersedes #` is used)

N/A - no Supersedes

- Superseded PRs + authors (`#<pr> by @<author>`, one per line): N/A - no Supersedes.
- Scope materially carried forward: N/A - no replaced PR.
- `Co-authored-by` trailers added in commit messages for incorporated contributors? No.
- If `No`, why (inspiration-only, no direct code/design carry-over): N/A - no incorporated superseded contributor work.

---

**Labels** live in the GitHub label UI, not in the body. The PR path labeler owns path/scope labels from `.github/labeler.yml`, and the PR size labeler owns canonical `size:*` labels. Maintainers and reviewers with label permissions still set `risk:*` and any missing manual labels via the sidebar. Contributors without label permission can note obvious label mismatches in a comment. Canonical colon-scoped labels use no-space spelling; during migration, copy exact live label spelling from the GitHub UI.

**Do not add bot/AI attribution footers** such as `Co-authored-by: Claude ...`
or `Created with Claude Code` to the PR body or commit-message tail. Human
co-author trailers are appropriate only for incorporated contributor work under
the supersede-attribution section and privacy contract.

**Privacy contract** (`docs/book/src/contributing/privacy.md`) is a merge gate. Never commit real identities, secrets, personal emails, or PII in diff, tests, fixtures, or docs.

prs.title: feat(zerocode): refresh the focused session without cancellation
prs.body:
## Summary

- **Base branch:** `master`
- **What changed and why:** Add F5 to refresh the focused Code or Chat session through the existing read-only session APIs. Keep local drafts, attachments, queues and interactions instead of invoking cancel-first recovery. Retain selection and reading position when their transcript entries still match; refuse replacement when they do not.
- **Scope boundary:** No polling, cancellation, automatic retries, cross-client streaming, new RPC method, authorization change or persistence migration.
- **Blast radius:** Shared ZeroCode Chat/ACP key handling, transcript projection and cached rendering. The daemon and other clients are unchanged.
- **Linked issue(s):** Refs #10695. This implements the manual-refresh slice.
- **Labels:** `enhancement`, `risk:medium`, `size:XL`, `zerocode`, `docs`.

### What this does, simply

ZeroCode lets you keep several agent conversations open. Another authorized client can send a message to one of those sessions, but the already-open pane can keep showing its older transcript. Closing and reopening the session reloads it, at the cost of disrupting the local view.

With this change, press F5 in Code or Chat to read the focused session again. A completed exchange returned by the daemon is added to the view without sending another prompt or cancelling a turn. Your unsent draft, attachments and queued messages stay in the pane. If the session is busy, the read fails, or selected content cannot be matched safely, the existing view stays available with a notice.

This is an explicit, point-in-time refresh. It does not stream another client's response or keep the pane synchronized in the background.

Refresh rebuilds the stored transcript. Local-only transcript rows, such as notices, can disappear.

### Scope and maintenance tradeoff

The daemon remains the history owner. Both panes use the existing shared Chat action and history projection. Most of the remaining client work matches transcript entries and preserves reading/selection anchors; calling recovery or resetting the pane would discard state that #10695 requires retaining. The diff also includes focused preservation regressions. Append-only histories reuse the existing rendered prefix. No new runtime or transport owner is introduced.

## Testing (required)

### How you can test

- **Reviewer testing requested?** Yes. I ran the two-client smoke myself (below); an independent run is welcome.
- **Interface(s) exercised:** `surface=tui`, Code/ACP and Chat.
- **Setup / preconditions:** Run this branch's ZeroCode against a compatible daemon. Open a harmless dedicated session and keep it focused. A second authorized RPC client must be able to resume that same session.
- **Steps to run:** Leave an unsent draft and a paused queued message in the pane. From the second client, submit a harmless prompt to the same session and wait for completion. Select unchanged text in the existing pane, then press F5. Also press F5 once while the second client still has a turn running.
- **Expected on this branch (after):** The completed exchange appears after refresh; the local draft, attachment ownership, paused queue, selection and reading position remain. Refresh during a running turn reports busy without cancellation.
- **Prior behavior on `master` (before):** F5 has no focused-session refresh action. The already-open transcript can remain stale until the session is reopened.

Run on head `204ca052d` (Linux x86_64, Rust 1.98.0, the CI toolchain):

```text

cargo clippy --locked -p zerocode --all-targets -- -D warnings   ok
cargo test --locked -p zerocode
  zerocode (lib)       52 passed; 0 failed

  terminal_disconnect  3 passed
bash scripts/ci/comment_hygiene_gate.sh          Comment hygiene gate passed.
bash scripts/ci/zerocode_no_zeroclaw_dep_gate.sh zerocode gate passed: no zeroclaw-* implementation dependencies.
```

The one failure, `connection_tests::insecure_tls_prompt_preserves_default_sigint`, also fails on clean `master` on these machines and is not touched by this PR.

- **CI checks relied on and why they cover this change:** [`CI Required Gate`](https://github.com/zeroclaw-labs/zeroclaw/actions/runs/40932393331) passed on the current head `204ca052d`: Formatting, Lint, workspace Test, ZeroCode RPC-only, MSRV and platform checks.
- **Known CI coverage gap:** The focused suite drives the real Chat action, RPC request sequence, asynchronous result application and production renderer with controlled daemon responses. It does not submit a turn through a second real client or exercise daemon persistence.
- **Beyond CI, what did you manually verify?** A live two-client run on the current head `204ca052d` (Linux, daemon and both clients from one debug build, local stub provider; [manifest](https://github.com/Audacity88/zeroclaw/blob/evidence-screenshots/pr-11457/live-204ca052d/MANIFEST.txt)). Client B resumed client A's session and completed a turn. F5 in A then imported that exchange and kept the unsent draft and the `notes.txt` attachment. F5 while B's slow turn was running showed the busy notice and left the transcript unchanged. That turn completed without being cancelled, and a second F5 imported it. Earlier, a two-client smoke on the experiment build [`20261015T062922Z-af67956b5e9d`](https://github.com/Audacity88/zeroclaw/tree/experiment/zerocode-builds/20261015T062922Z-af67956b5e9d) ([commit](https://github.com/Audacity88/zeroclaw/commit/af67956b5e9d1b9a9f0521dab4a1f48c999d6e71); dogfood base [`0341618f9d69`](https://github.com/Audacity88/zeroclaw/commit/0341618f9d69e31bf38300d134ba86e98491d49d), which carries this change). prs.body:
## Summary

- **Base branch:** `master` (all contributions)
- **What changed and why:**
  - Windows `SAFE_SHELL_ENV_VARS` (shell + skill tools) now forwards `APPDATA` and `LOCALAPPDATA`, matching the coding-CLI allowlist.
  - Hardware `SubprocessTool::SAFE_ENV_VARS` on Windows forwards the same two variables.
  - Source-level regression tests keep those entries from being dropped on non-Windows CI.
- **Scope boundary:** Does not change Unix allowlists, coding-CLI allowlists (already correct), or passthrough/env policy beyond these two names.
- **Blast radius:** Windows shell, skill, and hardware child processes only. Children that previously lacked profile roots will now see operator config/cred/cache paths under `%APPDATA%` / `%LOCALAPPDATA%`.

### What this does, simply

On Windows, ZeroClaw clears the child environment and then copies back a short allowlist before running shell, skill, or hardware tools. Most Windows CLIs (including `gh` and `npm`) look under those folders for login state and caches, so they behaved as if logged out or misconfigured even when the operator's own terminal was fine. The coding-CLI path already forwarded both variables; this PR brings shell, skill, and hardware children into line.

prs.title: fix(mcp-builder): support mcp>=2 streamable_http_client import and custom headers
prs.body:
Fixes #1668

### Problem
In `mcp>=2.0.0`, `streamablehttp_client` was renamed to `streamable_http_client`, and custom HTTP headers are configured via `create_mcp_http_client` / `http_client` rather than as a direct kwarg to `streamable_http_client`.

Because `skills/mcp-builder/scripts/connections.py` unconditionally imported `streamablehttp_client` at module scope, importing `connections` or running `evaluation.py` fails on startup when installing `requirements.txt` (which specifies `mcp>=1.1.0` without an upper bound):

```
Traceback (most recent call last):
  File ".../scripts/evaluation.py", line 19, in <module>
    from connections import create_connection
  File ".../scripts/connections.py", line 10, in <module>
    from mcp.client.streamable_http import streamablehttp_client
ImportError: cannot import name 'streamablehttp_client' from 'mcp.client.streamable_http'
```

### Solution
1. **Compatible import:** In `skills/mcp-builder/scripts/connections.py`, import `streamable_http_client` and `create_mcp_http_client` with fallback to `streamablehttp_client as streamable_http_client` for `mcp<2.0.0`.
2. **Context configuration:** In `MCPConnectionHTTP._create_context()`:
   - When `create_mcp_http_client` is available, create `http_client` with custom headers and pass to `streamable_http_client(url=self.url, http_client=http_client)`.
   - On `mcp<2.0.0`, pass `headers=self.headers` directly.
3. **Regression tests:** Added `skills/mcp-builder/scripts/test_connections.py` testing import resolution, stdio/sse/http transport factories, context manager creation, and validation error cases.

### Verification
- Ran `pytest skills/mcp-builder/scripts/test_connections.py -v`: all 5 tests passed.
- Verified `python skills/mcp-builder/scripts/evaluation.py --help` under `mcp 2.1.1` and Python 3.14: cleanly displays full usage and exits 0.
- Verified compilation with `python -m py_compile`.

prs.title: fix(skill-creator): isolate trigger evals and handle Windows and runtime failures
prs.body:
## Problem

Trigger evaluation can report false misses or invalid scores: per-worker command probes compete, select() on subprocess pipes fails on Windows, and unrelated tools stop the scan. Runtime failures also become non-triggers, incorrectly passing negative examples and misleading optimization.

Fixes #556.

## What changes

- Install one real candidate skill at `<temporary project>/.claude/skills/<name>/SKILL.md`, preserving its production name and candidate description. Parallel workers share it; concurrent runs use distinct UUID-based roots.
- Leave caller files untouched. The legacy `project_root` argument remains accepted but is no longer used.
- Reject same-name personal skill collisions, including those under `CLAUDE_CONFIG_DIR`.
- Resolve the Claude executable, including Windows npm shims. Read stdout/stderr with portable threads instead of select(). Close stdin and cap probes at eight turns.
- Keep scanning after Bash/Glob and other orientation tools. Match exact Skill names or skill-entrypoint Read paths, including Windows separators.
- Stop the probe process tree during cleanup: `taskkill /T /F` on Windows; a separate session/process group on POSIX.
- Treat error results, timeouts, truncated output and worker failures as invalid evaluations. Abort the batch instead of assigning zero trigger rates. Cancel pending work where possible; active workers finish their bounded cleanup.
- Preserve successful evaluation JSON. Initial optimization failures propagate; later failures preserve completed iterations. Empty and partial reports render correctly.
- Write candidate artifacts as UTF-8.

## Validation

Latest revision: Windows, Python 3.14.

```sh
# From skills/skill-creator
python -m unittest discover -s scripts/tests -v
uvx ruff check scripts/run_eval.py scripts/tests/test_eval_failures.py scripts/tests/test_stream_probe.py
git diff --check
```

- **21/21 tests pass.** Coverage includes artifact isolation, exact matching, late triggers, configuration collisions, invalid batch rejection, cleanup and partial-result recovery.
- A real Windows .cmd wrapper launches a Python child; the regression verifies that the child cannot continue after timeout. This test requires process-termination permissions and was run outside the restricted sandbox.
- Ruff passes for the files changed in the latest revision. Whitespace checks pass.
- Tests make no model calls and need no credentials. Instructions and limitations are in `scripts/tests/README.md`.

## Scope and limitations

The temporary project excludes caller-project files and configuration. Queries requiring local fixtures need those fixtures made available separately. Personal and managed Claude configuration is not fully isolated.

The original investigation included live routing experiments on Claude Code 2.1.149. Those historical observations are not a claim about every current version. This revision has not rerun live model evaluation or POSIX integration. The candidate uses the standard skill layout independently of legacy command behavior.

Related work: #794, #996, #1027, #1755 and #1757. This PR combines a real-skill artifact with portable stream handling, full-turn detection and explicit failure semantics.

## What changed
`skills/docx/scripts/accept_changes.py` now returns an Error when `soffice` times out instead of reporting success, and only claims success after checking that the output DOCX no longer carries revision marks (`w:ins` / `w:del` / `w:moveFrom` / `w:moveTo`) in `word/*.xml` parts.

Defect 1 in #1770: `soffice` operates in place on a copy and the macro stores/closes the document itself, so a timeout leaves the output in an unknown state (possibly untouched, possibly partly processed) while the caller was told "Successfully accepted all tracked changes". `__main__` keys on `"Error" in message`, so the process also exited 0.

## How verified
LibreOffice is not installed in this environment, so the fix is verified with mocked `subprocess.run` plus real DOCX fixtures:
- Timeout (`subprocess.TimeoutExpired`): returns an Error mentioning the timeout, never "Successfully".
- `returncode == 0` but the output still contains `<w:ins>`: returns "tracked changes remain in output document".
- `returncode == 0` with a clean output DOCX: still reports success.
- `_docx_still_has_tracked_changes`: True for each revision marker (`w:ins`, `w:del`, `w:moveFrom`, `w:moveTo`) and for a non-zip file, False for a clean DOCX.
- `python -m py_compile` clean; no new third-party imports (`zipfile` is stdlib).

prs.title: fix(skill-creator): support direct execution of package_skill.py and update usage paths
prs.body:
### Problem
Running \package_skill.py\ directly as a standalone script (e.g., \python skills/skill-creator/scripts/package_skill.py <skill-path>\) fails with \ModuleNotFoundError: No module named 'scripts.quick_validate'\. Additionally, the docstrings and CLI help messages contain outdated references to \utils/package_skill.py\ and \skills/public/...\.

### Root Cause
When executed directly as a script, Python places the script's immediate directory (\skills/skill-creator/scripts\) at \sys.path[0]\, preventing the top-level \scripts\ package from being resolved.

### Solution
1. Add the parent \skill-creator\ directory to \sys.path\ if not already present, allowing \ rom scripts.quick_validate import validate_skill\ to resolve under both direct script execution and module execution (\python -m scripts.package_skill\).
2. Update the docstring and CLI help usage examples to reference current repository paths (\scripts/package_skill.py\ and \skills/brand-guidelines\).

### Verification

- Direct execution from \skills/skill-creator\: \python scripts/package_skill.py ../brand-guidelines\
- Module execution from \skills/skill-creator\: \python -m scripts.package_skill ../brand-guidelines\
- Verified CLI usage message when called without arguments.

### Risk
Low. The change is limited to \package_skill.py\ and preserves the existing \scripts.quick_validate\ import. Direct and module execution were both verified successfully.

prs.title: Add document-typography skill: typographic quality control for generated documents
prs.body:
Prevents common typographic problems in AI-generated documents: orphan word wrap (1-6 words spilling onto the next line), widow paragraphs (section headers stranded at page bottom), and numbering misalignment.

These issues affect every document Claude generates. Users rarely ask for good typography, but they notice when it's bad.

**How it works**

The skill introduces a render-check-fix cycle: generate the document, convert to PDF, render pages as images, visually inspect, fix and regenerate. It also includes the M-count method — count how many capital M's (the widest character) fit on one line. Any real text will always be narrower, eliminating orphan wrap entirely.

**Included scripts**
- `measure_m_count.py` — Safe character limit per line using font metrics
- `check_orphans.py` — Reports lines at risk of orphan wrap
- `check_layout.sh` — One-command docx → PDF → page images
- `measure_line_width.py` — Visual line-width calibration

**Origin**

This skill emerged from iterative human-AI collaboration between [@PGTBoos](https://github.com/PGTBoos) and Claude. The user kept pointing out what the AI couldn't see (orphan words, widow paragraphs, layout balance) until the patterns were systematic enough to codify into a reusable skill. The M-count formula was the user's insight. The user actively wants to make LLMs more human-like, and sees this contribution as a help for both AI and humans writing skills.

- [x] SKILL.md with valid YAML frontmatter
- [x] Scripts are self-contained
- [x] Complements existing docx/pptx/pdf skills

prs.title: Improve frontend-design skill clarity and actionability
prs.body:
## Summary

This PR revises the frontend-design skill to improve clarity, actionability, and internal coherence. The goal was to ensure every instruction is something Claude can actually follow within a single conversation, and that the skill's guidance is specific enough to steer behavior without being prescriptive.

## Background

I've been exploring Anthropic's open-source ecosystem after building a [GUI for Bloom](https://www.justinwetch.com/blog/anthropicbloom) and [proposing new behaviors](https://www.justinwetch.com/blog/10behaviorsbloom) for it. Looking through the Skills repo, the frontend-design skill caught my attention. Reading through it, I noticed a few places where the instructions, while well-intentioned, weren't quite actionable from the model's perspective.

For example, the original skill said "NEVER converge on common choices (Space Grotesk, for example) across generations" and "No design should be the same." The intent is clear: avoid repetitive patterns. But Claude can't see its other generations. Each conversation is isolated. These instructions are impossible to follow because they reference information the model doesn't have access to.

This got me thinking about what I call "model theory of mind": reasoning about what the model can actually know and how it processes instructions. A prompt can sound good to humans but be confusing or non-actionable for the model. I wrote up my thinking in more detail [here](https://www.justinwetch.com/blog/scaffold).

## Key Changes

**Coherence fixes:**
- Removed instructions assuming cross-session awareness ("never converge across generations," "no design should be the same")
- Resolved internal contradictions ("pick an extreme" conflicted with "the key is intentionality, not intensity")

**Clarity improvements:**
- Replaced vague adjectives ("beautiful, unique, interesting") with concrete guidance
- Rewrote the Typography section to focus on actionable instructions rather than aesthetic judgments
- Added specific palette directions to Color guidance (bold/saturated, moody/restrained, high-contrast/minimal)

**Structural additions:**
- Added INSTEAD block to pair positive instructions with existing NEVER guidance
- Expanded aesthetic direction list (added dark/moody, lo-fi/zine, handcrafted/artisanal)
- Expanded spatial composition guidance (z-depth, full-bleed, dramatic scale jumps)
- Unified imperative voice throughout

## Validation

I built an evaluation system to test whether the changes actually improved outputs. The setup:

- 50 representative prompts covering different design contexts (landing pages, dashboards, portfolios, menus, band pages, etc.)
- Each prompt executed twice via API: once with original skill, once with revised skill
- Puppeteer captures full-page screenshots of both outputs
- Claude Opus 4.5 judges blind (screenshots anonymized as A/B) on five criteria: Prompt Adherence, Aesthetic Fit, Visual Polish, UX & Usability, Creative Distinction

Results across the Claude 4.5 model family: Haiku showed the strongest improvement (8-2), followed by Sonnet (7-3), then Opus (6-4). Across all three tiers, the revised skill won 21 of 28 decisive comparisons (75% win rate, p = 0.006).

Interestingly, the revised skill helped smaller models more than larger ones. My hypothesis is that Opus can compensate for ambiguous instructions, while Haiku benefits more from explicit guidance.

## More Detail

For a full walkthrough of the approach, reasoning, and specific edits: [Teaching Claude to Design Better: Improving Anthropic's Frontend Design Skill](https://www.justinwetch.com/blog/improvingclaudefrontend)

Happy to discuss any of the changes or adjust based on feedback.

# Add architecture-advisor skill: pattern selection with written justification

Fourth skill from the [harness](https://github.com/jordimarsal/harness) SDD
suite (MIT) — companion to the three skills in PR #2039. Where that PR covers
*how to run* feature work (specs, dispatch, review), this one covers *the
first decision*: which core architecture pattern a service should use.

## What it does

A decision procedure, not a lecture:

1. **Three selectors** — domain complexity, team size, scaling needs — answered
   in one line each.
2. **Catalog of 8 core patterns** (layered, hexagonal, clean, CQRS,
   microservices, modular monolith, event-driven, functional core/imperative
   shell), each with what/best-for/trade-offs/when-NOT-to-use.
3. **Per-pattern detail files** with principles, data flow and a "Do Not" list —
   the list of ways each pattern actually fails in practice.
4. **Overlay tables** chosen independently: API style (REST/GraphQL/gRPC/WS),
   frontend integration, data persistence.
5. **A justification block format**: pattern + selectors + accepted trade-offs +
   rejected alternative — written down so a reviewer can challenge the
   justification, not the choice.

Default when unsure: **modular monolith** until scale proves otherwise.

# Add harness SDD suite: spec-driven development, dispatch discipline, adversarial review

Three process skills extracted from [harness](https://github.com/jordimarsal/harness) (MIT), a multi-agent Spec Driven Development harness battle-tested on real projects (an Astro portfolio site, a Kafka telemetry pipeline, a Java/Spring Boot status API).

## What's in the suite

| Skill | What it does |
|---|---|
| `spec-driven-development` | EARS-formatted requirements, 3-file specs (`requirements.md`/`design.md`/`tasks.md`), human approval gates, and **objective** requirement-to-test traceability via a mechanical checker (`check_traceability.py`: every `R<n>` must map to a real, existing test — file stem, Python function, or JS/TS test title). Exit 0/1/2, JSON protocol. |
| `agent-dispatch-discipline` | The subagent orchestration protocol: one dispatch = one batch (2–4 tasks, never 5+), minimal dispatch anatomy, on-disk evidence checks after every batch (a chat claim is not evidence), the "Nothing was written" re-dispatch opener, fresh-session restarts at ~70% context. |
| `adversarial-review-gauntlet` | Sequential adversarial review G1 correctness → G2 adversarial → G3 maintainability → G4 evidence, with a mechanical G1 gate script (`gauntlet.sh`, same protocol/exit codes as the checker, which ships vendored so the skill is self-contained). A G1 REJECT stops everything. |

## Why here

They are pure process skills (no API keys, no machine-specific paths, no binaries): exactly the "reusable workflow" category — they teach any agent a strict, verifiable way to run feature work, and they compose (the gauntlet delegates G1 to the traceability checker).

prs.title: fix(slack-gif-creator): account for text bounds when centering
prs.body:
## Problem

`draw_text(..., centered=True)` subtracts half the width and height returned by Pillow, but ignores the bounding box left/top offsets. The captions therefore sit away from their requested center. On Pillow 12.3.0, a `gyp` caption requested at (64, 64) has an ink center at y=68; `Hello\nSlack` has an ink center at y=66.

## Change

Subtract the bounding-box origin as well as half its dimensions. Keep the existing integer rounding and non-centered drawing path unchanged. Document centered single-line and multiline captions, and add two rendering regressions. The tests compare against a centered crop of the native text layout, preserving whitespace inside the font bounds rather than assuming every font has identical ink margins.

## Verification

- Both final regression tests fail on unchanged upstream `dbd4588` with Pillow 12.3.0.
- `python -m unittest discover -s tests -v` from `skills/slack-gif-creator` passes both tests with Pillow 12.3.0 and the minimum supported Pillow 10.0.0.
- Actual three-frame 128x128 GIF generated through `GIFBuilder.save` and reopened with Pillow: three frames, correct dimensions. Rendered PNG inspected. Corrected ink center y=64 for both example captions.
- Exercised on Python 3.12.15, NumPy 2.5.4, imageio 2.38.1. No changes to palette optimization, timing, frame ownership, or font selection.

This is independent of the existing gradient, ndarray-normalization, frame-snapshot, and GIF-timing contributions.

prs.title: Add blast-radius skill
prs.body:
## What

`blast-radius` — a checklist for the moment before a bulk or destructive write:
archiving users, revoking access, deleting rows, mailing a batch.

It covers the gap between a query being right about *rows* and a bulk operation being
right about *the world*. The core move is to classify every affected row into
**act / exclude / unknown** before touching any of them, where *unknown is never act*,
then check the act bucket for people the rule was never meant to catch.

## Why

Every example in the skill is a real near-miss from running an internal platform, not an
invented scenario:

- "Archive everyone with no account on our chat platform" would have archived the
  **research director** and a physician hired three weeks earlier. That signal measured
  *never joined*, not *left* — of 505 active members, exactly one had ever left.
- "Revoke the 98 stale permission grants" would have cut off the **service account** and
  the team leads. Classified, only 18 were genuinely stale.
- One batch email would have gone to someone who already held an offer, **rotating their
  token and invalidating the accept link already in their inbox** — their status field
  said otherwise.
- "78 of 80 file weekly reports, so they're working" — 3,037 of 3,392 reports were
  auto-generated drafts.

None of these were caught by being careful. They were caught by splitting a count into
named rows before trusting it.

## Contents

```
skills/blast-radius/
  SKILL.md                    instructions (113 lines)
  LICENSE.txt                 Apache-2.0
  scripts/blast-radius.sh     optional PreToolUse hook
```

`scripts/blast-radius.sh` is opt-in and does nothing on its own — hooks load from
settings, not from the skill folder, so SKILL.md carries the `settings.json` wiring. It
exists because of the trigger problem: a skill about not trusting a query only helps if
it loads, and the agent that would blindly run the query is the one that will not think
to load it. An unfiltered write returns `permissionDecision: "ask"`; a filtered bulk
write returns the checklist as `additionalContext`; read-only commands and anything
already flagged `--dry-run` stay silent. It fails open — missing `jq`, unrecognised
input or any error exits `0` silently.

The skill is useful without it; drop the script if you would rather `skills/` stay
instructions-only.

## Notes

- Layout matches the per-skill convention in `skills/` — SKILL.md + LICENSE.txt, with
  aux files under `scripts/` as eight other skills do.
- `python3 skills/skill-creator/scripts/quick_validate.py skills/blast-radius` → valid.
- Hook smoke battery: 19/19, covering unbounded writes, filtered bulk writes, read-only
  fast paths, multiple leading `VAR=value` assignments, `#` inside string literals,
  malformed input and output shape.
- Also published standalone at https://github.com/kishormorol/blast-radius

Happy to rename, trim, or restructure to fit house style.

prs.title: fix(skill-creator): make the trigger-eval harness measure skill triggering
prs.body:
`skills/skill-creator/scripts/run_eval.py` and `run_loop.py` cannot currently measure whether a description triggers a skill. Every positive query scores 0% recall, and the same query alternates between 0.0 and 1.0 across runs — so `run_loop.py` optimizes descriptions against noise.

Five defects, all the same class: the experiment measures something other than the description.

## The defects

**The probe competes with the real skill.** `find_project_root()` walks up from cwd to the nearest `.claude/`, which lands in a tree that already registers the skill under test — the common case, since you run the eval from the repo holding the skill. Claude invokes the real name while the probe watches for its uuid-suffixed decoy, so every genuine trigger scores as a miss. That is the 100% precision / 0% recall signature. Each probe now builds and tears down its own root.

**The detector gives up at the first orienting command.** It returns `False` the moment a tool call is not `Skill` or `Read`. Reading the raw stream, Claude's opening move is usually an orienting call (`pwd`, `ls`, a Glob), and it consults the skill a turn later. That ordering is close to a coin flip, and it is the source of the non-determinism. A `Skill` call on the decoy now counts anywhere in the run, bounded by `MAX_PROBE_TURNS = 4` so a run that was never going to trigger stops early. A `Read` of the decoy file counts only as the first tool call: after Claude has explored the sandbox, where the decoy may be the only file, a Read can be exploration rather than a trigger.

**Probes share a directory.** With more than one worker, several decoy commands are live at once. They differ only by uuid, so a worker can watch its own copy while Claude invokes another's.

**No stdin redirect.** `claude -p` is spawned without `stdin`, so every probe waits 3s for piped input that never arrives.

**An installed copy still wins.** A private probe root isolates project scope, but a user-level `~/.claude/skills/<name>` entry or a user-enabled plugin reaches the probe anyway, and the real name outscores the decoy — the same false-miss, reported silently as 0%. This is easy to hit: testing a skill you actually use. Probes now run with `--setting-sources project,local`, which drops user-level skills and user-enabled plugins from the session, so the installed copy never competes. A name that is still registered after that is a built-in skill or command or a managed-policy install; a single pre-check reads the `system/init` event of one probe session before the pool starts and aborts with an error asking to rename the skill, instead of reporting a plausible zero.

## Probes cannot act on queries

Letting a run continue past its first tool call means negative queries ("clean up the build/ directory") get several turns. Under the caller's permission mode and allow rules, that would execute real tools against real paths. Probes therefore get only `--tools Skill Read Glob Grep`, no MCP servers (`--strict-mcp-config`), and, because user settings are excluded, the default permission mode. Trigger detection reads the tool call Claude emits, so nothing it needs is lost. An earlier deny-list approach (`--disallowedTools Bash Write Edit NotebookEdit`) still left Task, Workflow, CronCreate, RemoteTrigger, WebFetch, and every MCP tool available, so the allowlist replaced it.

## User-facing changes

`--project-root` becomes `--fixture`, reflecting what it now means: a *fixture copied into* each probe's sandbox. The old name invited pointing it at the real project — precisely the false-negative case the isolation exists to prevent. Skills whose queries only make sense somewhere specific need one: in a bare directory Claude answers "there's nothing here" rather than reaching for the skill, and every positive looks like a miss. The fixture's `.claude/skills` and `.claude/commands` are not copied (nor a `.claude` that is a symlink or a file), so the decoy is the only project-level registration; the rest of the fixture is copied intact, and the original is never modified, except through symlinks inside it, which are copied as links. The default remains a bare temp dir. A missing `--fixture` directory is rejected by argparse in both CLIs.

`--timeout` rises from 30s to 120s. With the turn cap in place it is a safety net rather than the expected duration of a negative.

As a side effect, the harness stops writing probe files into the caller's `.claude/commands/`. That path is not gitignored, so an interrupted run left untracked files staged for an accidental commit.

## Verification

Against `skills/mcp-builder`, two positives and two negatives, 2 runs per query, 4 workers:

| Query | Expected | Stock | This PR |
|---|---|---|---|

prs.title: Add three delivery-verification skills (iOS package gate, native ASC delivery, content language gate)
prs.body:
Three skills extracted from real shipping work on native iOS apps. Each one exists because a specific failure was **measured**, not imagined — and each one is built to distrust itself.

| Skill | What it refuses to let you believe |
|---|---|
| `ios-package-gate` | that `** ARCHIVE SUCCEEDED **` means your app is signed |
| `ios-appstore-native-delivery` | that "uploaded" means "installable" |
| `content-language-gate` | that "no violations found" means your scanner can see |

### `ios-package-gate`

Measured: `xcodebuild archive` printed `** ARCHIVE SUCCEEDED **` and the resulting bundle was `code object is not signed at all`. A pipeline that trusts build output will try to upload that. So this gate ignores the log and opens the package — 14 checks on the artifact: signature authority, `get-task-allow`, `beta-reports-active`, whether the embedded profile still carries `ProvisionedDevices` (i.e. it is a development profile), architecture, version fields, privacy manifest, icon, declared-vs-actual permissions, and whether `ITSAppUsesNonExemptEncryption` agrees with what the source actually imports.

Run against three different apps; rejected known-bad in three distinct ways (unsigned archive → 7 failures; signature and profile stripped → 2; undeclared permission → named the exact missing key).

One design note worth flagging, because it is the kind of thing that makes a shared gate harmful: the permission check originally came from an app whose flow asks for nothing, so it asserted *"there must be no permission strings at all."* Run against a second app it went red on a **legitimate** microphone and photo-library permission — the gate was writing one product's assumption onto another as a defect. The rule is now "permissions must match what you declared"; an undeclared one is still red, which is the real risk.

### `ios-appstore-native-delivery`

The `xcodebuild` path rather than Expo/EAS, with four traps that each cost real time:

1. Under automatic signing `CODE_SIGN_IDENTITY` **stays** `Apple Development`. Writing `Apple Distribution` yields `conflicting provisioning settings`. The distribution identity is swapped in by `exportArchive`, not by `archive` — and the `archive` output cannot be uploaded. Five attempts to find this.
2. `ARCHIVE SUCCEEDED` does not prove signing (see above).
3. `POST /v1/apps` → **403 `The resource 'apps' does not allow 'CREATE'`**. Creating the app record is a web-UI step. Until it exists, `altool` reports `Cannot determine the Apple ID from Bundle ID`, which reads like a signing failure and is routinely misdiagnosed as one.
4. JWT `exp` must be ≤ 20 minutes, or a 401 surfaces downstream as an unrelated `KeyError: 'data'`.

It keeps `"No errors uploading"`, `processingState: VALID`, and "reachable by the internal group" as **three separate claims** (installing on a device is a fourth). Bounded polling, no blind retry, never re-uploads the same binary. Tester identity is read from `/v1/users` and confirmed by reading the group back — nothing is guessed, no other user is added.

**Honest limit, stated in the SKILL.md itself:** the chain *after* `altool --upload-app` — processing poll, group creation, tester — is written and reviewed but has **never run against a real upload**, because the app record did not exist. I would rather ship that caveat than imply coverage I do not have.

### `content-language-gate`

Scans product text against forbidden-language classes from a rule file and counts originality (repeated strings are the App Review 4.3(b) template signature). Three properties make it trustworthy:

- **It self-tests every run.** Known-bad decoys go through its own patterns first; if it fails to catch them it prints `gate is BLIND` and refuses to treat a clean result as evidence. Measured reason: an earlier version matched a verb stem, mistook ordinary phrases for clinical diagnosis, and produced **8 false violations** — writing its own defect onto the product.
- **An empty scan is not a pass.** Wrong glob → `NOTHING WAS SCANNED`, exit 1. Silence is the most common way a text gate lies.
- **Fields are never merged when counting uniqueness.** Measured: a predecessor counted `text + "|" + short` as one key; because `text` always differed, repeated `short` strings were mathematically invisible — it reported `433/433 unique` while 12 strings repeated 3–4 times. 28 excess copies were hidden by the merge.

Ships a runnable synthetic example, including the two arms that prove the gate can fail.

### Shape

All three are parameterized — no bundle ids, team ids, project paths or credentials in any file. The ASC key id, `.p8` path and keychain service come from the environment with **no built-in default** (a default would also make the script silently look for the wrong key on another machine). All example content is synthetic.

Exit codes carry the real verdict, so each one works directly as a CI gate.

prs.title: fix(pptx): make clean.py slide resolution namespace-aware and fail closed (#1953)
prs.body:
## Summary

Addresses #1953 in `skills/pptx/scripts/clean.py`:

Previously, `clean.py` extracted slide relationship IDs from `ppt/presentation.xml` using a regex:
```python
re.findall(r'<p:sldId[^>]*r:id="([^"]+)"', pres_content)
```
If `presentation.xml` was missing, malformed, used single-quoted XML attributes (`r:id='rId1'`), or used an alternative namespace prefix (`<ppt:sldId>`), the regex returned no IDs. The safety guard then failed to trigger, causing `remove_orphaned_slides()` to delete **every** slide on disk and all associated resources (charts, drawings, media).

## Changes

1. **Robust XML Parsing**: Replaced regex extraction with `defusedxml.minidom` (already utilized throughout `clean.py`) to parse `sldId` elements and resolve `r:id` across namespaces and quotation styles.
2. **Fail-Closed Safety**:
   - Refuses to clean (`RefusedToClean`) if `ppt/presentation.xml` is missing while slides exist on disk.
   - Refuses to clean (`RefusedToClean`) if `ppt/presentation.xml` is malformed and fails to parse.
   - Refuses to clean (`RefusedToClean`) if no on-disk slides match the referenced slides list.
3. **Regression Tests**: Added `skills/pptx/tests/test_clean.py` covering missing/malformed `presentation.xml`, single-quoted attributes, alternative namespace prefixes, and mismatch detection.

Fixes #1953

prs.title: skill-creator: quick_validate rejects empty name/description and checks referenced files
prs.body:
## Problem

`quick_validate.py` currently passes two damage classes that matter for skill integrity:

1. **Empty-string frontmatter values.** All format checks sit behind truthiness guards
   (`if name:` / `if description:`), so `name: ""` parses as an empty string, skips every
   check, and validates as "Skill is valid!". (Unquoted `name:` becomes `None` and is
   accidentally rejected by the type check — so the behavior differs by quoting style.)
2. **No reference-existence check.** SKILL.md may link to bundled files
   (`[guide](references/x.md)`) that don't exist on disk; nothing catches it.

## Repro (upstream main @ 8a1541c; quick_validate.py last touched in 1ed29a03)

```bash
mkdir -p /tmp/qv-demo/blank /tmp/qv-demo/dead-ref
printf -- '---\nname: ""\ndescription: ""\n---\n\n# T\n' > /tmp/qv-demo/blank/SKILL.md
printf -- '---\nname: t\ndescription: demo skill for validation.\n---\n\nSee [g](references/g.md).\n' > /tmp/qv-demo/dead-ref/SKILL.md
python3 quick_validate.py /tmp/qv-demo/blank      # before: "Skill is valid!"  after: rejects empty name
python3 quick_validate.py /tmp/qv-demo/dead-ref   # before: "Skill is valid!"  after: "Referenced file(s) not found: references/g.md"
```

## Change

- Reject empty `name`/`description` after stripping (presence of the key was already
  required; the value now must be non-empty too).
- Add a reference-existence check scoped to **markdown link targets** under
  `scripts/`, `references/`, `assets/`, skipping fenced code blocks and
  placeholder-looking paths. Inline-code mentions in prose are intentionally out of
  scope for a quick check — skill-creator's own SKILL.md uses illustrative example
  paths (e.g. `references/aws.md` in a routing pattern), and checking only link
  targets keeps false positives at zero (verified against skill-creator itself and
  several real-world skills).

## Context

Found during fault-injection experiments on skill integrity (blanking frontmatter,
deleting referenced attachments): the validator reported "Skill is valid!" for every
damaged variant. A community fork of skill-creator already ships a similar
`validate_path_references`; this brings the idea upstream in a false-positive-safe form.

prs.title: fix(skill-creator): do not pass negative evals on worker errors
prs.body:
## Problem

The trigger evaluator treats a failed trial as `False` (skill did not trigger). For a negative eval query, that becomes a PASS. Claude CLI failures and worker exceptions can therefore inflate specificity and let the description optimizer select a broken run. The HTML report and verbose accuracy also count failed negative trials as correct.

## Fix

Raise on a nonzero `claude -p` exit or a streamed `result` with `is_error`. Keep the existing per-query warning/continue behavior for worker exceptions, but record their count and force that query to fail. Exclude failed negative trials from the report's correct-run total and the verbose true-negative count.

## Verification

Five regressions failed before their respective fixes: nonzero CLI exit returned `False`, CLI error result returned `False`, a worker exception made a negative query pass, and both the report and verbose output counted a failed negative trial as correct. All five pass with `/opt/homebrew/bin/python3.11 -m unittest scripts.test_run_eval_errors -v` from `skills/skill-creator`.

I fixed the no-holdout report case you noted. The report normalizes only test_results=None to an empty list; numeric zero and False still fail as malformed input. prs.title: fix(skill-creator): reject duplicate eval queries before evaluation
prs.body:
## Problem

`run_eval` groups finished trials by query text. If an eval set contains the same query twice, the two items silently collapse into one result and `summary.total` undercounts. With conflicting `should_trigger` values, the expected label depends on worker completion order. In `run_loop`, duplicates can also land on opposite sides of the train/holdout split; the result is then attributed to training, corrupting the holdout score.

## Fix

Reject duplicate query text before launching workers. The error points users to `runs_per_query` for repeated trials.

## Verification

- Added a regression that failed before this change (`ValueError` was not raised) and now passes.
- Confirmed unique queries still yield two separate results.
- Ran `/opt/homebrew/bin/python3.11 -m unittest scripts.test_run_eval -v` from `skills/skill-creator` (2 passing tests).

prs.title: fix(pptx): detect dangling third axis in 3D line charts
prs.body:
## Problem
The PPTX chart validator declares that `line3DChart` needs three axes, but its broken-reference check stopped as soon as it found two live references. A 3D line chart with a dangling third reference therefore passed the check. It also counted repeated references to the same axis separately, so `1, 2, 1` appeared to satisfy a three-axis requirement.

## Fix
Use each chart type's `AXID_MINIMUM` and count distinct resolved axis IDs. Diagnostics now report the correct minimum.

## Regression evidence
- Before: the missing-third-axis test found no problem for references `1, 2, 999`; the repeated-axis test found no problem for `1, 2, 1`.
- After: both invalid charts are reported; the three-distinct-live-axis control passes.
- `PYTHONPATH=skills/pptx/scripts python3.11 -m unittest discover -s skills/pptx/scripts/tests -p test_chart_axes.py -v` — 3 passed.
- `python3.11 -m compileall -q skills/pptx/scripts/office/helpers/pptx_chart.py` — passed.

The OOXML `CT_Line3DChart` schema specifies exactly three `axId` elements: https://c-rex.net/samples/ooxml/e1/part4/OOXML_P4_DOCX_line3DChart_topic_ID0E3EJQB.html

## Problem

`add_slide.py` documents that a duplicate must not share the source slide's speaker notes. It removes `notesSlide` relationships using a regex that only recognizes unprefixed `<Relationship>` elements. The OOXML relationship namespace can validly use a prefix such as `<rel:Relationship>`. Allow a namespace prefix on relationship element names when filtering a copied slide's `.rels` file. Other relationships remain intact.

Before this change, the copied slide still had both links and the test failed (`{'image', 'notesSlide'} != {'image'}`). prs.title: fix(web-artifacts-builder): support current TypeScript and calendar API
prs.body:
## Problem

The documented `init-artifact.sh` workflow generates a project that does not pass its own `pnpm build` with the current Vite/TypeScript template. The script adds `baseUrl` to both tsconfig files, and TypeScript 6 exits with TS5101 because that option is deprecated. It also installs the latest `react-day-picker` (currently major 10), while the vendored `calendar.tsx` uses major 9's `ClassNames` API; once TS5101 is removed, the calendar fails with TS2353 (`table` is not a valid key).

## Fix

Keep the `@/*` path mappings without `baseUrl` (supported by current TypeScript), and constrain `react-day-picker` to major 9, which matches the vendored calendar component. This does not touch `react-resizable-panels`; open PR #1894 handles that separate major-version mismatch.

## Verification

Ran the unmodified initializer with Node 24, pnpm 11, current create-vite/TypeScript in a disposable project. `pnpm exec tsc -b` failed first at TS5101. Removing `baseUrl` exposed the calendar TS2353 error; installing `react-day-picker@9` removed calendar errors, leaving only the resizable errors covered by #1894. Ran this branch's initializer fresh and applied #1894's intended `react-resizable-panels@^3` pin locally: `pnpm build` passed, including TypeScript and Vite. The fixture test verifies the generated tsconfigs and installed day-picker major; both checks fail on `main` and pass here. `bash -n` and `git diff --check` pass.

The generated build still requires #1894 (or its equivalent) until that PR merges. This PR does not duplicate its resizable change.


### Review follow-up: alias resolution

I verified the reviewer’s Parcel concern with a real project using `tsconfig.json` paths `@/* -> ./src/*` and **no `baseUrl`**. On Node 24.19.0, pnpm 11.25.0, and Parcel 2.16.4, the repository's `bundle-artifact.sh` installed its resolver stack, built successfully, and inlined the bundle. An import of `@/lib` resolved to `src/lib.ts`; both the emitted JavaScript and `bundle.html` contain the expected `ALIAS_RESOLVED` marker. Thus the current Parcel fallback resolves the alias with the TypeScript 6-compatible config.

prs.title: fix(docx): declare XML namespaces on root before appending comment elements
prs.body:
## Problem

Closes #1821.

In `skills/docx/scripts/comment.py`, `_append_xml` imports and appends comment nodes into existing XML parts (e.g. `word/comments.xml`, `word/commentsExtended.xml`, `word/commentsIds.xml`, `word/commentsExtensible.xml`).

When `word/comments.xml` does not exist, the script copies from its bundled template which already declares `xmlns:w14`. However, when a document already includes an existing `comments.xml` that does not declare `xmlns:w14` (for example, documents generated by Pandoc, which declare only `w`, `m`, `r`, `o`, `v`, `w10`, `a`, `pic`, and `wp`), `_append_xml` imports child elements carrying `w14:paraId` into the existing root and serializes the DOM.

Because the imported element relies on prefix `w14` but the document root has no `xmlns:w14` binding, `dom.toxml()` emits XML with unbound prefix `w14`. The resulting `.docx` is malformed and fails validation:
```
xml.etree.ElementTree.ParseError: unbound prefix: line 2, column 2
word/comments.xml: Line 2: Namespace prefix w14 for paraId on p is not defined, line 2, column 51
```

A similar unbound prefix risk exists for `w15` in `commentsExtended.xml`, `w16cid` in `commentsIds.xml`, and `w16cex` in `commentsExtensible.xml` if those parts already exist without their respective namespace declarations.

## Fix

In `_append_xml`, iterate through all namespace declarations in `NS` and ensure any missing prefix bindings are explicitly set as `xmlns:{prefix}` attributes on `root` before importing and appending child nodes:

```python
    for prefix, uri in NS.items():
        if not root.hasAttribute(f"xmlns:{prefix}"):
            root.setAttribute(f"xmlns:{prefix}", uri)
```

This guarantees that all prefixed attributes used in appended templates (`w`, `w14`, `w15`, `w16cid`, `w16cex`) are properly declared on the enclosing root element, producing strictly well-formed XML regardless of which tool generated the source document.

## Verification

Tested with Python 3.10 and `defusedxml` / `xml.etree.ElementTree`:

| Scenario | Pre-fix | Fixed |
|---|---|---|
| Existing `comments.xml` declaring only `xmlns:w` | `ParseError: unbound prefix: line 1, column 141` | `ET.fromstring` succeeds; 1 comment parsed |
| Appending second comment | N/A (failed on first) | `ET.fromstring` succeeds; 2 comments parsed without duplicate namespace attributes |
| `commentsExtended.xml` append | Missing declaration risk | Validated clean XML with `w15` prefix preserved |
| Syntax verification | Clean | `python -m py_compile skills/docx/scripts/comment.py` clean |

No external dependencies added (uses existing `NS` mapping and DOM methods).

issues.title: Security: Community skills distributed under anthropic/ namespace enable trust boundary abuse
issues.body:
## Summary

Community-made skills are being distributed under the `anthropic/` namespace, impersonating official Anthropic skills. This creates a trust boundary vulnerability where users may grant elevated permissions to community skills they believe are official.

## Discovery

During a comprehensive security audit of 580+ installed Claude Code skills, we found 6 skills placed under `~/.claude/skills/anthropic/`:

| Skill | author field | allowed-tools |
|-------|-------------|---------------|
| anthropic-expert (root) | not set | Read, Grep, Glob |
| claude-code | not set | Read, Grep, Glob |
| claude-command-builder | not set | Read, Write, Edit, Grep, Glob, **Bash** |
| claude-mcp-expert | **raintree** | Read, Write, Edit, Grep, Glob, **Bash** |
| claude-hook-builder | not set | Read, Write, Edit, Grep, Glob, **Bash** |
| claude-settings-expert | not set | Read, Write, Edit, Grep, Glob |
| claude-skill-builder | **raintree** | Read, Write, Edit, Grep, Glob, **Bash** |

**None of these exist in the official `anthropics/skills` repository.** Two skills explicitly list `author: raintree`, confirming they are community-made.

## Security Concern

### Trust Boundary Abuse

1. Users see `anthropic/` in the skill path and assume official Anthropic provenance
2. This lowers their guard when approving operations — especially Bash execution and settings.json modifications
3. `claude-hook-builder` can write PostToolUse hooks to `settings.json`, enabling arbitrary command execution after every tool use
4. `claude-settings-expert` can directly edit `settings.json` and documents `bypassPermissions` (as a warning, but the JSON structure is shown)

### Attack Scenario

```
User installs "anthropic/" skills from a community collection
  → Trusts them as official due to namespace
  → Approves Bash operations without scrutiny
  → claude-hook-builder writes a PostToolUse hook
  → All subsequent tool executions trigger arbitrary commands
```

## Suggested Mitigations

1. **Reserved namespace**: Prevent community skills from using `anthropic/` as a directory name in skill registries
2. **Namespace verification**: Add a verification mechanism (e.g., signed manifests) for official Anthropic skills
3. **Documentation**: Warn users in the skills documentation that directory names do not imply official provenance

## Note

The skills themselves do not appear to contain actively malicious code. The `claude-hook-builder` skill includes appropriate "USE AT YOUR OWN RISK" warnings. The concern is purely about the trust boundary created by the `anthropic/` namespace impersonation.

issues.title: run_eval.py: claude -p never triggers skills/commands (0% trigger rate across all queries)
issues.body:
## Bug Description

`run_eval.py` creates a command file in `.claude/commands/` with the skill description in YAML frontmatter, then runs `claude -p` with test queries to check if Claude invokes the `Skill` or `Read` tool for that command. In practice, **no query ever triggers the skill** — all should-trigger queries get 0/3 trigger rate, including an explicit "run /lucas:memory-layer please".

## Reproduction

Tested with 8 different skills (144 total queries across all eval sets). Every should-trigger query scored 0/3 triggers. Every should-not-trigger query also scored 0/3 (correctly, but vacuously).

Diagnostic test with maximally obvious trigger:
```json
[{"query": "I need to use the lucas memory layer skill right now, run /lucas:memory-layer please", "should_trigger": true}]
```
Result: 0/3 triggers.

## Environment
- Claude Code v2.1.71
- macOS Darwin 25.3.0
- Model: claude-opus-4-6
- Ran from external terminal (no active Claude Code session)

## Analysis

The issue appears to be that `claude -p` does not auto-trigger commands placed in `.claude/commands/` the same way an interactive Claude Code session triggers skills from `~/.claude/skills/`. Possible causes:

1. **Commands vs Skills**: Commands in `.claude/commands/` may not appear in Claude's `available_skills` list the same way skills do, or may only be invocable via explicit `/command-name` syntax
2. **`claude -p` mode**: The `-p` (pipe/prompt) mode may not load commands/skills at all, or may not present them to the model
3. **Simple query threshold**: Claude may not consult skills for queries it can handle directly — but even explicit "run this skill" failed, ruling this out as the sole cause

## Expected Behavior

At minimum, an explicit request like "run /skill-name please" should trigger the command (rate > 0/3). Description-matched queries should trigger at a reasonable rate.

## Suggested Fix

- Verify that `claude -p` actually loads and presents `.claude/commands/` files to the model
- Consider placing test skills in `~/.claude/skills/` instead of `.claude/commands/` if skills and commands are triggered differently
- Add a `--debug` flag to `run_eval.py` that dumps what Claude actually sees (system prompt, available skills list) to verify the command file is being presented

issues.title: Proposing a second skill: compact-memory (symbolic notation for compact agent state)
issues.body:
Following up on my earlier question about whether external skill contributions are welcome (#1328) with a second concrete one, since these are independently useful.

This skill is compact-memory. A long-running agent spends a lot of context on its own notes and persistent memory, written in prose. Prose is redundant and it drifts: the agent paraphrases an earlier note or quietly softens a rule when it reads it back. The skill has the agent write its internal state in a small fixed symbolic notation instead, one fact per line with a consistent operator set. The result is smaller and reads back with one unambiguous meaning, which is what makes the compression safe rather than lossy.

It is self-contained: a single SKILL.md with the notation and the write discipline, no dependencies, and I would license it Apache-2.0 to match the repo. It pairs with the critical-qa skill from #1328 and three others I have packaged together (cheapest-tier routing, pre-ship web verification, claim verification) if a small bundle is more useful than single skills.

Same question stands: is a PR with a skills/<name>/SKILL.md folder following ./template the path you prefer, or an issue first? Happy to do whichever fits your review flow.
